### BOOK THREE [space] 183

...the greater side subtends <term>subtends|The side of a triangle that sits directly opposite a specific angle.</term> the greater given angle. For if the side that subtends the greater angle is not greater, it is either equal or smaller. But if it were indeed equal, the angles which they subtend would also be equal (by the fifth proposition). If, however, it were smaller, the angle which it subtends would also be smaller, according to the preceding proposition. For it has been shown that the greater side subtends the greater angle, and the smaller side the smaller. But the angles would behave in the opposite way. Therefore, the side is greater than the other side. 

It is also possible to show the proposed point without this division, by first demonstrating a certain small <term>assumption|original: "sumptiunculam"; a minor lemma or supporting premise used to prove a larger point.</term>, which is as follows: 

<margin>Assumption</margin>
If an angle of a triangle is bisected <note>original: "bifariam sectus"; cut into two equal parts.</note>, and the straight line bisecting the angle is drawn to the base, dividing the base into unequal parts: the sides containing that angle will be unequal, and the greater side will be the one that meets the greater segment of the base, while the smaller side meets the smaller segment. 

<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
Let there be a triangle **abc**, and let the angle at <margin><unclear>...mus</unclear></margin> point **a** be bisected by the straight line **ad**, and let **ad** itself cut the base **bc** into unequal parts; let the part **cd** be greater than the part **bd**. I say that side **ac** is greater than side **ab**. 

<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
Let **ad** be extended to point **e**, and let **de** be made equal to **ad**. And since **dc** is greater than **db**, let **df** be made equal to **bd**, and let **ef** be connected, and let it be extended as far as point **g**. Therefore, since **ad** is equal to **de**, and **bd** is equal to **df**, these two sides are equal to those two sides, and they contain equal angles, which are at the vertex <note>original: "ad verticem"; these are "vertical angles," which are opposite each other where two lines cross and are always equal.</note>. The base **ba** is therefore equal to the base **ef**, and thus all parts are equal to all parts. For which reason, angle **def** is also equal to angle **dab**. But this is not unequal to **dag**. Therefore, side **ag** is also equal to side **eg**, by the sixth proposition. Thus, side **ac** is greater than side **ef**. But side **fe** is equal to side **ab**. Therefore, side **ac** is greater than side **ab**, which was to be demonstrated.

<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>
Having assumed this, we shall show that the greater side subtends the greater angle. Let there be a triangle **abc** having the angle at point **b** greater than the angle at point **c**. I say that side **ac** is greater than side **ab**. Let **bc** be bisected at point **d**, and let **ad** be connected, and let **de** be drawn equal to **ad**, and let **be** be connected. Therefore, since **bd** is equal to **dc**, and **ad** is equal to **de**, the two sides are equal to the two sides, and they contain equal angles, those which are at the vertex. And the base **be** is therefore equal to the base **ac**, and all to all—

<margin><unclear></unclear></margin>

To construct a triangle from three straight lines which are equal to three given straight lines. It is necessary, however, that any two of the remaining lines, however they are taken, be greater than the third. <margin>Proposition 22. Problem 8.</margin>

We have transitioned back to Problems, <margin>Commentary 27.</margin> and Euclid instructs us to construct a triangle from sides that are equal to three given straight lines, provided that any two of those lines are greater than the remaining one. Indeed, he first recognized that it is impossible for a triangle to be constructed from those very same lines which have already taken their specific positions; however, it can be done from lines that are equal to them. <note>Euclid distinguishes between using the physical lines provided and using new lines of equal length to form the shape.</note> Next, he notes that it is necessary for the straight lines that will complete the triangle to have two sides greater than the third. For every two sides of a triangle are greater than the remaining side, however they are taken, just as was previously demonstrated. <margin>In Proposition 20.</margin> For this reason, he added that it is necessary—even when the first straight lines exist—to construct the triangle from three lines equal to them: it is essential that two be greater than the remaining one, however they are chosen, or there will be no triangle made from those three equal straight lines. Furthermore, he has also refuted all "Instances" <note>term: Instances <gloss>original: "Instantias"</gloss> — counter-arguments or specific cases intended to disprove a general rule</note> which are brought against the construction, and which can be resolved by this single addition <note>The "addition" refers to the condition that two sides must exceed the third.</note>. The present Problem is therefore among the **Determinate**, <margin>On Determinate, Indeterminate, Possible, and Impossible Problems, see the first commentary above.</margin> and not the **Indeterminate**. For among Problems, just as among Theorems, some are Indeterminate, while others are Determinate. For if we had simply spoken in this way—"to construct a triangle from three straight lines equal to three given straight lines"—the Problem is **Indeterminate** and **Impossible**. But if we add, "of which any two are greater than the remaining one, however taken," it is **Determinate** and **Possible**. For this [condition] makes it so. Just as—

<margin>Objections to this Problem.</margin>
Just as there is a division of theorems into **True** and **False**, there is also a division of problems into the **Possible** and the **Impossible**. Moreover, we shall learn how the objections brought against a construction are refuted by looking a little more closely at the matter. For we shall follow the words of the **Geometer** <note>original: "Geometrę," referring here to Euclid, the author of the Elements.</note>. Let there be three straight lines **a**, **b**, and **c**, of which any two, however they are taken, are greater than the remaining one, and let it be required to perform the work. Let a certain straight line **de** be placed, finite on one side—for example, at point **d**—but infinite on the other. And let **df** be placed equal to **a**; then **fg** equal to **b**; and **gh** equal to **c**. With center **f** and the distance **fd**, let circle **k** be described. Again, with center **g** and distance **gh**, let circle **l** be designated. And let the circles intersect each other. Indeed, the author of the *Elements* <note>Euclid</note> 
<margin>† He assumed [this].</margin> 
† assumed this would happen. "From where, then, does this result?" someone might ask; for perhaps they only touch one another, or perhaps they do not even touch. For one of three things must happen to them: they must either intersect one another, or touch, or stand apart from one another. 

<margin>The Response.</margin>
I say, therefore, that they necessarily intersect each other. For let them first be supposed to touch one another. Since the point **f** is the center of circle **k**, the line **df** is equal to **fn**. And since the point **g** is the center of circle **l**, the line **hg** is equal to **gm**. Therefore, the two lines **df** and **gh** together are equal to one, namely **fg**. But they were positioned so as to be greater than it, just as **a** together with **c** is greater than **b**; for they are equal to those lines. Therefore, they are both equal to it and greater than it, which is impossible to happen...

...it cannot happen. Again, if it were possible for the circles to stand apart from each other, such as these circles **k** and **l**. Since the point **f** <note>In this context, the Latin 'Signum' (sign/mark) refers to a geometric point.</note> is the center of circle **k**, the line **d-f** is equal to **f-n**. And since the point **g** is the center of circle **l**, **h-g** is equal to **g-m**. Therefore, the whole line **f-g** is greater than the two lines **d-f** and **h-g** combined. For the line **f-g** exceeds **d-f** and **g-h** by the segment **n-m**. 

However, it had been assumed that the lines **d-f** and **h-g** were greater than **f-g**, just as the given lines **a** and **c** were greater than **b**. For **d-f** was set equal to **a**; **f-g** was set equal to **b**; and **h-g** was set equal to **c**. It is therefore necessary that the circles **k** and **l** intersect one another. 

For this reason, the author of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid, the Greek mathematician who compiled the foundational 'Elements' of geometry.</note> correctly assumed that the circles intersect each other. Indeed, he assumed that of the three straight lines, any two are greater than the remaining one, however they are chosen—not equal to the one, nor smaller than it. It is necessary that if the circles touch each other, the lines are equal; but if they are distant from each other, the two lines are smaller than the remaining one.

->To construct a rectilinear angle equal to a given rectilinear angle, at a given point on a given straight line.<-
<margin>Proposition 23, Problem 9.</margin>

This is also a problem which is a discovery of Oenopides <note>Oenopides of Chios was an ancient Greek mathematician of the 5th century BC.</note> rather than Euclid, as Eudemus <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a student of Aristotle and the first historian of mathematics.</note> says. <margin>Commentary 28. This problem was found by Oenopides according to Eudemus.</margin> It requires the construction of an angle equal to another rectilinear <note>A shape formed by straight lines.</note> angle at a given point on a given straight line. In this, Euclid necessarily added that the given angle must be "rectilinear," since it is not possible for an angle equal to *every* kind of angle to be constructed on a straight line. 

For it was shown <margin>In commentary 2 of this book.</margin> that only two kinds of curvilinear <note>A shape formed by curved lines.</note> angles are equal to rectilinear angles: namely, the angle of the lune-shaped figure <term>lune</term><note>A crescent-like shape formed by two intersecting circular arcs.</note>, which has already been shown to be equal to every rectilinear angle; and the angle of that figure which resembles an axe <term>securis</term><note>Latin for 'axe'; in geometry, a figure bounded by four circular arcs, often called a 'pelekus' in Greek.</note>, which is equal to two-thirds of a right angle.

<summary>This page concludes a proof on circle intersections based on the triangle inequality and introduces Euclid's 23rd Proposition, attributing its origin to the mathematician Oenopides of Chios.</summary>

192 ->B O O K<-

<margin>Note that the angle of a figure resembling an ax is a type of **lunate** <note>original: *lunularis*; a crescent-shaped figure formed by two intersecting circular arcs.</note> angle, and it is called a **Pelecoid** angle <note>original: *Pelecoides*; from the Greek *pelekys* for "ax."</note>.</margin>

<margin>Another more refined demonstration of this problem.</margin>

A lunate figure of this kind, which is called a **Pelecoides**, is formed by two circles intersecting each other through their centers. However, the fact that this construction occurs upon a certain straight line makes the resulting angle a determined one, rather than one of an indefinite kind; it is either a **rectilinear** <note>An angle formed by straight lines.</note> or a **mixed** <note>original: *mixtum*; an angle formed by the intersection of a straight line and a curved line.</note> angle. Since no mixed angle can be equal to a rectilinear one, it is manifest that this angle must also be entirely rectilinear. Therefore, the instructor of the *Elements* <note>A reference to Euclid, the author of the foundational geometry textbook *The Elements*.</note> simply used the preceding problem and, having devised a triangle from three straight lines that are equal to three given lines, achieved the goal. 

You may take up the construction of this triangle through a more refined teaching in this manner. Let the given straight line be **a b**, the given point upon it be **a**, and the given rectilinear angle be **c d e**. It is necessary, therefore, to perform what has been commanded. Let **c e** be joined, and let **a b** be extended on both sides as far as the points **f** and **g**. Let **f a** be made equal to **c d**; let **a b** itself be made equal to **d e**; and let **b g** be made equal to **e c**. 

With center **a** and at the distance of **a f**, let circle **k** be marked out. And again, as in the preceding step, with center **b** and at the distance of **b g**, let circle **l** be described. Therefore, the circles intersect one another, just as was shown above. Let them intersect at points **m** and **n**, and from point **n** let straight lines be connected to the centers, and likewise from point **m**. Since, therefore, **f a** is equal to both **a m** and **a n**, and **c d** is equal to **f a**, it follows that **a m** and **a n** are also equal to **c d**. 

Again, since **b g** is equal to both **b m** and **b n**, and **g b** is not unequal to **c e** <note>A common Latin double-negative phrasing meaning "is equal to."</note>, the lines **b m** and **b n** are also equal to **c e**. Furthermore, **a b** itself is equal to **d e**. Therefore, the two lines **a b** and **a m** are not unequal to the two **d e** and **d c**, and the base **b m** is equal to the base **c e**. Consequently, the angle **m a b** is equal to the angle at point **d**. 

Once more, the two lines **n a** and **a b** are equal to the two **c d** and **d e**, and the base **n b** is equal to the base **c e**. Thus, the angle **n a b** is also equal to the angle **c d e**, and the task has been performed twice over. For we have constructed not just one, but two angles equal to the given angle on either side of the straight line **a b**, as in...

<margin>**Doubt**</margin>
For what reason, then—just as in the fourth theorem <note>Euclid's Book I, Proposition 4: the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem.</note> he demonstrated at the same time that the areas of the triangles are also equal—did he not also add in this one that, besides the inequality of the bases, the areas are also unequal? 

<margin>**Solution.**</margin>
In response to this doubt, let it be said that the logic is not the same for equal angles and bases as it is for unequal ones. For when the angles and bases are equal, the equality of the triangles follows; however, when they are unequal, it is not necessary that an inequality of the areas follows. Instead, the triangles can be both equal and unequal; that which has the larger angle and larger base can be larger, or it can be smaller. For this reason, the author of the *Elements* <note>Euclid.</note> left out the comparison of the triangles' areas. Furthermore, the contemplation of these matters requires a treatment of parallel lines.

**S** <note>This large decorative initial marks the beginning of Baroci's own commentary</note> I MUST also offer my opinion: whoever this unknown author may be, he has clearly erred; the Philosopher <note>Referring to Proclus (c. 412–485 AD), the famous Neoplatonist whose commentary on Euclid was a primary source for Renaissance mathematicians like Baroci</note>, however, did not err. For it must be known that the triangles themselves, which the founder of the *Elements* <note>Euclid</note> proposes, will be either <term>equicrura | isosceles: triangles with two equal sides</term> or <term>scalena | scalene: triangles with no equal sides</term>. Indeed, they cannot be equilateral <note>triangles with three equal sides</note>, since the vertical angles are unequal, while two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other, one to one. If they were equilateral, the angles would also be equal, which is not supposed. 

If, therefore, the triangles were isosceles, just as the founder of the *Elements* also took them, the straight line which was last drawn will necessarily fall upon the <term>subtending line | base: the side of a triangle opposite a specific angle</term>, as the unknown author also shows. But if they are scalene, as Proclus also understood them, it can happen that the straight line which was last drawn falls either upon the subtending line itself, or above it, or even below it. And according to every position, the theorem contains the truth within itself, as anyone can see in Proclus himself. Unjustly, therefore, does the unknown author attack Proclus. For Proclus did not assume the last drawn line to be outside or upon the subtending line [only] in isosceles triangles, but stated it simply. 

When we affirm something indeterminately, we understand it in those cases where it can occur, but not in those where it cannot. It must be said, therefore, on behalf of the unknown author, that he wrote the present Scholium either as if for the unlearned, for the sake of ambition (since he shows such a great man to be deceived), or for the sake of exercise and the mental stimulation of those who excel in talent, or perhaps he even hallucinated <note>original: "hallucinatus est"; meaning he was simply mistaken or deluded in his logic</note>. The present theorem is the opposite of the eighth <note>Proposition 8: the "Side-Side-Side" congruence theorem</note>, and the converse of the preceding one <note>Proposition 24</note>. For following the pairing of the *Elements*, the author <note>Euclid</note> has presented theorems regarding the equality and inequality of angles and bases, accepting in each of the pairings some as "preceding" and others as "converse." In the preceding theorems, he uses direct demonstrations; in the converse ones, he uses the method of reduction to the impossible <note>original: "ad impossibile Deductionibus"; a proof where one assumes the opposite of what they want to prove and shows it leads to a logical contradiction</note>.

He did this also with any single triangle, sometimes showing that the equality of the angles subtended <note>i.e., the angles opposite the sides</note> by the sides follows from the equality of the sides themselves; at other times showing that inequality follows from inequality. Again, conversely, he asserts that the equality of sides follows from the equality of angles, and inequality from inequality. 

But coming to the point: since it is clear how the geometer [Euclid] demonstrates this, we will leave those who are possessed by a desire for learning to read it from his books. However, we will briefly narrate the proofs which others bring forward for the same theorem. And first, we shall present that which Menelaus of Alexandria <note>A 1st-century mathematician and astronomer famous for his work on spherical geometry</note> discovered and handed down.

<margin>Proposition 26
Theorem 17.</margin>

<margin>Commentary 31.
A most beautiful division of the comparison of Triangles.</margin>

Anyone wishing to compare Triangles with one another in terms of their Sides, Angles, and Areas, must necessarily either seek the equality of Angles by taking only the Sides as equal; or investigate the equality of Sides by taking only the Angles as equal; or examine the equality of both Angles and Sides by mixing Angles and Sides together. Thus, when Euclid assumed only the Angles were equal, he could not show the Sides of the Triangles were also equal. For triangles with equal angles <note>known today as "similar" triangles</note> can be very small or very large, since they may be surpassed by others in their Sides and the spaces they enclose, even while having angles individually equal to each other. 

But when he assumed only the Sides were equal, he demonstrated that everything was equal through the eighth Theorem <note>The "Side-Side-Side" (SSS) congruence theorem.</note>, in which there are two Triangles that have two Sides equal to two Sides, each to each, and the Base equal to the Base; these are shown to be equiangular, and to have the power of enclosing equal Spaces. The author of the **Elements** <note>referring to Euclid</note> omitted this addition <note>regarding the area and angles</note> as it follows necessarily from the fourth theorem <note>The "Side-Angle-Side" (SAS) theorem.</note> and requires no further Demonstration. 

In taking both Sides and Angles, he ought to have taken either one Side equal to one and one Angle equal to one; or one Side and two Angles of the triangles equal to two; or conversely, one Angle and two Sides; or one Angle and three Sides; or one Side and three Angles; or even more than one Side and more than one Angle. However, when he took only one Angle and one Side, he by no means proved the Proposition—namely, the equality of the rest. For it is possible for two Triangles to be equal in only one Side and one Angle, yet be entirely unequal in all other respects. For let there be a straight Line $ab$ erected Perpendicularly upon the straight Line $cd$; let $bd$ be greater than $bc$, and let them be connected...

One may take one side and two angles and show the rest to be equal, and this is done through the present <term>Theorem</term> <note>A mathematical statement that has been proven based on previously established statements. Here, it refers to Euclid's Proposition 26.</note>. However, to assume one side and three equal angles is again superfluous. For even when only two [angles] are equal, the equality of the rest has already been shown. Again, by taking one angle and two equal sides, he demonstrated the equality of the rest in the fourth <term>Theorem</term> <note>referring to Proposition 4, the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem</note>. But to take one angle and three equal sides is superfluous; for assuming only two are equal concluded the equality of the rest. Furthermore, to undertake [a proof with] two sides and two equal angles, or two sides and three equal angles, or two angles and three sides, or three angles and three sides—all of these are superfluous. For those suppositions that require fewer elements are entirely accompanied by more, provided that the suppositions are taken with the <margin>† proper</margin> † conditions. Therefore, three suppositions requiring demonstration have arisen for us: one which assumes only three sides; one which assumes one side and two angles, which the Geometer <note>Usually a reference to Euclid himself.</note> now proposes; and its opposite. And for this reason, we have only these three theorems concerning the equality of triangles which involve sides and angles. For all other suppositions are either invalid for showing what is sought, or they are valid but superfluous, because the same results are achieved by their very nature through fewer suppositions. Just as, therefore, when he assumed two sides equal to two sides and one angle equal to one angle, he did not indeed take just *any* angle, but (as was proposed by him) the one contained by the equal straight lines; in the same way, when assuming two angles equal to two and one side equal to one side, he does not assume just any side, but either the one adjacent to the equal angles, or the one subtending <note>To "subtend" means to be opposite to an angle.</note> under one of the equal angles. For neither in the fourth [theorem] can just *any* equal angle be taken, nor in the present theorem can just any side show the rest to be equal. [Diagram 1: A triangle with vertex 'a' at the top. The base is a horizontal line with points 'b', 'd', and 'c' from left to right. Lines connect 'a' to 'b', 'a' to 'd', and 'a' to 'c'. This illustrates the "ambiguous case" where two different triangles can share two equal sides and a non-included angle.]

Two triangles having two sides $a$ $b$ <note>The text is discussing the relationship between sides $ab$, $ac$, and $ad$.</note> equal to two sides $a$ $c$ and $a$ $d$, and having one angle (the one at point $b$) equal to one angle (the one at point $c$), do not necessarily have their remaining sides equal; for example, side $b$ $d$ is not equal to side $d$ $c$, for they are unequal. Nor, for that matter, are the remaining angles equal. The cause of this is that we chose an equal angle that was not the one **contained by the equal sides**. <note>original Latin: "non eum, qui ab æqualibus Lateribus continetur." This refers to the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) requirement in geometry.</note> In the very same way, the present theorem will also seem to falter unless we accept it according to the condition just mentioned: that the equal side must either **subtend** <term>subtend: in geometry, to be the side opposite to an angle</term> one of the equal angles, or be **adjacent** to the equal angles. 

For let there be a right-angled triangle $a$ $b$ $c$, having a right angle at point $b$, and let side $b$ $c$ be greater than side $b$ $a$. 

[Diagram 2: A geometric diagram showing two triangles sharing a common side 'bc'. Triangle 'abc' has a right angle at 'b'. Side 'ab' is vertical, 'bc' is horizontal. The line 'ab' is extended downwards to point 'd'. A line connects 'c' to 'd'. Point 'f' is on the line 'bd'. This diagram visualizes a "false proof" or fallacy.]

Let $a$ $b$ be extended, and let there be constructed upon the straight line $b$ $c$, at the point $c$ upon it, an angle $b$ $c$ $d$ equal to angle $b$ $a$ $c$. Let the lines $b$ $d$ and $c$ $d$ be extended until they coincide at point $d$. There are thus two triangles, $a$ $b$ $c$ and $b$ $c$ $d$, sharing one common side $b$ $c$, and having two angles equal to two angles: specifically, angle $a$ $b$ $c$ is equal to $c$ $b$ $d$ (for they are both **right angles**), <note>original Latin: "Recti. n. sunt"</note> and $b$ $a$ $c$ is equal to $b$ $c$ $d$, for they were constructed to be so. It would therefore seem (as it appears) that the triangles are equal. However, it is shown that triangle $b$ $d$ $c$ is larger than triangle $a$ $b$ $c$. 

The cause of this error is that in triangle $a$ $b$ $c$, we took the common side $b$ $c$ as the one **subtending** <gloss>opposite to</gloss> one of the equal angles (specifically the one at point $a$); but in triangle $b$ $c$ $d$, that same side is **adjacent** to the equal angles. It was necessary, therefore, in both triangles, for the side to either subtend one of the equal angles or be adjacent to the equal angles. By failing to observe this, we might claim that triangle to be equal which is necessarily larger. For how is triangle $b$ $c$ $d$ not larger than triangle $a$ $b$ $c$? For let it be constructed upon the straight line $b$ $c$ at the given point $c$...

### What the Purpose of the Second Part of the First Book of the Elements Is: A Single Chapter.

[Large decorative initial D] **Regarding the origin of TRIANGLES**, <margin>Continuation of the Book.</margin> and their equality or inequality, we have learned whatever could be said in an elementary introduction from what has already been stated. Next, Euclid describes **Quadrilateral Figures**, primarily teaching us about **Parallelograms**, while also bringing in the doctrine of **Trapezoids** along with the contemplation of these. For a quadrilateral is divided (as we said elsewhere previously in the Suppositions) <margin>In the commentary on Definition 18 of Book 2.</margin> <note>original: "In cō 18. Libri 2." Proclus likely refers to his earlier discussion of Euclid's definitions; though the margin says Book 2, it refers to the preceding section of this commentary.</note> into the Parallelogram and the Trapezoid: and the Parallelogram into certain other species, and the Trapezoid likewise. 

But since the Parallelogram is ordered because of its participation in equality, while the Trapezoid does not have the same or a similar order, it is not without reason that his discourse is primarily about Parallelograms, though he contemplates the Trapezoid together with them. For from the cutting <note>or "sectioning"</note> of Parallelograms, the origin of Trapezoids will appear, as will be manifest to us as we proceed. <margin>Below in Proposition 35.</margin> 

Since, moreover, it is impossible for anything to be said about the construction or equality of Parallelograms without the consideration of **Parallel lines** (for as is clear from the name, a *Parallelogram* is that which is circumscribed by parallel straight lines lying opposite one another), he necessarily takes the beginning of his teaching here from Parallels. Having progressed a little from these, he enters the teaching of Parallelograms, using one middle theorem between the elementary instruction of the former and the latter. Indeed, this seems to investigate a certain <term>Symptoma; a property or characteristic following from a definition</term> that exists in Parallels; but first, it hand down the origin of the Parallelogram. For such is what he says: *Straight lines which join equal and parallel straight lines in the same directions are themselves also equal and parallel.* <margin>Proposition 33.</margin> For in this theorem...

<margin>Three properties which belong to parallels by themselves</margin>
Moreover, three things must be assumed which belong to parallels by themselves, and which express them essentially, and are interchangeable with them—not only all three together, but each one even when taken separately from the others. The first of these is that, when a straight line cuts parallel lines, the **alternate angles** are equal; the second is that, when a straight line cuts parallel lines, the **internal angles** are equal to two right angles; and the remaining one is that, when a straight line cuts parallel lines, the **exterior angle** is equal to the interior and opposite angle. For any one of these <term>symptoms<note>original: "Symptomatū". In classical geometry, a 'symptom' refers to a defining property or essential characteristic of a figure that follows from its construction.</note></term>, once demonstrated, is sufficient to affirm that the straight lines are parallel. In this way, other mathematicians have also been accustomed to discourse on lines, providing the "symptom" of each species.
<margin>Apollonius, Nicomedes, Hippias, Perseus</margin>
For **Apollonius** showed what the symptom is in any of the conic lines; and **Nicomedes** in the <term>conchoids<note>A family of shell-shaped curves used in ancient Greek geometry to solve problems like trisecting an angle.</note></term>; and **Hippias** in the <term>quadrants<note>original: "Quadrantibus". This refers to the 'quadratrix,' a curve used by Hippias of Elis for squaring the circle and trisecting angles.</note></term>; and **Perseus** in the <term>spiric sections<note>Curves formed by the intersection of a plane with a torus (a donut shape).</note></term>. For after their origin is established, that which is assumed to belong to them by themselves and according to their very nature distinguishes the form established for us from all others. In the same way, therefore, the author of the *Elements* also first investigates the symptoms of parallels.

### FOURTH BOOK. 217

...two assumptions of the angle are supposed equal to each other, while according to one, they are equal to two right angles <note>In geometry, "two right angles" is the equivalent of a 180-degree straight line</note>; in these cases, however, it is the opposite: according to two [assumptions] they are equal to two right angles, while according to one, they are equal to each other. <margin>Why Euclid omitted three cases of angles.</margin>

It seems, moreover, that the Geometer <note>The "Geometer" refers to Euclid</note> chose these suppositions because they are either more abundant in affirmation or are simpler; and therefore, from those angles which are not on the same side, he took only the internal ones, which he called **Alternate**; but from those which are on the same side, he took both the internal ones and one internal with one external; the remaining cases he avoided, as if they were declared more by negation, or as being more varied. Nevertheless, whether this is the cause or another must be said, it is manifest from these things how many consequences follow from the suppositions themselves.

->**THE TEXT**<-

**If a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the external angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles: the straight lines themselves will be parallel to one another.**

<margin>Proposition 28 Theorem 19.</margin>

<margin>Commentary 2.</margin>

The preceding theorem <note>Proposition 27</note> showed that straight lines were parallel to each other by taking angles that were not on the same side—specifically those lying within the straight lines; this theorem, however, proposes the remaining two suppositions, one of which separates the angles according to the categories of [**exterior**] and [**interior**], while the other supposes both to be interior, and shows the same conclusion. 

<margin>Doubt</margin>

<margin>Aeneas of Hierapolis wrote a compendium of the Elements.</margin>

It might perhaps seem that the author of the *Elements* divided the theorems inappropriately. For it was necessary either to take the three suppositions separately and make three theorems, or to collect them all into one theorem, as did **Aeneas of Hierapolis**, who wrote a compendium of the *Elements*; or, if he wished to divide them into two, to make an orderly division, taking separately those suppositions in which the angles are equal, and separately that one in which they are equal to two right angles. In the present case, however, in one theorem he supposed the **Alternate** angles to be equal, while in the other he supposed the external to be equal to the internal, and the interior angles on the same side to be equal to two right angles. 

<margin>Solution.</margin>

What, then, was the cause of this division? Did he not look to the equality of the angles to each other, or to the equality of two right angles, and by this reasoning...

->**TEXT**<-

A straight Line falling upon parallel straight Lines makes the alternate Angles equal to one another: and the external [angle] equal to the internal and opposite [angle] on the same side: and the internal [angles] on the same side equal to two Right angles.

<margin>Proposition 29. Theorem 20.</margin>

The present Theorem is the converse of both the preceding ones. For that which was the goal in both of those <note>Propositions 27 and 28</note> becomes the assumption here; and what was given in those, it now proposes to show. <margin>Commentary 3.</margin> And this difference of Converses should not be passed over in silence: that everything which is converted is either one-to-one (as the fifth to the sixth), or one to many (as what is proposed here follows from the preceding ones), or many to one (as will be clear to us shortly). <margin>A certain difference of Converses. In commentary 32 of the Proposition.</margin> In the present Theorem, the founder of the Elements <note>Euclid</note> first made use of this Petition <margin>Fifth Postulate.</margin> <note>original: "Petitione"; in classical geometry, a "Petition" is a Postulate—a statement assumed to be true without proof</note> which says: if a straight Line falling on two straight Lines makes the internal angles on the same side less than two right angles, those straight Lines, when produced to infinity, will meet on those sides where the Angles are less than two Right angles. When explaining those things that come before the Theorems, <margin>In book 3, chapter 1, and in commentary 3.</margin> we said that it was not granted by everyone that this is self-evidently clear without demonstration. For how can something be like that [self-evident] when its converse is written in the Theorems as something demonstrable? For that Theorem which says that "in every Triangle, any two interior Angles are less than two Right angles" <note>Euclid I.17</note> is the converse of this Postulate. Furthermore, since the fact that straight Lines incline toward each other more and more as they are produced is not a certain Sign of meeting <note>original: "coincidentiæ"</note>, because other lines have also been found which incline more and more but never meet <note>A reference to asymptotic lines, which get closer forever without touching</note>, as was also said before. <margin>At the end of the second book and in commentary 3 of the third book. For if **ak** and **cl** meet, the angles **kfh** and **lgh** no longer remain the same, and a certain part of the straight line **fg** is left outside the straight lines **ak** and **cl**. And thus two lines, namely **fk** and **gl**, are again greater than the base by as much as they intercept in the inner part of the straight line **fg**.

<margin>Proposition 31.
Problem 10.

Commentary 5.</margin>

<margin>Instruction.</margin>

<margin>Communalities between this and the twelfth problem.</margin>

<margin>In commentary 22 of the third book.</margin>

<margin>Differences between this and the twelfth Proposition.</margin>

It was necessary not only to have learned the properties of **Parallels** in themselves from the discourses of the author of the *Elements* <note>Euclid</note>, but also to describe their origin through **Geometric** methods, and to have understood in what manner one straight **Line** might be made **Parallel** to another. For in many places, the origins of things render the essence of the subjects clearer to us. This, therefore, the author of the *Elements* achieves through the present **Problem**. For since he had taken a **Point** <term>Signum: literally "a sign" or "mark," used here to mean a geometric point</term> and a straight **Line**, he draws a **Line** parallel to the straight **Line** through that **Point**. 

However, it is necessary for us to assume beforehand that the **Point** must lie entirely outside the straight **Line**. For we will not place the point upon the straight line itself simply because it was said to be "through a given point." Indeed, if it were on the line, there would be no other line besides the given straight **Line** that could be drawn **Parallel** through it. Therefore, since he has distinguished between the **Point** and the straight **Line**, he indicated that the **Point** is to be taken outside the straight **Line**. He also made this manifest regarding the **Perpendicular** line by adding the phrase: "upon a given infinite straight line from a given point which is not on it, to drop a perpendicular." 

Thus, one thing is common to both of these **Problems**: first, that from the same **Point**, two **Perpendiculars** are not dropped to the same straight **Line**; and second, that through the same **Point**, two **Parallels** are not drawn to the same straight **Line**. For this reason, the author of the *Elements* spoke in the singular in this way, saying to draw "a straight line"—in the former case a **Perpendicular**, and in this case a **Parallel**. But while that former case was demonstrated previously, this one is manifest from what has already been proven. For if two **Parallels** were drawn to the same straight **Line** through the same **Point**, they would also be **Parallel** to each other while coinciding at the given **Point**, which is entirely impossible. 

It is also necessary to observe the differences between these two **Propositions**: "from a given point" <note>original: à dato Signo</note> and "through a given point" <note>original: per datum Signum</note>. For sometimes the **Point** is the beginning of the **Line** which is being drawn, and therefore the drawing happens *from* it; but sometimes the point is located *on* the straight **Line** being drawn, and therefore the drawing happens *through* it. The word "through" was not used because the straight **Line** cuts the given **Point**, but because it coincides with it, and marks its interval with respect to that straight **Line** by the distance between the **Point** and the straight **Line**. For as much as the given **Point**... <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

<margin>Proposition 32
Theorem 22.</margin>

Whatever was lacking in the sixteenth and seventeenth theorems, this one adds. <margin>Commentary 6.</margin> For we learn from this theorem not only that the exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either interior and opposite angle <note>This refers to Euclid’s Proposition 1.16, which states that an exterior angle is simply *greater* than either opposite interior angle, without specifying by how much.</note>, but indeed by how much it is greater. Since it is equal to both, it is greater than either one by the amount of the other. Nor do we merely know from these things that any two angles of a triangle are less than two right angles <note>In classical geometry, "two right angles" is the standard way to describe a straight line or 180 degrees.</note>, but also by how much they are less: namely, by the remaining of the three angles. Therefore, those earlier theorems were in a certain way more indefinite; but this one brings a scientific boundary to both. 

We should not, however, say that those earlier theorems were superfluous. <margin>He responds to a silent objection.</margin> For they have brought us the greatest utility in many demonstrations, from which we shall also show this one. It is necessary for our knowledge, as it proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect, to pass from indeterminate apprehensions to determinate and certain statements.

Since we now hold that the three angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles, we must take up a certain path by which <margin>A digression in which there are four most beautiful considerations.</margin> we may find how many right angles the angles of all other rectilinear multi-angled figures <term>multi-angled figures: polygons</term> are equal to—for instance, those of a quadrilateral, a pentagon, and consequently all many-sided figures.

By whatever number of joined triangles the first constructed figure differs from its sides, all other figures differ by that same number. Thus, every many-sided figure has two more sides than the number of triangles into which it is dissolved. 

And yet, it has been shown that every triangle has angles equal to two right angles. Therefore, doubling the number of those constituent triangles will provide the multitude of right angles to which each many-sided figure's angles are equal. For this reason, every four-sided figure has angles equal to four right angles, since it is composed of two triangles; every five-sided figure has six, and so on in the same manner. This is the first thing to be taken from the present theorem concerning all multi-angled and rectilinear figures together.

Next, let us state briefly another point following from this: <margin>Second [consideration].</margin> every rectilinear figure, when each of its sides is produced <term>produced: extended or lengthened</term> once, has exterior angles equal to four right angles. For the total sum of the successive angles must be double the number of sides, since at each side they are constituted as equal to two right angles. However, when the right angles that are equal to the internal angles are subtracted, the remaining angles on the outside become equal to four right angles. For example, if the figure is a triangle, while each of its sides is produced once, angles equal to six right angles are created.

However, we must not pass over in silence a very clever point <margin>A most beautiful digression on universal consideration. Some theorems are universal, others are not.</margin> that appears in this theorem: namely, that some theorems are **universal**, while others are **not universal**. We shall explain how we define each of these when we divide the subject of inquiry, which has one part that is universal and another that is not. For although every theorem might perhaps seem to be universal, and everything shown by the founder of the *Elements* <note>Euclid of Alexandria, the author of the foundational textbook of geometry.</note> seems to be of this kind—just as in the present case it seems to be stated universally of all parallelograms not only that they have opposite sides and angles equal, but also that a diagonal bisects each one—nevertheless, we say some are shown universally and others not.

For a thing is customarily called "universal" in two ways: <margin>The double meaning of universal. See the same in Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics*, Book 1, text 11.</margin> in one way, it describes what is true of **all** things of which it is predicated; in another way, it includes **everything** that possesses the same <term>property</term> <note>original: *symptoma*; in this context, it refers to an essential characteristic or attribute of a geometric figure.</note>. For example, it is "universal" that every **isosceles triangle** has three angles equal to two right angles, because this is true of all isosceles triangles. But it is also "universal" that **every triangle** has three angles equal to two right angles, because this includes everything in which this property inherently exists. Therefore, we say that this property—having three angles equal to two right angles—is first shown of the **triangle** as a whole <margin>The proper meaning of "Universal."</margin>.

According to this meaning, then, we call some theorems universal and others not. We say the present theorem has one universal goal and another that is not. For this property—having opposite sides and angles equal—is **universal**, since it belongs to parallelograms alone. But this property—the diagonal bisecting the area—is **not universal**, because it does not include everything in which this property is observed. Indeed, this is also true for **circles** and **ellipses**. It seems that the first notions of such things are more specific; but as they progress, they come to include the whole. For it is not possible to say what is common to Numbers, Magnitudes, Motions, and Sounds—in all of which "alternating ratio" <note>original: *alterna Ratio*. A rule in proportions where if A is to B as C is to D, then A is to C as B is to D.</note> exists. Furthermore, it is difficult to express what is common to the Ellipse, the Circle, and the Parallelogram; for one is a rectilinear figure, the second is circular, and the third is mixed. Therefore, when we think we are showing it universally—he who demonstrates that every diameter <note>The author uses "diameter" where we would typically use "diagonal" for a parallelogram.</note> of a Parallelogram bisects it—we do not see the common reason why this is true. This property, then, is not universal even in Parallelograms of this sort, for the reason already mentioned. That [universal property] is: **Every Parallelogram has opposite sides and angles that are equal.** For if any figure is assumed to have opposite sides and angles that are equal, it will be shown to be a Parallelogram.

<margin>Converse of the first and second properties of this Theorem.</margin>
For let there be such a figure **a b c d**, and a diagonal **a d**. Since sides **a b** and **b d** are equal to sides **a c** and **c d**, and the angles contained by them are equal, and the base is common, everything will also be equal to everything. Therefore, Angle **b a d** is equal to Angle **a d c**, and Angle **a d b** is equal to Angle **c a d**.

<margin>End of the Digression. Instruction. Whence the name "Parallelogram" arose.</margin>
Therefore, the side **a b** is parallel to **c d**, and **a c** is parallel to **b d**. On account of which, the figure **a b c d** is a Parallelogram. Let these words suffice concerning these matters. It seems that the founder of the *Elements* <note>original: *Elementorum institutor*, referring to Euclid.</note> also composed the name "Parallelogram" itself, taking the occasion from the preceding theorem. For since he had shown that straight lines which join equal and parallel straight lines on the same side are themselves also equal and parallel, it is clear that he pronounced the opposite sides—both those that join and those that are joined—to be parallel.

<margin>What a Parallelogram is properly, and what a Parallelogram is according to Euclid.</margin>
He rightly called a figure contained by parallels a **Parallelogram**, just as he called that which is bounded by straight lines **rectilinear**. And it is manifest that the founder of the *Elements* placed the Parallelogram among the quadrilaterals <note>Four-sided figures.</note>. In the process of generation, it is said that one proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect. Therefore, the transition from the senses to contemplation, and from contemplation to the mind, occurs not without merit. Just as among the Phoenicians, on account of trade and commerce, a certain knowledge of numbers took its beginning, so indeed among the Egyptians, Geometry was discovered for the reason already mentioned <note>The author likely refers to the need for land surveying after the Nile floods.</note>. When Thales first traveled to Egypt, he transferred this knowledge into Greece. He discovered many things himself, and explained the principles of many others to those who succeeded him—touching upon some matters more universally, and others more through the senses. After him, Ameristus, the brother of the poet Stesichorus, is remembered as one who touched upon and had a taste for the study of Geometry; Hippias of Elis also made mention of him as one who won glory in Geometry.

After these, Pythagoras transformed that philosophy which concerns Geometry into the form of a liberal education <note>term: liberal education (Latin: *liberalis doctrina*). This refers to the "liberal arts" suitable for a free person, focusing on theoretical understanding rather than just practical application.</note>, considering its principles from a higher perspective and investigating its theorems immaterially and intellectually. He indeed discovered the treatment of those things which cannot be explained in Geometry <note>original: *quae explicari in Geometria non possunt*. This likely refers to irrational numbers or incommensurable magnitudes.</note>, and the constitution of the cosmic figures. Following him, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae attempted many things pertaining to Geometry. Then Oenopides of Chios, who was somewhat younger than Anaxagoras, both of whom Plato mentions in the *Rivals* as those who achieved glory in Mathematics.

Succeeding them, Hippocrates of Chios—who discovered the squaring of the lune <note>term: squaring of the lune. A "lune" is a crescent shape; Hippocrates proved that certain crescents could have the exact same area as a square, a major step in the history of geometry.</note>—and Theodorus of Cyrene became distinguished in Geometry. For Hippocrates was the first of those recorded to have written *Elements*. When Plato succeeded them, he caused both Geometry itself and the other Mathematical Sciences to receive the greatest increase because of the immense zeal he applied to them. This is manifest in his own writings, which are filled with mathematical discourses, and by his awakening everywhere an admiration for these subjects in those who touch upon Philosophy. At this time also lived Leodamas of Thasos, Archytas of Tarentum, and Theaetetus of Athens, by whom the theorems were increased and reached a more skillful arrangement. Neoclides was younger than Leodamas, and his pupil was Leon, who added many things to what their predecessors had devised. Thus Leon also constructed *Elements* more accurately, both in terms of the number and the utility of the things demonstrated in them; he also discovered the "determination" <note>term: determination (Greek: *diorismos*). The criteria for whether a geometric problem has a solution or is impossible.</note>, namely, when a sought problem is possible and when it is impossible. Eudoxus of Cnidus, a little younger than Leon and a companion of Plato, first [increased] the multitude of those theorems...

...Perhaps it will seem entirely worthy of wonder to those who are unlearned in this kind of contemplation <note>unlearned: those unfamiliar with the formal proofs of geometry</note> if Parallelograms established upon the same Base, and within the same Parallels, are equal to one another. <margin>The doubt of the unlearned.</margin> For how can this be possible, since the length of the spaces established upon the same Base grows toward infinity? For as much as we extend the Parallel lines, by so much can we also increase the Lengths of the Parallelograms. By what means, then, while this occurs, does the equality of the Spaces remain? Perhaps someone might not unfairly ask this. For if the Width is indeed the same (since the Base is one and the same) but the Length is greater, in what way will the Space not also be greater? <margin>The present Theorem is among the number of "admirable" theorems in the mathematical sciences.</margin> This Theorem, therefore, and that which follows from it concerning Triangles, is from the number of those called "admirable theorems" in the mathematical disciplines. For mathematicians have also established a "Place" <note>original: *Locus*. In classical logic and rhetoric, a "topic" or "category" of argument; here used to describe a class of mathematical paradoxes.</note> in theorems, just as the Stoics <note>An influential school of ancient Greek philosophy.</note> did in arguments, which is called "admirable," <margin>What the "Admirable Place" is among mathematicians and among Stoics.</margin> and they suggest this Theorem is among those of that kind. Thus, the common crowd is immediately stunned when the multiplied Length does not destroy the equality of the Spaces, provided the Base remains the same.

It must be said, however, that the equality and inequality of the Angles has the greatest power for increasing or diminishing Spaces. <margin>Response to the doubt of the unlearned.</margin> For as much as we make the Angles unequal, by so much more do we diminish the Space, if the Length and Width were to remain the same. Therefore, an increase of the Length is necessary so that we may preserve the equality. <margin>Demonstrates that an increase in Length is necessary to preserve the equality of the spaces.</margin> For the sake of example, let there be a Parallelogram **abcd**, and let the side **ac** be extended to infinity, and let this perhaps be a rectangle, and let another be established on the Base **bd**, and let it be **befd**. It is therefore clear that the Length has been increased. For the side **be** is greater than the side **ab**, since the Angle located at point **a** is a right angle. But this happened by necessity, since the Angles of the Parallelogram **befd** itself were made unequal—some indeed Acute, others indeed Obtuse. This happens because the side **be** approaches the side **bd** in a certain way and contracts the Space. For the sake of example, let **bg** be taken equal to **ab**, and let a Parallel to **bd** be drawn through point **g**, which shall be **gh**. Therefore, the Length of the Parallelogram **bdgh** is equal to the Length of the Parallelogram **abcd**, and the Width is the same, yet the Space...

The limit of the increase in length is the location of the parallel lines themselves. For when both parallelograms are rectangular and have equal perimeters, the square is shown to be larger than the rectangle <note>literally "the part longer on one side"</note>. But when both have equal sides and equal perimeters, the one that is rectangular is shown to be larger than the one that is not rectangular. Hence, a square appears larger than all those shapes that have the same perimeter; but a rhomboid is smaller than all of them.

From this, it is also clear that it was not without reason that he taught what a trapezium is in the postulates: namely, that it is a quadrilateral in genus, but not a parallelogram. Because it does not have equal opposite sides and angles, it falls out of the category of parallelograms.

Therefore, the parallelogram **ab** is equal to the parallelogram **de**. Again, if someone supposes the side **ac** of the parallelogram **ab** itself to be cut by the side **dc**, and the parallelograms to lie just as **adbe** and **bdcf**, we shall show that these are also equal.

**Parallelograms which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.**

The preceding theorem <note>Proposition 35</note> assumed the same bases, but this one assumes bases that are indeed equal, but different from one another. It is common to both, however, to suppose the parallelograms are in the same parallels. It is necessary, therefore, that they fall neither inside the underlying parallel straight lines, nor outside. For parallelograms are said to be in the same parallels when their bases and the sides lying opposite to them are joined to the same parallels. Furthermore, although the author of the Elements <note>Euclid</note> took the bases as being entirely separate, he still proved the theorem. However, nothing prevents us from assuming them to be placed so that they have a certain common part. For let there be parallelograms *ab* and *cd* on equal bases *eb* and *fd* having a common part, and in the same parallels; I say that they are equal. Let the straight lines *ec* and *bg* be connected.

<margin>Scholium <note>original: "Scholiũ"; a marginal note or explanatory comment, usually by an editor or student.</note></margin>
**HERE** you must observe, dear reader, that the present tenth commentary of Proclus was found by us to be incomplete in all the manuscripts that have come into our hands up to this time. Therefore, I have decided that it should be printed in its current order just as it presents itself, so that those few things found within it would not be hidden from you. However, so that you may clearly recognize its imperfections, I must run through several points, in which I will briefly encompass everything that would be contained in it if it were whole. 

Our author Proclus, having first handed down the commonalities and differences between the present and preceding theorems, and having taught in passing how parallelograms are said to be within the same parallel lines, prepared himself in his usual manner to explain the **Cases of Construction.** <note>In geometry, "cases" refer to the different ways a figure can be drawn while still satisfying the conditions of a theorem.</note> Now, the cases (as you can see in his work) are three in total, and they present themselves to us according to the first mental concept; out of these, one is indeed that which Euclid undertook in his own Construction. The remaining two are those which Proclus proposed to declare himself. When he had indeed declared these and shown that the Theorem universally obtains the truth in these three cases, he immediately added what was to be explained next: namely, the **Division** of these three cases 
<margin>Division of the Cases.</margin>
together with the **Demonstration** of the Theorem in all parts of those cases. 

Indeed, the Division is as follows: Since there are three cases of construction for Parallelograms existing on equal bases and within the same parallels, their bases are either entirely separate from each other (as the founder of the *Elements* <note>original: "Elementorum inſtitutor"; referring to Euclid.</note> supposed), or they are joined at only one point <note>original: "Signo"; literally a sign or mark, used here to mean a geometric point.</note> (as Proclus shows in his second description), or they had a certain common part (as the same author shows in the first). Each of these three cases still has seven parts.

For if two isosceles <term>isosceles: a triangle with at least two sides of equal length</term> triangles are proposed, one of which has two equal sides of five units and a base of eight; the other has two equal sides of five units and a base of six—measured, for example, in cubits or fingers—those who are unskilled in these matters are greatly deceived in their choice. But a man of Geometry will not be ignorant of the fact that the **Areas** are equal, even though the perimeters were unequal. For each area is twelve. If you draw a **Perpendicular** line from the vertex <note>The highest point of the triangle</note>, you will divide the bases in half. ->**THE TEXT**<-
<margin>Proposition 38, Theorem 28.</margin>
**Triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.**

The present theorem is indeed a <term>local theorem<note>original: "Theorema locale". In classical geometry, a "local" theorem refers to properties depending on the position or "locus" of the figures, such as their placement between parallel lines.</note></term>, as it corresponds proportionally to the <margin>Commentary 12.</margin> parallelograms and assumes the position of triangles upon equal bases. It seems to me that Euclid treats these four theorems—two of which were demonstrated regarding parallelograms, and two regarding triangles (some with the same base, others with equal bases)—by providing a single demonstration in the <note>Euclid’s "Elements" consists of thirteen books; Book VI introduces the more advanced theory of proportions.</note> sixth book through the first theorem. It also seems that he does this hidden from the common student. For when he shows that triangles and parallelograms which are under the same <term>altitude<note>The "altitude" or height is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel lines holding the shapes.</note></term> have the same ratio to each other as their bases have, he demonstrates nothing other than all these things more universally through <term>Proportion</term> itself. 

For the same altitude is nothing other than being in the same parallels; all figures that are in the same parallels are under the same altitude, and vice versa. Indeed, the <margin>What the Altitude of figures is.</margin> altitude is the perpendicular line which extends from one parallel to the remaining one. Therefore, in that later book [Book VI], it is shown through Proportion that triangles and parallelograms situated under the same altitude (that is, situated in the same parallels) relate to each other as their bases do. Thus, if the bases are equal, the spaces are equal; if the bases are double, the spaces are double; and if the bases have another ratio, the spaces will have that same ratio to each other. 

In the present case, however, since it was not fitting for him to use Proportion before he had taught it, he is content with equality and identity alone; for from the equality of the bases, the identity of the triangles is gathered. Therefore, these four theorems are encompassed in that one [in Book VI]. This is not only because a single demonstration shows whatever is contained in these four, but also because <margin>† Altogether what is perfected in the case of bases.</margin> it adds something more: namely, the identity of ratios, even if the bases are unequal.

Since our purpose was to demonstrate equality, we previously established four theorems: two regarding parallelograms and two regarding triangles, situated either upon the same bases or upon equal bases. But now, in turning back <note>original: "conuertentes," referring to the proof of the converse theorems</note>, we have omitted those converses concerning parallelograms, while we have judged those concerning triangles to be worthy of memory. 

The reason for this is that the method of demonstration is identical in those cases as well, proceeding through a "reduction to the impossible" <term>reductio ad impossibile: a proof method that shows a statement must be true by proving that its opposite leads to a logical contradiction</term> and a similar construction. We are satisfied to have shown the way in the simpler cases—I mean the triangles—leaving it to those who are more curious to reason out the same things in the remaining figures. It is easy to recognize at the same time that the path in those cases is the same. For when we take equal parallelograms on the same base, or even on equal bases, we shall say that they are also within the same parallels. For if they are not, one of them will fall either inside or outside the parallels drawn for the other. However it falls, once we have accepted that figure and the parallels within it, we shall demonstrate what is also shown in the case of triangles: namely, that the whole would be equal to its own part. This, however, is impossible.

It is worthy of note, however, that since there is a threefold Conversion of Theorems (for either the whole is converted to the whole, as we said of the eighteenth and nineteenth; or the whole to the part, as in the sixth and fifth; or part to part, as in the eighth and fourth. For in the preceding [theorems], the "Sought" was that the Triangles be equal; here, however, that is not only the "Given," since it has additionally taken a part of the assumption that was in the previous ones. For that phrase [ **on the same side** ] was additionally assumed from the outside.

**Equal triangles, which are on equal bases and on the same side, are within the same parallels.**

The method of conversion <note>original: "modus Conversionis"; a logical process where the conclusion of a previous theorem is taken as the starting assumption for a new one</note> is the same in this case, and the demonstration is similar. However, since there are three variables in these stated propositions—being on equal or the same bases, being within the same parallels, and the triangles or parallelograms being equal in area—it is clear that by always joining two of these and leaving one out, we can "convert" the statement in various ways.

Finally, when we take the areas to be equal and situated within the same parallels, we may show the remainder: that they are either on the same or on equal bases. This would produce another four theorems, which the founder of the *Elements* omitted entirely. <margin>Digression. Here he draws out another converse of this theorem, according to another method of conversion.</margin>

The parallelogram is double the triangle **a c d**; however, triangle **a d c** is equal to triangle **e d c**, and furthermore, the parallelogram is double that triangle **e c d**. Therefore, it is clear that when the base is the same, the parallelogram is shown to be double the triangle. If, however, the bases are equal, it will be shown in the same way, by our drawing the <term>diagonal</term> <note>original: "Dimetientem"; literally the "measurer through," used here for the line splitting the parallelogram.</note> of the parallelogram. For since the triangles are equal, the parallelogram which is double one will also be double the other. Indeed, the triangles are equal because of the equality of their bases and the identity of their height. Rightly, therefore, the Geometer <note>A traditional title for Euclid, the author of the *Elements*.</note> omitted these also, for the demonstration is the same. For they will either share the same part, or they will be joined at only one point, or they will be separate from one another. But however these may vary, there is one demonstration for all cases. Moreover, we will demonstrate the converse of this theorem in the same way. One of these is: if a parallelogram is double a triangle, and they have either the same base or equal bases, <insert>and if they are on the same side</insert>, they will be within the same parallels. For if they are not, the whole would be equal to its part, and the same reasoning will hold. For the vertex of the triangle must fall either inside or outside the parallels. Whichever way it stands, the same impossibility follows once a parallel to the base is drawn through the vertex of the triangle. The other [converse] is: If a parallelogram is double a triangle, and both are within the same parallels, they will be upon one base or upon equal bases. For if they were on unequal bases, when we take equal ones, we would show the whole to be equal to its part. Therefore, all these theorems end in this common impossibility <note>This refers to a "reductio ad absurdum," a proof where the starting assumption leads to a logical contradiction, such as a part being equal to the whole.</note>. Thus, the author of the *Elements* left us to investigate the variety found in these, while he restricted his consideration to the simpler and more fundamental cases. For if it had a double ratio, it would be a parallelogram, since it is a quadrilateral. I say, however, that it is either more than double or less. ->FOURTH BOOK<-                                                                    257

...commentaries of the third part holds the first place, yet he did not connect the third part to the second, nor did he discuss the purpose of the third part in the same way he did at the beginning of the fourth book. Furthermore, whereas at the end of the third book he concluded the first part with an epilogue before proceeding to the exposition of the twenty-seventh Proposition <note>Euclid's *Elements*, Book 1, Prop. 27</note>—which enjoys the beginning of the second part—he interposed an entire chapter in which he showed the second part joined to the first, and declared what was to be treated therein by the founder of the *Elements* <note>original: "Elementorum institutore"; referring to Euclid</note>. Clearly, this ought to have been done in this location as well, especially since the purpose of the third part appears most prominently in this Theorem. But there is no one who does not see that at the end of the fourteenth Commentary, he made no epilogue for the second part, but without any intervening medium, he moved on to the interpretation of the thirty-fifth Proposition. Moreover, at the beginning of the fifteenth, he neither linked these two parts together, nor made any mention of those things treated by Euclid in the third part. I believe this was not done without reason. For since our author Proclus <note>Proclus Lycaeus (412–485 AD), the Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Euclid is a primary source for the history of geometry</note> wished to divide his commentaries on the first book of the *Elements* into exactly four books, he could not do these things between the fourteenth and fifteenth Commentaries, lest he pervert the order of the Commentaries and, in a way, create the beginning of a fifth Book. Therefore, it remains that at the end of the fifteenth, he briefly touched upon both the continuation of those parts and the purpose of the last part, neither deviating from the series of Commentaries nor undermining the four-part distribution of the books. By this first reason, then, it is clear to us that the present Commentary we are discussing contained a more prolix <note>lengthy or wordy</note> discourse than what is found within it.

Secondly, however, because he undertook a digression into a most beautiful and difficult matter, it certainly requires more words to explain all parts of that subject matter. <margin>Second reason.</margin> For while Euclid has up to this point compared Parallelogram to Parallelogram, and Triangle to Triangle, and Parallelogram to Triangle upon the same or upon equal Bases and within the same Parallels, our author Proclus likewise—who throughout his Commentaries has looked to the benefit of students—has proposed here, for the sake of our exercise, <margin>What Proclus teaches in his digression.</margin> to compare a <term>Trapezium</term> <note>In this context, a quadrilateral with only two parallel sides</note> to a Triangle and a Parallelogram, and likewise to another Trapezium upon the same or equal Bases and within the same Parallels. I say "Trapezium" in the sense of that which is properly called a Trapezium by Posidonius and by Proclus, namely that which has only two parallel sides. For <term>Trapezoidea</term> <note>Irregular quadrilaterals with no parallel sides</note>, which Euclid also called by the common name "Trapezia," have no property resulting from parallels, nor can they be within the same Parallels, since they do not have parallel sides. Nor is the reason valid...

->**FOURTH**<- <note>original: "Q V A R T V S." This likely refers to the fourth section or chapter of the commentary.</note> 263

The figure, and the remaining five sides $b, f, k, l, h$, are equal. These, moreover, were the **complements**. <note>In geometry, "complements" are the two areas of a parallelogram that remain after drawing two smaller parallelograms along its diagonal.</note> But if the parallelograms were neither joined at a single point nor distant from one another, but instead intersected each other, the proof will be the same in this manner. For let there be a **parallelogram** $a b$, and a **diagonal** $c d$ <note>original: "dimetiens," literally "the measurer through," used here for the diagonal line of the figure</note>, and let there be parallelograms about it: one indeed being $e c f l$, and the other, by which this one is cut, $d g k h$. I say that the complements $f g$ and $e h$ are equal. For since the whole triangle $d g k$ is equal to the whole triangle $d h k$, and the triangle $k l m$ (which is a part of it) is equal to triangle $k l n$—since $l k$ itself is also a parallelogram—the remaining **trapezoid** $d l n h$ <note>In this period, "trapezium" or trapezoid often referred to any four-sided shape that was not a parallelogram.</note> is therefore equal to the remaining trapezoid $d l m g$. Furthermore, triangle $a d c$ is equal to triangle $b c d$, and triangle $f c l$ is equal to triangle $e c l$ in the parallelogram $e f$, and trapezoid $d g m l$ is equal to trapezoid $d h n l$. Therefore, the remaining quadrilateral $g f$ is not unequal to the remaining quadrilateral $e h$. The theorem has thus been shown according to all **cases**. There are, however, only three cases, neither more nor fewer. For the parallelograms which consist about the same diagonal will either intersect each other, or touch each other at a single point, or be distant from each other by some part of the diagonal.

<margin>Why there are only three cases for this theorem.</margin>
<margin>A lesson: From where this name "Complements" arose.</margin>
<margin>Why Euclid did not define complements in the Definitions.</margin>
<margin>Which parallelograms are said to be "about the same diagonal."</margin>

But the founder of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid, the author of the *Elements of Geometry*.</note> adopted the name "Complements" from the nature of the thing itself, insofar as these areas also "complete" the whole besides the two parallelograms [along the diagonal]. For this reason, it was not thought worthy of mention by itself in the **Definitions**. Indeed, it needed variety for its own declaration, so that we might recognize what a parallelogram was, and which those parallelograms were that are about the diagonal of the whole parallelogram. For once these things were declared, the **Complement** would also become known in this way. Moreover, those parallelograms are "about the same diagonal" which have any part of the total diagonal as their own diagonal; but those which do not, are not. For when the diagonal of the whole parallelogram cuts any of the sides of the internal parallelogram, then that parallelogram is not "about the same diagonal" as the whole. For example, as in parallelogram $a b$, the diagonal $c d$ cuts the side $e h$ of the parallelogram $c e$. Therefore, parallelogram $e c$ is not about the same diagonal as parallelogram $c d$.

<margin>What these names—**application** <note>original: "παραβολὴ" (parabole)</note>, **excess** <note>original: "ὑπερβολὴ" (hyperbole)</note>, and **defect** <note>original: "ἔλλειψις" (ellipsis)</note>—signified among the ancients, and what they signify among more recent writers. <margin>There are three "givens" in this problem.</margin>

<margin>Instruction.</margin>

These things are indeed ancient, as the associates of **Eudemus** <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a historian of mathematics and pupil of Aristotle.</note> say, and were discoveries of the **Pythagorean Muse** <note>A reference to the followers of Pythagoras, to whom many early geometric discoveries were attributed.</note>: specifically, the **Application of Areas**, along with their **Excess** and **Defect**.
