<meta>This page continues the discussion on the historical conflict between the Protestant Reformation and the Roman Catholic Church, specifically focusing on the Council of Trent.</meta>

266

## III. Protestantism and the Council

This context explains the attitude of the Protestants toward the Council. 

If the Council were to act as a judge over them, they first had to be recognized as members of the Church; however, the Pope had already struck them with excommunication. If it was meant to be a free, Christian assembly in German lands, there was no mention of this in the papal indiction <note>The formal proclamation or summons of the Council.</note>. In that document, the very dogma against which they protested was already established as the sole law of the Church; the opening of the bull stated it was: "for the uprooting of heresies" <note>original: "ad extirpationem haeresum"</note>.

Therefore, an assembly was called not to investigate, but to judge and condemn. 

Added to this was the method of voting. At the earlier Councils of Constance and Basel, voting had been conducted by nations to break the overwhelming influence of the Italians. In Trent, however, voting was done by head <note>per capita</note>, and since the majority of the prelates were Italian, the influence of the Curia <note>The administrative apparatus of the Holy See and the papal court.</note> was secured. 

Hence the saying: "The Holy Spirit is sent from Rome to Trent in mailbags" <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus in manticis Roma Tridentum mittitur." This was a famous satirical remark suggesting that the bishops at the Council did not act under divine inspiration, but rather under constant, direct instructions sent by the Pope from Rome.</note>. 

The Protestants therefore demanded a <term>free, Christian council in German territories</term> <note>original: "Concilium liberum, christianum, in partibus Germaniae"</note>:

1. ***Free***, meaning independent of the Pope; for since he had already condemned their teaching, he could not simultaneously be the judge in his own cause.
2. ***Christian***, meaning a place where not only prelates, but also delegates of princes and cities—even laypeople—would have a seat and a vote, and where Holy Scripture alone should serve as the standard for decisions.
3. ***In German territories***, because the conflict had arisen here and the investigation could be conducted most easily here.

<summary>This page explains the Protestant rejection of the Council of Trent, citing the Pope's prior condemnation of their views and the unfair voting structure that favored Italian interests. The text outlines the three Protestant requirements for a legitimate council: independence from the Pope, inclusion of laypeople/Scripture-based decisions, and a German location.</summary>
<keywords>Council of Trent, Protestantism, Papal Curia, Council of Constance, Council of Basel, voting by nation, sola scriptura, excommunication</keywords>

# BOOK TWO. 83

<margin>Third cause, which is an accumulated Multitude.</margin>
...[parts], while dividing others into dissimilar parts. Thirdly, it is strengthened by an <term>accumulated multitude</term> <note>original: "accumulata multitudine"; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the way a single principle multiplies into many diverse forms</note>, and for this reason, it extends Forms of every kind and produces multiform Principles of Figures. And propagating itself, it certainly does not cease until it reaches a certain ultimate point and opens up every variety of Forms. And just as in that higher realm the One is shown to be in that which is, and that which is in the One, so indeed it shows even in rectilinear Figures the Circular ones, and conversely the rectilinear ones encompassed in the Circular. And it manifests its whole nature specifically in each one, and all these in all things; since the Whole is also simultaneously in all and in each one separately. 

<margin>Fourth cause, which is the Number Three.</margin>
Thus, it holds this power from that order. Fourthly, it receives the measures of the progression of forms from the first of the Numbers <note>The number three was considered the first "actual" number in this tradition, as one and two were seen as the parents of number.</note>. From this, it also establishes all things according to Numbers, some according to simpler ones, others according to more composite ones. Indeed, Triangles, Quadrangles, and Pentagons, and all Polygons progress together with the infinite changes of Numbers. 

<margin>Number is in Arithmetic, while Figure is in Geometry.</margin>
But the reason why this happens is unknown to the common people; however, for those who know where Number resides and where Figure resides, the logic of the cause to be rendered is manifest. 

<margin>Fifth cause, which is the second Totality.</margin>
Fifthly, from another "second Totality," which is also divided into similar parts, it is filled with that division of Forms which divides them into other similar Forms. By this, the Triangular <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Ratio"; often used to translate the Greek "Logos," meaning a formative or rational principle</note> is divided into Triangles, and the Quadrangular into Quadrangles. And that which I have said, we also achieve when exercising ourselves in <term>Images</term> <note>Geometric drawings were seen as "images" or shadows of higher mathematical truths.</note>, even though it existed long before in the primary principles. 

Nevertheless, by looking to these assignments, we can provide many causes for Figures, reducing them to their first principles. And indeed, the one more common Figure has obtained an order of this kind, and receives perfection from so many causes. 

<margin>How Figure is attributed to the Gods.</margin>
From here, it proceeds to the classes of the Gods, and according to different forms it is attributed to some, and acts in a different way upon others. To some, it provides simpler Figures, but to others, more composite ones derived from these. And to some, it assigns primary figures, those produced on Surfaces; but to others (those entering the <term>fullness</term> <note>original: "tumorem"; literally "swelling," referring to the three-dimensional volume of solid shapes</note> of solid Bodies), it assigns the Figures suitable to them that are in Solids. Since all things exist in all things, the Forms of the Gods are indeed accumulated and full of all powers: but with a specific property producing one thing after another. For one god holds all things Circularly, another Triangularly, and another Quadrangularly; and in the same way among the Solids.

->**THE TEXT**<-
A **Circle** is a **Plane Figure** contained by one **Line**, which is called the **Circumference**, to which all the straight **Lines** falling from one **Point** of those which lie within the **Figure**, are equal to one another. And the **Center** of the circle is what that **Point** is called.
[End of decorative border]

<margin>Definition 15.</margin>
<margin>Definition 16.</margin>

<margin>Commentary 13.</margin> **The Circle** is the first, simplest, and most perfect of all **Figures**. <margin>The circle is the most excellent of all figures.</margin> For it surpasses all **Solids** because it exists in a simpler state; and it excels those figures that exist on **Planes** by its uniformity and identity. It corresponds in proportion to the "End," to "Unity," and finally to the better level of coordination. For this reason, if you were to divide the figures of the world and those that are above the **World**, you would always find the **Circle** to be of a more divine nature. For if you divide the whole into the **Heavens** and the realm of **Generation**, <note>original: "Generationem"; in ancient philosophy, this refers to the sublunary world of change, birth, and decay.</note> you will assign the **Circular** form to the heavens, and the **Straight** form to **Generation**. For whatever is **Circular** within things that can be generated—namely in their changes and **Figures**—comes down from the heavens above. For through the heaven's rotation, **Generation** revolves back upon itself, and it reduces unstable change to an ordered continuation. 

But if you should distribute those things which lack bodies into the **Soul** and the **Mind**, <note>original: "Mentem"; likely referring to the Greek *Nous* or pure intellect.</note> you would say that the **Circle** belongs to the **Mind**, and the **Straight** to the **Soul**. On this account, the **Soul** is also said to move **Circularly** according to its conversion toward the **Mind**, and the **Soul** has the same relationship to the **Mind** as **Generation** has to the **Heavens**. <margin>Socrates in the *Timaeus*.</margin> For it moves **Circularly** (says Socrates) because it imitates the **Mind**. But the generation and progress of the **Soul** happens according to a **Straight Line**. For it is characteristic of the **Soul** to apply itself to different **Forms** at different times. 

However, if you wish to divide these into **Body** and **Soul**, you would establish that everything corporeal participates in a portion of the **Straight**, while everything **Animal** <note>In the sense of *anima*, or "having a soul/life force."</note> participates in the identity and likeness of the **Circle**. For the former is composite and varied in its powers, much like **rectilinear Figures**; but the latter is simple and intelligent, moving by itself and acting by itself, turned toward itself, and acting upon itself. <margin>Timaeus.</margin> Hence, furthermore, when **Timaeus** had also established the **Elements** of the universe with **rectilinear Figures**, he provided them with **Circular** motion and shaping from that **Soul** which dwells within the **World**. <margin>Epilogue.</margin> Nevertheless, it is manifest from what has already been said that the **Circle** everywhere holds the first place in respect to other **Figures**. 

<margin>Digression.</margin> It is worthwhile, however, to look also at its entire sequence, beginning from above and descending to the lower things, and perfecting all things according to the capacity of those things which receive its fellowship. <margin>The circle provides perfection to all things. To the Gods.</margin> To the **Gods**, therefore, it provides a turning back toward their causes and a union; and it provides this: that they may remain in themselves and not depart from their own blessedness... union...

->BOOK TWO, 85<-

...strengthening these unities as Centers for the lower things that desire them, while firmly situating the multitude of powers within those things around those same Centers, and containing them through their simplicity. <margin>To the essences of Minds.</margin> To the essences of **Minds** <note>original: "Mentium essentijs"; in this Neoplatonic context, "Mind" or "Intellect" refers to a level of reality higher than the human soul, representing pure, eternal thought.</note> this suggests that they act perpetually within themselves, are filled by knowledge from within themselves, and hold their intellectual concepts in a contracted form. Within themselves, they perfect their own acts of understanding. For every Mind proposes an "intelligible" object to itself, and this object acts as a Center for that Mind. The Mind itself enfolds and acts around that Center, and is united within itself by all its various mental operations.

<margin>To Souls,</margin> To **Souls**, however, it illuminates the power of living by their own means, of moving by themselves, of turning toward the Mind, and of leaping around the Mind. It allows them to return to their own specific cycles, unfolding the "indivisibility" of the Mind into a sequence of thought. For again, the intellectual arrangements will provide Centers for the Souls, and the Souls will act in a circle around them. Indeed, every Soul—according to its own intellectual part—has received the "Supreme One" as its Center <margin>"One" here stands for Mind.</margin> <note>The author clarifies that for a Soul, the "One" it focuses on is the higher Intellect.</note>. Yet, according to its own multiplicity, the Soul revolves in a circle, desiring to embrace its own Mind.

<margin>To Celestial bodies</margin> To the **Celestial bodies**, it grants a likeness to the Mind: a similarity, an equality, and a comprehension of all things in their furthest reaches. It gives them their revolutions, which occur in determined measurements, their everlasting existence, and finally, the fact that they lack a beginning and an end—and everything of that kind.

<margin>To the Four Elements.</margin> To the **Elements** that exist beneath the hollow of the Moon's orbit, it grants the cycle that occurs through change: a likeness to the heavens, that which is "uncreated" within things that are born, that which remains stable within things that move, and that which exists as "Limited" within things that can be divided. For all things always exist because of the Circle of Generation, and a balance is maintained in all things because of the reciprocal nature of decay. For if generation did not return in a cycle, the order of these things and their entire adornment would vanish in a short span of time.

<margin>To Animals and Plants.</margin> Again, to **Animals** and **Plants**, it brings that similarity found in reproduction; for these arise from seeds, and from these, seeds are produced in turn. Generation is perfected by these alternating steps—a revolution from the imperfect to the perfect, and back again—so that decay exists alongside birth. 

<margin>To those things which occur contrary to nature.</margin> Even to those things which occur **contrary to nature**, it imposes an order. It reduces their indeterminate variety to a Limit, and even these things it adorns becomingly with the final traces of its powers. Therefore, even these things revolve according to determined Numbers; not only fertility, but even sterility exists according to the alternating revolutions of these Circles (as the speech of the Muses shows). <margin>The Muses in Book 8 of the Republic. Socrates in the Republic.</margin> <note>This refers to a famous passage in Plato’s *Republic* (Book 8) where Socrates discusses the "Nuptial Number" and the cyclical decline of states and people.</note> And although all evils are cast down from the Gods into the realm of mortals, even these things revolve (as Socrates says), and even for these things there is a Circular revolution and a Circular order.

->SECOND BOOK. 87<-

...therefore <note>original: "tra)" — this appears to be the end of a word like *intra* (inside) or *extra* (outside) from the previous page</note> he added this: that the lines falling from one Point to the Boundary of the Circle are equal. For there are infinite points within it, but of all these, only one has the power of the Center. And because this one Point—from which all lines meeting the Circumference of the Circle are equal—is either inside the Circle or outside (for any Circle has a Pole <note>In this context, a "Pole" refers to a point outside the plane of the circle, such as the apex of a cone, that is equidistant from the circumference.</note> from which all lines drawn to its Circumference are equal), <margin>Sixth.</margin> he therefore added that these are "of the points which are within the Figure." Nor did he do this without reason, choosing only the Center and not the Pole. For he wishes to observe all things in a single Plane, whereas the Pole is higher than the underlying Plane. Necessarily, therefore, he also added at the end that this Point—which indeed lies within the Circle and from which all lines falling to the Circumference are equal—is the Center of the Circle. <margin>Definition of the Center.</margin> For there are only two such Points: the Pole and the Center. But the former is outside the Plane, while the latter is within it. For example: if you imagine a <term>gnomon</term> <note>An upright rod or tool used to measure shadows or define right angles.</note> standing in the Center of a Circle, <margin>What the Pole of a Circle is, and its definition.</margin> its upper extremity is the Pole. For all lines drawn from it to the Circumference of the Circle are demonstrated to be equal to one another. Similarly, in a Cone, the vertex of the whole Cone is the Pole of the Circle existing at the Base. <margin>Epilogue.</margin> Thus far, it has been determined what a Circle is, what a Center is, what the Circumference placed in the Circle is, and what the whole Circular Figure is.

Now, therefore, let us return from these things to the contemplation of the Exemplars <term>Exemplars</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, these are the divine, perfect patterns or "Forms" upon which physical reality is modeled.</note>, <margin>Digression: Contemplation of the Center, the distances from the Center, and the Circumference in the Exemplars.</margin> and in those let us understand the Center everywhere according to a unique, indivisible, and firm excellence. Let us understand the distances from the Center according to the progressions which occur from the One toward an infinite multitude of power. And let us understand the Circumference of the Circle according to the return of those progressions back to the Center, through which the multitudes of powers are rolled back into their own union; all hasten toward it and desire to act around it. <margin>How these communicate with those.</margin> And just as in a Circle all things exist together—the Center, the Intervals, and the external Circumference—so truly in those higher realms, some do not pre-exist in time while others follow, but rather all are one: the staying, the progression, and the return. <margin>How they differ.</margin> But these differ from those in that the higher things subsist indivisibly and without any dimension; however, these geometric things exist with dimension and divisibly—the Center in one place, the Lines from the Center in another, and the external Circumference terminating the Circle in yet another. But there, all are in the One. If you take that which performs the role of the Center, <margin>Beautiful.</margin> you will find all things in it. If you take the progression distant from it, you will have all things in this also. If you take the return, it is the same. When, therefore, you look upon all things in relation to one another, and the lack <note>original: "defectum"</note> arising from dimension... <margin>How he who truly is may be found.</margin>

SECOND [BOOK]. 89

<margin>The circle is the first of figures, and the triangle the first of the straight-lined figures. Epilogue.</margin>

...the cause of the first of the straight-lined figures within itself. For this reason, the Sages—and especially the most secret of the Theologians <note>original: "Theologicorumque maximè arcani." This likely refers to Pythagorean or Neoplatonic thinkers who assigned mystical or divine meanings to geometric shapes.</note>—gave it its name. The **diameter** of a circle is a straight line drawn through the **center**, which is terminated on both sides by the **circumference** of the circle, and divides the circle into two equal parts.

<margin>Definition 17.</margin>

<margin>Commentary 14.</margin>

<margin>In what way the **Diameter**, the **Diagonal**, and the **Axis** differ.</margin>

Euclid himself clearly shows that he is not defining every kind of diameter, but only the circular one. This is because squares also have a "diameter" <note>original: "Dimetiens." In ancient geometry, this term was often used for what we now call a diagonal.</note>, as do all parallelograms, and even spheres among solid figures. However, in these cases, it is also called a **diagonal**; in the sphere, it is also called an **axis**. In circles, it is called only the **diameter**. Indeed, people are accustomed to call it the axis for the ellipse, the cylinder, and the cone; but for the circle, they properly call it the **diameter**.

<margin>The term "diameter" is only used properly in a circle.</margin>

Therefore, in its nature, this is a straight line. Although many straight lines exist in a circle—just as there are infinite points—just as only one of these points is called the **center**, so too is this line alone called the **diameter**: the one which passes through the center, neither ending inside the circumference nor extending beyond its boundary, but being bounded on both sides by it. These points show how it is formed. Furthermore, the addition at the end—that it also divides the circle into two equal parts—indicates its specific action upon the circle, unlike all other straight lines drawn through the center which are not bounded on both sides by the circumference.

<margin>Thales.</margin>

They say that **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624 – 548 BC), often considered the first Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> was the first to demonstrate that a circle is divided into two equal parts by its diameter. The cause of this equal division is the passage of the straight line through the center without wavering. For since it is drawn through the middle, and always maintains the same motion across all its parts toward either side without bending, it cuts off an equal amount on both sides of the circle's circumference. If you also wish to show this through a mathematical method,

<margin>Demonstration.</margin>

imagine the diameter being drawn and one part of the circle being folded onto the other. For if they are not equal, one will fall either inside or outside...

They are biform <note>original: "biformes," meaning having two forms or composed of two different types of lines</note>, just as the **Monadic Circle** <note>The "Monadic Circle" refers to the ideal, singular Circle that exists as a primary principle in Neoplatonic geometry</note> was, and they consist of dissimilar parts. For any figure that is bounded by two limits, or is contained by two circumferences—such as the **Lunule** <note>original: "Lunularis," a crescent shape formed by two intersecting arcs</note>—or by a straight line and a circumference, as with the figures already mentioned; or by two "mixed" <term>lines</term> <note>A "mixed line" in this period usually refers to a curve that is neither a perfect circle nor a straight line, such as an ellipse</note>, such as if two ellipses were to intersect each other (for they would enclose a figure intercepted between them); or by a mixed line and a circumference, as when a circle cuts an ellipse; or by a mixed line and a straight line, such as half of an ellipse. The **Semicircle**, however, is composed of dissimilar lines, yet they are simple lines, and they touch each other by being placed together. Therefore, before the discourse defines the **Triadic** <note>three-sided or triangular</note> figures, it rightly comes to the **Biform** figure after the Circle. For two straight lines can never enclose a space. But a straight line and a circumference can enclose two spaces <note>This likely refers to the two segments created when a chord cuts a circle</note>. And two circumferences can similarly enclose space, either by forming angles, as in the **Lunular Figure**; or by completing a figure without angles, such as if you imagine **concentric circles**. For the middle space intercepted between the two is bounded by two circumferences: one inner and the other outer, and no angle is formed. For they do not intersect each other, as happens in the **Lunule** and in the figure that is **convex on both sides** <note>a lens shape</note>. Furthermore, it is manifest that the center of the semicircle is the same as the center of the circle. For the **Diameter** <note>original: "Dimetiens"</note>, having the center within itself, completes the semicircle, and all lines drawn from this center to the semi-circumference are equal; for this is a part of the circle’s circumference. Moreover, equal straight lines fall from the center to all parts of a circle’s circumference. Therefore, the center of the semicircle and the circle is one and the same. And it should be noted that of all figures, this is the only one that has the **Center** on its own perimeter—of all plane figures, I mean. From this you may gather that the Center has three possible locations: either within the figure, as in the Circle; or on the perimeter, as in the Semicircle; or outside, as in certain **Conic Lines** <note>such as the exterior focus of a hyperbola</note>. Thus, the semicircle has the same center as the circle. What then does this indicate, or of what things does it offer an image, except that all figures which have not entirely departed from the primary principles, but participate in them in some way, are able to be concentric with them and participate in those same causes? For the semicircle communicates with the circle in two ways: both according to the diameter and according to the circumference. Accordingly, the center is also common to them. And perhaps the semicircle is even likened to the second principles following the simplest...

After the **Monadic** <term>Monadic (from *monas*): representing unity or the number one</term> figure, which has the nature of a principle for all figures, and the biform <note>original: *biformemque*; referring to its dual nature of having both a straight and a curved line</note> **Semicircle**, the progression of rectilinear figures is handed down according to the progression of numbers unto infinity. For that reason, mention was also made of the semicircle, as it shares boundaries partly with the Circle and partly with Rectilinear figures.

Just as the **Binary** <note>The number two</note> is the mean between **Unity** <note>The number one</note> and **Number**. For if Unity is added to itself, it produces more than if it is multiplied <note>1 + 1 = 2, whereas 1 × 1 = 1</note>; Number, on the other hand, produces more if it is multiplied than if it is added <note>For example, 3 × 3 = 9, while 3 + 3 = 6</note>. The Binary, however, whether it is multiplied by itself or added to itself, produces an equal result <note>2 + 2 = 4 and 2 × 2 = 4</note>. Therefore, just as the Binary is the mean between unity and multitude, so also the Semicircle shares with Rectilinear figures in its base, and with the Circle in its circumference.

Rectilinear figures proceed in order by number, beginning from the **Ternary** <note>The number three</note> unto infinity. Therefore, Euclid also began from here. To be sure, trilaterals are also multilaterals; but they also have a proper name besides the common denomination. Since, however, we could by no means follow the others because of the infinite progression of numbers, we were content with the common denomination. He made mention only of trilaterals and quadrilaterals because the **Ternary** and **Quaternary** <note>The number four</note> are the first in the order of numbers; the former indeed being purely odd among the Odd numbers...

Among those enclosed by simple lines, some are bounded by lines of the same species, such as *rectilinear* figures; others by lines of different species, such as *semicircles*, *segments*, and *apsides* <note>original: "apsides"; here referring to arches or segments of a circle smaller than a semicircle</note>, which are smaller than semicircles. By one line: the *circle* itself. 
By two lines: some are "deangular" <note>literally "without angles"</note> such as the *corona* <note>original: "corona"; a ring-shaped area or annulus</note>, which is bounded by concentric circles; others are angular, such as the *lunula* <note>original: "lunula"; a crescent or "little moon" shape formed by two intersecting arcs</note>. 
By more than two lines: this process continues to infinity. For certain figures are bounded by three, four, or more successive circumferences. For instance, if three circles touch one another, they enclose a certain three-sided space bounded by three circumferences; if four circles, a space bounded by four circumferences, and so on. 

<margin>A figure is called "mixed" in two ways. Mixture occurs in two ways. See above in commentary 7.</margin>

Among those bounded by straight lines, some are enclosed by three, others by four, and others by many lines. For a space is not enclosed by two straight lines, and much less by one. Therefore, every space enclosed by one or two boundaries is either mixed or circular. 

A figure is "mixed" in two ways: either because mixed lines enclose it—such as the space intercepted by a *cissoid* <note>original: "cissoide"; an ivy-shaped curve</note> line—or because lines of different species bound it, such as the *apsides*. Indeed, "mixture" occurs in two ways: either by **apposition** <note>original: "appositionem"; placing different types of lines side-by-side to form a boundary</note> or by **confusion** <note>original: "confusionem"; a blending where the individual nature of the lines is merged into a new type of curve</note>.

<note>This section presents Euclid’s classic definitions of triangles, translated here from the Latin version of the text.</note>
Among three-sided figures, an **equilateral** triangle is that which has three equal sides.

An **isosceles** <note>literally "equal-legged," from the Latin *equicrus*</note> triangle is that which has only two equal sides.

But a **scalene** triangle is that which has three unequal sides.

Furthermore, among three-sided figures, a **right-angled** triangle is that which has one right angle.

An **obtuse-angled** triangle is that which has one obtuse <note>greater than 90 degrees</note> angle.

But an **acute-angled** triangle is that which has three acute <note>less than 90 degrees</note> angles.

<margin>Definitions 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29.</margin>
<margin>Commentary 17. The double division of triangles.</margin>
The division of triangles sometimes begins with their angles, and at other times with their sides. The division by sides comes first as something better known; that by angles follows as something more specific. <margin>Division of triangles by sides.</margin> Indeed, these three types of angles—right, obtuse, and acute—apply only to figures made of straight lines. Equality and inequality of sides, however, can also be found in figures that are not straight-lined <note>such as those bounded by curves</note>.

<margin>Division of triangles by angles.</margin>
Therefore, he [Euclid] says that some triangles are equilateral, others isosceles, and others scalene. For they either have all sides equal, all unequal, or only two equal. And again, he says that some triangles are right-angled, some obtuse-angled, and some acute-angled. <margin>Why Euclid provides a double division of triangles.</margin> He defines a right-angled triangle as having one right angle, just as an obtuse-angled one has one obtuse angle. Indeed, it is impossible for a triangle to have more than one right or obtuse angle. An acute-angled triangle, however, is one that has all its angles acute; for here it is not enough to have only one acute angle. If that were the case, all triangles would be considered acute-angled, because every triangle—whether you like it or not—has at least two acute angles. Only the acute-angled triangle has three.

<margin>A four-sided triangle, called "point-shaped" (*acidoides*).</margin>
It seems to me that Euclid made these separate divisions for angles and sides for this specific reason: namely, that not every "triangle" <note>in the sense of a figure with three interior corners</note> is also three-sided. For there are four-sided triangles, which are called *acidoides* <note>original Greek: ἀκιδοειδῆ</note>, meaning "point-shaped," by mathematicians; and by Zenodorus <note>a Greek mathematician known for studying isometric figures</note> they are called *koilogonia* <note>original Greek: κοιλογώνια</note>, meaning "having a hollow angle" <note>This refers to what we now call a "non-convex" or "concave" quadrilateral, which looks like an arrowhead</note>. For imagine one of the three-sided ones, and upon...

For this reason, Philolaus also gathers their union under one angle. The first division of **Quadrilateral Figures** <note>Four-sided shapes</note> must be made into two branches: some of them are called **Parallelograms**, while others are **Non-Parallelograms**. Among the Parallelograms, some are both right-angled and equilateral, such as **Squares**; <margin>Commentary 18. The division of Quadrilateral Figures according to Posidonius.</margin> others are neither, such as **Rhomboids**; <note>original: "Rhomboidea"; a parallelogram where opposite sides and angles are equal, but it is neither a square nor a rectangle.</note> others are right-angled but not equilateral, such as **Rectangles**; <note>original: "altera parte longiora"; literally "longer in one part."</note> and others, conversely, are equilateral but not right-angled, such as **Rhombuses**. For a shape must either have both—namely, equality of sides and rightness of angles—or neither, or one of the two, and this last case happens in two ways. Therefore, the Parallelogram is established in a fourfold way. Among the **Non-Parallelograms**, <margin>There are seven species of Quadrilateral Figures.</margin> some have only two parallel sides but not the remaining two, while others have no parallel sides at all. The former are called **Trapezia**, while the latter are **Trapezoids**. Among the Trapezia, some have equal sides by which these parallel sides are joined <note>meaning the non-parallel legs are equal</note>, while others have unequal sides. The former are called **Isosceles Trapezia** <note>original: "Aequicrura"; literally "equal-legged."</note> and the latter are **Scalene Trapezia**. Thus, the Quadrilateral Figure is established for us in seven modes. For one is the **Square**; the second is the **Rectangle**; the third is the **Rhombus**; the fourth is the **Rhomboid**; the fifth is the **Isosceles Trapezium**; the sixth is the **Scalene Trapezium**; and the seventh is the **Trapezoid**. 

Truly, **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and mathematician (c. 135–51 BCE) who sought to refine Euclid's definitions.</note> made a perfect division of rectilinear quadrilaterals into these members, since he also established seven species of these, just as there are of triangles. <margin>Euclid's Division.</margin> **Euclid**, however, was not at all able to divide them into Parallelograms and Non-Parallelograms, because he had neither mentioned parallels yet nor taught us about the Parallelogram itself. This property is to have opposite sides and angles equal. For the **Square**, the **Rectangle**, and the **Rhombus** itself have opposite sides and angles that are equal. <margin>In Proposition 34 of the first book. <margin>Continuation of the Book. From Chapter 8 of the previous Book.</margin> **S**ince the principles of Geometry are divided into three parts—into Hypotheses, Postulates, and Axioms <note>The Latin text uses *Pronuntiata* (Proclamations) for what are commonly called Axioms or Common Notions in geometry.</note>—we have already set forth the difference between these in the previous sections. But our present purpose is to discuss the **Postulate** and the **Axiom** specifically and more accurately, since we are now mainly occupied with them. We have already explained the Hypotheses, which are also called Definitions, in what has been said. 

<margin>The commonalities of Postulates and Axioms according to the opinion of the author and Geminus. Their differences.</margin> It is common to both Axioms and Postulates that they require no demonstration <note>original: "demonstratione"</note> nor any geometric proof; rather, they are accepted as self-evident and become the principles for everything else. They differ from one another, however, in the same way that **Theorems** were distinguished from **Problems**. For just as in Theorems we propose to perceive and understand that which follows from the subject matter, while in Problems we are commanded to construct and do something; in the same way, in Axioms we accept those things which are self-evident to the mind and ready at hand in our untaught concepts. <note>Proclus is arguing that Axioms are things we "just know" intuitively, while Postulates are things we "just do" to start a construction.</note> In Postulates, however, we seek to accept those things which are easy to do and construct, where the Mind <note>original: "Cogitatio"</note> is not exhausted in accepting them, and which require no variety and no Construction. 

Therefore, clear and indemonstrable knowledge, and construction-free acceptance, distinguish Postulates from Axioms. Just as demonstrative knowledge and the acceptance of the things sought together with Construction separated Theorems from Problems. For everywhere, the principles must surpass those things that follow the principles in simplicity, in being indemonstrable, and in the fact that they provide their own credibility. 

<margin>Speusippus</margin> Indeed, universally (says Speusippus) <note>Speusippus was Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy; he argued that all geometric propositions should be called 'theorems'.</note> of those things which the Mind hunts for, it brings some forth without any varied or winding path, and for the future inquiry...

<summary>In this opening to Book Three, Proclus distinguishes between the fundamental starting points of geometry: Postulates (tasks to be done) and Axioms (truths to be known), comparing them to the relationship between Problems and Theorems.</summary>

The mind prepares itself and possesses a clearer grasp of these things than of visible objects. While it cannot achieve some things immediately, it progresses by passing through them, attempting to hunt them down by following a logical sequence. <margin>Example</margin> For example, it accepts the drawing of a straight line from one point to another as something self-evident and easy to perform. Since it is formed by the steady flow of a point and proceeds forward together, because it never deviates more or less to one side, it arrives at the second point. Again, if one of the endpoints of a straight line remains fixed while the other moves around it, a circle is described without any difficulty. However, if one wishes to describe a <term>spiral</term><note>The original uses the term "Helix." In this context, it refers to a two-dimensional spiral, like those studied by Archimedes.</note> of a single revolution, they require a more complex device, for it is generated by several different motions. Likewise, if one wishes to construct an equilateral triangle, they will also need a specific method for that construction. For the Geometric Mind will say: <margin>Generation of a Plane Spiral</margin> "When I have understood a straight line where one end remains fixed while the other moves around it, and a point moves along that line starting from the fixed end, I have described a spiral of one revolution." For when the end of the straight line (which describes the circle) and the point moving along that straight line both arrive and coincide at the same spot, they create such a spiral for me. <margin>Construction of an Equilateral Triangle</margin> "And again, when I have described equal circles and drawn straight lines from their common intersection to the centers of the circles, and then drawn a straight line from one center to the other, I will have an equilateral triangle."

Thus, these things are far from being perfected by simple apprehension or a primary notion, for we are content just to follow their origin. Therefore, whether these things are acquired more easily or with more difficulty, and whether they are demonstrated through more or fewer intermediate steps, depends on the skill of those approaching them. But truly, the need for demonstration and construction arises from the nature of the things sought, which falls short of the clarity found in <term>Postulates</term><note>Latin: *petitiones*. These are fundamental assumptions that allow a mathematician to perform a specific action, like drawing a line.</note> and <term>Axioms</term><note>Latin: *pronuntiata*. These are self-evident truths that do not require proof, often called "common notions."</note>. Both, therefore, ought to be simple and easy to grasp. A Postulate, I say, commands us to devise and prepare certain material to assign a property, which should be simple and easy to perceive. An Axiom, however, speaks of something that is an essential attribute in itself, known to the listeners on its own—for instance, that fire is hot, or any of those other things which are most manifest. Regarding those who doubt such things, we say they lack either their senses or a punishment. <note>This is a reference to a classical philosophical stance (often attributed to Aristotle) that self-evident truths are so obvious that denying them suggests a lack of basic perception or a stubbornness that deserves discipline rather than argument.</note> For this reason, the Postulate and the Axiom belong to the same category, but they differ in the manner already stated: for both are indemonstrable principles, yet the latter is so in one way, and the former in another, as we have said. Now, some people call all of these "Postulates"...

<margin>Commentary 1.</margin>

THese three, both because of their ease and because they command us to prepare something, must necessarily be placed among the **Postulates** according to the opinion of **Geminus** <note>Geminus of Rhodes (1st century BCE), a mathematician whose works are largely lost but preserved in commentaries like this one.</note>. If, therefore, we understand a **Point** to be moved in an undeviating and shortest motion, we will arrive at another **Point**, and the first **Postulate** is completed, and we have understood nothing varied. If, however, since the **Straight Line** itself is terminated by a **Point**, we similarly understand its **Extremity** to be moved by the shortest and undeviating motion, the second **Postulate** will be prepared from a ready and simple apprehension. If, moreover, we understand a finite straight **Line** to remain fixed according to one of its **Extremities**, but to be moved around that which remains fixed according to the other, then the third **Postulate** will be completed. For the **Center** indeed is the **Point** that remains; the **Distance**, however, is the straight **Line**.

### BOOK THREE 107

An indivisible thing <note>Referring to a mathematical point, which has no parts</note> has its own motion. But we, looking toward the motions of physical bodies, attribute those motions that occur in things lacking dimension <note>original: *intervallo*, referring to the spatial "interval" or extension between points</note> to them. Therefore, indivisible things are free from physical space and external motions; but another species of motion, and another kind of space related to those motions, is considered within them. Indeed, we say that a <term>Point</term> <note>original: *Signum*, literally "sign," used here as a synonym for a geometric point</note> has a position in the <term>Imagination</term> <note>original: *Phantasia*; in this context, it refers to the mental faculty where geometric forms are visualized</note>, and we do not ask how that which is moved somewhere <margin>† is situated</margin> can still remain indivisible and be contained by a place. For the space of those things that have dimension possesses dimension itself; but the space of indivisibles has no dimension.

Therefore, some species are proper to geometric things, and others are those constituted by them; there is one motion of bodies, and another of those things conceived in the Imagination; likewise, there is one place for things with parts, and another for those without parts. It is necessary to distinguish these so as not to confuse the essences of things, nor to disturb them. It seems that the first of these three <term>Postulates</term> <note>original: *Petitionum*, the standard term for Euclid's postulates</note> <margin>Digression.</margin> declares to us through images how those things that exist are contained within their causes (which are indivisible), and are limited by them; and that even before they are formed, they are everywhere encompassed by them. For when points exist, a straight line is drawn from one to the other, is terminated by them, and is received between them.

The second postulate shows how those things, by having their own causes, proceed toward all things while maintaining a continuity in them, from which they are never severed; rather, because of the cause of infinite power, they strive to reach everywhere. The third shows how those things that have proceeded forth return again to their own principles. For the revolution of a point moving around a fixed point, which produces a circle, imitates this circular return <note>The author is linking the geometric construction of a circle to the Neoplatonic concept of "proceding" from a source and "returning" to it</note>. However, one must know that the ability to be extended to infinity is not inherent in all lines; <margin>End of the Digression. Lesson.</margin> for it is not in the circular line, nor the <term>Cissoid</term> <note>An ivy-shaped curve</note>, nor in any of those that describe a closed figure, nor even in those that make no figure. For a <term>Helix</term> <note>A spiral</note> of a single revolution is not produced to infinity, for it is established between two points; nor are any other lines that are formed in this way. Furthermore, it is not possible to extend every kind of line from every point to every point, for not every line can exist between all points. So much for these matters. Let us proceed to the rest.

<margin>Commentary 2.</margin>

<margin>The fourth Postulate <note>original: "Petitio"</note> is excluded from the number of Postulates, according to the opinions of both Geminus and Aristotle. The same was noted above in the first commentary of this book.</margin>

<margin>Proof of the fourth Postulate.</margin>

<margin>In the 10th definition.</margin>

<margin>Pappus’s lesson.</margin>

This current Postulate is granted by us as something manifest and needing no proof; thus, it is not a "Postulate" according to Geminus's opinion, but rather an Axiom <note>original: "Pronuntiatum." Geminus was an ancient Greek mathematician who distinguished between "postulates" (which ask you to do something) and "axioms" (which state a self-evident property).</note>. For it describes a property that belongs to right angles in themselves, without commanding us to perform any simple construction. Furthermore, it is not a Postulate according to Aristotle’s classification either. For in his view, a Postulate requires some form of proof <note>Aristotle argued that if a student does not intuitively accept a premise, it must be proven to them, making it a "postulate" rather than a "common notion."</note>. But if we say that it is indeed demonstrable and seek its proof, then according to Geminus’s view, it still should not be placed among the Postulates. Thus, the equality of right angles is apparent even according to our common notions. Since the right angle holds the status of a unit or a limit <note>original: "Termini rationem." The author views the right angle as a fixed "standard" compared to the infinite variety of acute or obtuse angles.</note> compared to the infinite increase or decrease of other angles on either side, it is equal in respect to any other right angle. Indeed, we first establish a right angle in this way: by making the angles on both sides of a standing straight line equal to one another. If it is necessary to provide a geometric proof for this, let there be two right angles, one **a b c** and the other **d e f**.

I say that they are equal. For if they are not equal, let one of them be larger, such as the one at point **b**. Therefore, if line **d e** is applied to line **a b**, line **e f** will fall inside. Let it fall as line **b g**, and let line **b c** be extended as far as

[A geometric diagram is placed here, to the right of the preceding six lines. It shows a horizontal line labeled **k**, **b**, **c**, **h**. A vertical line **a**-**b** meets it at **b**. A slanted line **b**-**g** originates from **b** and falls inside the angle **a b c**. To the right is a separate right angle formed by vertical line **d**-**e** and horizontal line **e**-**f**.]

point **h**. Since angle **a b c** is a right angle, angle **a b h** will also be a right angle, and they will be equal to each other. For we have it in the Definitions that a right angle is equal to the angle adjacent to it. Therefore, angle **a b h** is larger than angle **a b g**. Let line **g b** be extended again as far as **k**. Since angle **a b g** is a right angle, its adjacent angle will also be a right angle, and therefore equal to **a b g** itself. Thus, angle **a b k** is equal to angle **a b g**, which would make angle **a b h** smaller than angle **a b g**; but it was also larger, which is impossible. Therefore, one right angle is not larger than another. This has also been shown by other commentators and did not require much deliberation. Pappus, however, rightly reminds us that the converse of this Postulate is not true—namely, that everything equal to a right angle is necessarily a right angle. While this is undoubtedly true if the angle is formed by straight lines <note>original: "rectilineus"</note>, an angle formed by curved lines <note>original: "curuilineum"</note> could also be equal to a right angle.

**THIRD [BOOK]** 109

I have also shown an angle equal to a Right Angle. And it is manifest that we shall not say that an angle of this kind can be a "Right Angle." For in the division of rectilinear <note>original: "rectilineorum" — angles formed by straight lines.</note> angles, we accepted the Right Angle as being constituted by a straight line standing inflexibly upon a subject straight line. <margin>In the 10th definition.</margin> For this reason, an angle equal to a right angle is not entirely a "Right" angle, since it is not even rectilinear. Therefore, let two equal straight lines **a b** and **b c** be understood, forming a right angle at the point **b**; and in these, let the semicircles **a e b** and **b f c** be described by their center and interval. Since, therefore, the semicircles are equal, they will coincide with each other, and the angle **e b a** is equal to the angle **f b c**. Let the remaining common part, namely **e b c**, be added.

[Diagram 1: A geometric figure showing a right angle formed by lines 'ab' and 'bc'. Two semicircles are drawn: one with diameter 'ab' passing through point 'e', and another with diameter 'bc' passing through point 'f'. Points 'a', 'b', 'c', 'e', 'f' are labeled.]

Therefore the whole Right angle is equal to the <term>horn-like angle</term> <note>original: "Corniculari" — an angle formed between the circumference of a circle and a straight line, or between two curves; so called because it resembles the curve of a horn.</note>, specifically to **e b f**, yet the horn-like angle is not a Right Angle. In the same way, even if the angle **a b c** is <term>Obtuse</term> or <term>Acute</term>, a horn-like angle will be shown to be equal to it (for this is that class of curvilinear angles which corresponds with rectilinear ones). Beyond this, one must only notice that in the Right angle and in the Obtuse angle, it is necessary to add the middle angle contained by the line **c b** and the circumference **b e**; but in the Acute angle, it must be taken away, for the straight line **c b** cuts the circumference **b e**. Therefore, let the exemplary descriptions of both suppositions be set down. These things have thus been described, which indeed show both that all Right angles are equal to one another, and that an angle equal to a Right angle is not necessarily a "Right Angle" itself. For if it is not rectilinear, in what way could anyone call it "right"? Moreover, it is manifest from this <term>Postulate</term> <note>original: "Petitione" — referring here to Euclid's Fourth Postulate: "That all right angles are equal to one another."</note> that the "Rightness" of an angle is related to equality, just as "Sharpness" <note>Acuteness</note> and "Bluntness" <note>Obtuseness</note> are related to inequality. For indeed, Rightness and equality belong to the same coordination (for both exist under the <term>Limit</term> <note>original: "Fine" — referring to the Pythagorean principle of *Peras*, representing order and boundaries.</note>), as does similarity. But Sharpness and Bluntness belong to the same series as inequality, just as dissimilarity; for all these are produced from the Limit and from <term>Infinity</term> <note>original: "Infinitate" — referring to *Apeiron*, the principle of the unlimited or disordered.</note>.

[Diagram 2: A geometric figure showing two intersecting semicircles forming a curvilinear angle. Points 'a', 'b', 'c', 'e', 'f' are marked.]

These are those things which, according to the opinion of everyone, are called indemonstrable **Axioms**, insofar as they are judged by all to be so, and no one doubts them. For frequently they also call propositions "Axioms" <note>original: "Pronuntiata"</note> simply, whatever kind they may be, whether they are properly "immediate" <note>self-evident</note> or even if they require some reminder. <margin>Apollonius is condemned for having demonstrated the **Axioms**, as was mentioned above in chapter 1 of this book.</margin>...notion of [this]. We are therefore far from praising **Apollonius the Geometer**, who (it seems) also wrote demonstrations for the **Axioms** <note>original Latin: *Pronuntiata*; these refer to Euclid's "Common Notions," self-evident truths that require no proof.</note>, since he is said to be of an opposite mind to **Euclid**. For Euclid indeed enumerated even demonstrable things among the **Postulates** <note>original: *Petitionibus*</note>, while Apollonius attempted to find demonstrations even for things that cannot be demonstrated. 

<margin>Indemonstrable things differ by nature from those that can be demonstrated, and the sciences concerning them are different. See Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics*, Book 1, texts 5 and 6.</margin>However, these two types of things differ from one another by their very nature, and the kind of science required for each is different. I speak of those sciences which concern **immediate propositions** <note>Propositions that are self-evident and do not require a "middle term" to prove their truth.</note>, which fall within our knowledge entirely because of their clarity; and those sciences which employ demonstrations, which receive their principles from the former, and once received, use them appropriately in their own conclusions. 

<margin>The demonstration of Apollonius.</margin>That the demonstration of the first **Axiom**, which Apollonius persuaded himself he had discovered, does not possess a **Middle Term** <term>Middle Term: In logic, the link that connects the subject and the predicate in a proof.</term> more known than the conclusion—indeed, one even more doubtful—anyone will be able to realize if they look into it even slightly. 

"For let **a**," he says, "be equal to **b**, and **b** equal to **c**; I say that **a** is also equal to **c**. For since **a** is equal to **b**, it occupies the same place as **b**. And since **b** is equal to **c**, it also occupies the same place as **c**. Therefore, **a** also occupies the same place as **c**. They are, therefore, equal." 

In this argument, he must pre-suppose two things: first, that things which occupy the same place are equal to one another; and second, that things which occupy the same place as the same thing also occupy the same place as each other. 

<margin>The first property of Axioms.</margin>It is manifest, however, that these assumptions are more obscure than the present **Axiom**. For in what way are things that fill the same place "equal"? Is it according to the **Whole**, or according to a **part**? Or according to the configuration of a **Ratio**? For this reason, it is not at all to be admitted that we should move toward the concept of "place," which is more unknown to us than the things which exist within that place. Indeed, discovering the very essence of "place" is difficult and ambiguous. 

<margin>The second property of Axioms.</margin>Lest we use a long-winded speech: all **Axioms** must be handed down as immediate and self-manifest, since they are known and credible in themselves. For he who brings a demonstration to things that are most manifest does not confirm the truth concerning them; rather, he diminishes the clarity which we have in our unlearned **innate notions** <note>original: *prenotionibus*; the "common notions" or sparks of knowledge we are born with.</note>. This must be understood beforehand regarding the **Axioms** as the judgment of their specific property: that all of them belong to the common genus of the **mathematical sciences**. Each of these is said to be verified not only in **Magnitudes**, but also in **Numbers**, **Motions**, and **Times**. And this is necessary. For the **Equal** and the **Unequal**, and the **Whole** and the **part**, and...

-> THIRD BOOK 113 <-

And these principles are common to both discrete <note>original: "discretis"; referring to numbers</note> and continuous <note>original: "continuis"; referring to lines or shapes</note> quantities. Therefore, any contemplation concerning Time, Motion, Numbers, or Magnitudes requires these principles as self-evident truths. In all these fields, that saying is true: **things equal to the same thing are also equal to one another**; as is any other of the Common Notions <term>Common Notions (Pronuntiata): these are basic mathematical axioms, like "1+1=2," that Euclid assumed everyone would agree are true without needing a proof</term> that we might take up. Since these principles are universal, each person uses them according to their specific subject matter as much as is required: one uses them for Magnitudes, another for Numbers, and another for Times. In this way, specific conclusions are reached in each individual science, even though the Common Notions themselves are universal. Furthermore, <margin>How specific conclusions are made from common principles. Same as above in the first chapter.</margin> one should not try to reduce the number of these axioms to a minimum, as **Heron** <note>Heron of Alexandria (c. 10–70 AD), a Greek mathematician and engineer</note> does, who proposed only three Common Notions. For that principle, **The whole is greater than its part**, is also a Common Notion, and the Geometer assumes this everywhere in his proofs; so too is the principle, **Things that coincide with one another are equal**. Indeed, <margin>Heron proposed only three Common Notions.</margin> this latter principle is immediately useful for the proof of the fourth proposition <note>This refers to Proposition 4 of Euclid's "Elements," which deals with the congruence of triangles</note>. Nor should one add other things to the list, some of which are specific only to geometric matter—such as the claim that "two straight lines do not enclose a space"—since Common Notions must be of a universal nature, as we have said. Others are simply consequences of those axioms already established, <margin>He prunes the 6th, 7th, and 10th Common Notions. Common Notions are of a common genus. Same as above in Chapter 1.</margin> such as the statement that "doubles of the same thing are equal." For this follows from the axiom: "if equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal." For those things that are equal to a **Half**, when they are combined with that same Half, they become **Doubles** of the same thing, and they are equal to each other because the amount added was equal. By this same reasoning, not only doubles, but triples, and all multiples of the same thing, will appear equal. To these Common Notions, **Pappus** <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290–350 AD), one of the last great Greek mathematicians of antiquity</note> says certain <margin>Certain other Common Notions which are added by Pappus.</margin> others should be added, such as: **If unequal things are added to equal things, the difference between the wholes is equal to the difference between the things added.** And conversely: **If equal things are added to unequal things, the difference between the wholes is equal to the difference of those things that were unequal at the start.** These are also self-evident, yet they are demonstrated in this manner: Let **a** and **b** be equal, <margin>Proof of the first Common Notion added by Pappus.</margin> and let unequal things **c** and **d** be added to them. Let **c** be greater than **d** by the amount **e**, and let the remainder be **f**.

**S**ince all systematic knowledge is twofold, and one part is concerned with immediate Propositions, while the other is concerned with those things which are shown and compared from them <margin>Commentary 5. Science is twofold.</margin>—and generally unfolds its treatment around those things that follow from the principles—this [science], in turn, has divided itself in Geometric discourse into the performance of Problems and the discovery of Theorems. For the former [Problems] command us to undertake Origins, and Positions, and Applications, and Descriptions, and Inscriptions, and Circumscriptions, and Fittings-together, and Contacts, and all such things <margin>The function of a Problem.</margin>; but the latter [Theorems] strive to persuade us of the Properties <note>original: "Symptomata" — here referring to the essential attributes or characteristics that belong to a geometric figure.</note> and those things that are inherent in the subjects of Geometry by their very nature, and to convince us by demonstrations. <margin>The function of a Theorem.</margin> For concerning whatever it is possible for a Question to be asked, about all those things does Geometry speak, referring some to Problems and others to Theorems. <margin>Concerning what things Geometry speaks.</margin> For it seeks "what it is," and this in two ways: for it either seeks the reason and the understanding, or it seeks the understanding and the very essence of the subject. <margin>Geometry seeks the four things which are usually sought.</margin> I say, for example, when it asks what a "line of similar parts" is: for seeking this, it either desires to find the definition of such a Line—that a Line of similar parts is one which has all parts fitting all others—or it seeks to take up the actual species of lines with similar parts, such as whether it is a Straight line, or a Circular line, or a Helix <note>A spiral shape.</note> around a Cylinder. <margin>Geometry seeks "What is it?" in two ways.</margin> Furthermore, before this,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four types of scientific inquiry (existence, essence, quality, and cause) as applied to geometry, specifically addressing whether geometry investigates the "cause" of things.</meta>

116 BOOK I

<margin>How Geometry seeks "whether it exists."</margin>
[Geometry] seeks **[whether it exists]** <note>original: "si est"</note> for its own sake, and this is especially true in its **Determinations** <note>The section of a proof that defines the specific conditions under which the goal can be achieved.</note>, where it discusses whether what is sought is impossible or possible, to what extent it holds true, and in how many ways. Furthermore, it seeks **[what kind of thing it is]** <note>original: "quale quid est"</note>; for when it considers the essential properties of a Triangle, a Circle, and Parallel lines, it is clear that it is investigating "what kind" of things they are. 

<margin>How, and what kind of thing it is.</margin>
<margin>Proclus responds against the opinion of Amphinomus and Aristotle, following the opinion of Geminus.</margin>
<margin>Argument.</margin>
However, many have believed that Geometry does not at all contemplate the cause or the **[wherefore]** <note>original: "propter quid," referring to the formal cause or reason why a thing is true.</note>. This was the opinion of Amphinomus, following the lead of **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher who argued that mathematics describes "that" something is, but not always "why" it is.</note>. "But someone will find," says **Geminus** <note>A Greek mathematician and astronomer (c. 1st century BC).</note>, "the investigation of this even in Geometry. For how is it not the task of the Geometer to seek the cause of why an infinite number of equilateral polygons can be inscribed in circles, while it is impossible to inscribe an infinite number of equilateral and equiangular solid polygons <term>polyhedra</term>—constructed from similar planes—within spheres?" 

<margin>How and when Geometry seeks the "wherefore" (the cause).</margin>
To whom would it belong to investigate and discover this, if not the Geometer? Therefore, when Geometers use a **syllogism through impossibility** <note>A "reductio ad absurdum" proof, which proves a point by showing that its opposite is impossible.</note>, they only desire to find the **symptom** <note>A property or characteristic.</note>; but when they use a direct demonstration, then again, if the demonstrations are made in a particular case, the cause is not yet manifest. If, however, they are made in a universal sense and apply to all similar cases, immediately the **[wherefore]** becomes clear. 

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
But let these remarks suffice regarding the things sought. 

<margin>The parts of Problems and Theorems.</margin>
<margin>The function of the Proposition.</margin>
<margin>The function of the Exposition.</margin>
<margin>The function of the Construction.</margin>
<margin>The function of the Demonstration.</margin>
<margin>The function of the Conclusion.</margin>
Every **Problem**, and every **Theorem**, that is complete in its finished parts, ought to contain all these in itself: the **Proposition**, the **Exposition**, the **Determination**, the **Construction**, the **Demonstration**, and the **Conclusion**. 
*   Of these, the **Proposition** <note>Also called the enunciation.</note> states what is sought, given certain data; for a perfect Proposition consists of both. 
*   The **Exposition** <note>Or "Setting-out."</note> takes the given data by itself and prepares it for the inquiry. 
*   The **Determination** <note>Or "Specification."</note> explains separately exactly what the thing sought is. 
*   The **Construction** adds those things that are missing from the data to help "hunt down" what is sought. 
*   The **Demonstration** skillfully gathers the proposed conclusion from what has been granted. 
*   The **Epilogue**, or **Conclusion**, turns back again to the Proposition, confirming that which has been shown. 

<margin>Three parts are most necessary, which must always be present in both Problems and Theorems: the Proposition...</margin>
And these are indeed all the parts of Problems and Theorems; but the most necessary, which exist in all of them, are the **Proposition**, the **Demonstration**, and the **Conclusion**. For it is necessary to know in advance what is sought, to show this through intermediary steps, and to conclude that which has been shown; it is impossible for any of these three to be missing. 

The remaining parts are used in many places, but in many other places they are omitted because they provide no utility. For instance, the **Determination** and the **Exposition** are not found in that Problem which says: *To construct an isosceles triangle which has each of the angles at the base double the remaining angle.* <note>This refers to Euclid's Elements, Book IV, Proposition 10.</note>

For the **Exposition** and **Specification** belong to the **Given**. Indeed, they would be the same as the **Proposition** itself. <margin>Exposition and Specification belong to the Given.</margin> For what else would you say to specify the aforementioned problem, except that it is necessary to find such an Isosceles triangle? And that was exactly what the **Proposition** stated. If, then, the **Proposition** does not have this specific **Given** and that specific **Sought**, the **Exposition** is silent because there is no **Given**, and the **Specification** is omitted so as not to be identical to the **Proposition**. You will find many other such problems, especially in Arithmetic and in the Tenth Book <note>Referring to Book X of Euclid's Elements, which deals with irrational magnitudes.</note>, such as finding two straight lines commensurable in power that contain a medial area, <margin>Proposition 29 of the Tenth Book of the Elements.</margin> and all others of that kind. Every **Given** can be provided in these four ways: by **Position**, by **Ratio**, by **Magnitude**, or by **Form**. <margin>Instruction.</margin> For a **Point** <note>original: "Signum," used here as a geometric point.</note> is given by **Position** only, while a **Line**...

<margin>The "Given" is understood in four ways; therefore, the **Exposition** <note>The "Exposition" or *ekthesis* is the step in a geometric proof where the specific given elements are identified on a diagram.</note> is also performed in four ways.</margin>

From this, since a **Position** can vary, the **Construction** also admits variety. Since, therefore, the **Given** is understood in four ways, it is manifest that the **Exposition** is also performed in four ways. At times, it even connects two or even three of these modes.

<margin>Geometric **Demonstration** is twofold. The perfection of a demonstration.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding that which is called a **Demonstration**, we will find that it sometimes possesses the qualities proper to a true **Demonstration**, showing the thing sought through "Intermediate Definitions" <note>Definitions that act as the logical middle ground to connect a premise to a conclusion.</note>. <margin>The Geometric **Conclusion** is twofold.</margin>
And it must not be overlooked that although geometric discourses always possess **Necessity** <note>Logical certainty.</note> because of their underlying subject matter, they are not always perfected through strictly demonstrative methods. For example, when it is shown that a **Triangle** has three internal angles equal to two right angles because the exterior angle of a **Triangle** is equal to the two internal and opposite angles <note>This refers to Euclid’s Elements, Book I, Proposition 32.</note>, how can this be a demonstration based on a cause? For how is the "Middle Term" <note>The logical link in a syllogism.</note> not merely a sign? Even if the external angle did not yet exist, the internal angles would still be equal to two right angles, for the **Triangle** exists even if the side is not extended.

However, when it is shown through the drawing of **Circles** that a constructed **Triangle** is equilateral, the understanding is reached through the cause. For we shall say that the similarity and equality of the **Circles** are the cause of the equality of the sides of the **Triangle**.

Furthermore, they are accustomed to making the **Conclusion** twofold in a way. For once they have shown it for the **Given** case, they also conclude universally, returning from the particular conclusion to the universal one. For since they do not rely on the specific properties of the objects before them, but rather place the **Given** before our eyes—describing an **Angle** or a straight **Line**—they believe that whatever is concluded in this specific case is also concluded in every similar case. Therefore, they transcend to the universal so that we do not think the **Conclusion** is only particular. They transcend by the best possible reason, since they use the things placed before them for the demonstration not insofar as they are *these* specific things, but insofar as they are similar to others. For they do not perform the bisection of an **Angle** because the proposed **Angle** is of a certain size, but only because it is "rectilinear" <note>Made of straight lines.</note>. Indeed, the specific **Quantity** belongs to the proposed **Angle** alone, but being **Rectilinear** is common to all rectilinear angles. Suppose the given **Angle** is a **Right Angle**. If I were to include its "Rightness" in the demonstration, I could not transcend to every species of rectilinear angle. But if I do not include its Rightness... [Catchword: *subiungo*]

Now the Proposition <margin>The Proposition of the first Problem of Euclid.</margin> in this case consists of both the **Given** and the **Sought**; for the Given is a finite straight line, and what is sought is in what way an equilateral triangle might be constructed upon it. And indeed, the Given precedes, and the Sought follows, so that you might also weave them together: "If there is a finite straight line, it is possible for <margin>Note that every Problem can be reduced to a Theorem.</margin> an equilateral triangle to be constructed upon it." For without a straight line existing, a triangle could not be constructed, as it is contained by straight lines; nor could it be without being finite, for an angle cannot be made unless it occurs at one point, and an infinite line has no end point.

After the Proposition follows the Exposition: <margin>Exposition and Determination of the first problem of Euclid.</margin> "Let there be a finite straight line, this one:" and you see that the Exposition mentions only the Given itself, by no means adding the Sought. After this comes the Determination: "It is necessary to construct an equilateral triangle on the given finite straight line." In a way, the Determination is the cause of our attention. For it makes us more attentive to the Demonstration by pronouncing the thing sought, just as the Exposition makes us more teachable by placing the Given before our eyes.

After the Determination, the Construction follows: <margin>Construction.</margin> "With one of the endpoints of the straight line as a center, and the remaining distance as an interval <note>original: "interuallo," here meaning the radius or distance from the center to the other end of the line</note>, let a circle be described. And again, with the remaining endpoint as a center, and with the interval that was previously the center, let a circle be described; and from the point of the common intersection of the circles to the endpoints of the straight line, let straight lines be extended." 

And you see that in the Construction I use Postulates <note>original: "Petitionibus," referring to Euclid's basic geometric assumptions.</note>. <margin>Geometers use Postulates in construction, but Axioms in demonstration.</margin> Specifically this one: "To draw a straight line from any point to any point." And this one: "To describe a circle with any center and interval." For universally, Postulates bring utility to Constructions, while Axioms <note>original: "Pronuntiata," or Common Notions</note> bring utility to Demonstrations. 

Thus follows the Demonstration: <margin>Demonstration.</margin> Since either of those points which are on the given straight line is the center of the circle surrounding it, the straight line which touches the common intersection is equal to the given straight line. For this reason, since the remaining point of those on the given straight line is also the center of the circle containing it, the straight line touching the common intersection of the circles is equal to the given straight line. The reminder of these things comes from the definition of a circle, which stated that all lines from the center to the circumference are equal. Therefore, both [new lines] are equal to the same [given line]. And those things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another...

<margin>A beautiful consideration of the phrases "Which was to be done" and "Which was to be demonstrated."</margin>
To these conclusions, he added the phrase [**which it was necessary to have done**] <note>This is the Latin translation of the Greek *hoper edei poiēsai*, commonly known today by the Latin abbreviation **Q.E.F.** (*Quod erat faciendum*).</note>, showing this to be a **Problematic Conclusion**. For in Theorems, he adds the phrase [**which it was necessary to have shown**] <note>This is the Latin *quod ostendisse oportuit*, known as **Q.E.D.** (*Quod erat demonstrandum*).</note>. The former [Problems] declare the actual making or doing of something, while the latter [Theorems] declare the showing and discovery of the nature of that which already exists. 

Altogether, he places these phrases after the Conclusions to show that all parts of the **Proposition** have been fulfilled, joining the end back to the beginning, and imitating the Mind as it revolves and returns to its starting point. He does not always add the same phrase, but sometimes [which was to be done] and sometimes [which was necessary to have shown]

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
because of the difference between **Problems** and **Theorems**. We have therefore practiced all these things and made them clear in this one first Problem. It is necessary, however, for those who listen to seek these things in the remaining propositions as well: which of these headings are included and which are omitted; in how many ways a "Given" is defined; and from which principles we derive either the **Constructions** or the **Demonstrations**. For a clear contemplation of these matters provides no small exercise and meditation on geometric discourse. 

But since these things are also determined, come, let us briefly discuss those things annexed to them: what is an **Assumption**, what is a **Case**, what is a **Corollary**, what is an **Objection**, and what is an **Induction**.

<margin>What an Assumption is.</margin>
They say that an <term>Assumption</term> <note>original: *Sumptio*. In modern geometry, this is often called a **Lemma**—a preliminary proposition used to prove a larger one.</note> is frequently spoken of regarding every Proposition that is taken up for the construction of another Proposition; they say that the demonstration of that thing is made from so many "Assumptions." 

Properly, however, among those who work in Geometry, an **Assumption** is a Proposition in need of credibility. For when we take something in either a Construction or a Demonstration that has not yet been shown but requires a reason, we then consider that which is taken—being in itself ambiguous—to be worthy of inquiry. We call it an **Assumption**, which differs from a **Postulate** <note>original: *Petitio*</note> and an **Axiom** <note>original: *Pronuntiatum*</note> insofar as it can be demonstrated, whereas Postulates and Axioms are accepted without demonstration to produce belief in other things. In the discovery of Assumptions, the best thing is an aptitude of thought for this purpose; for many people are naturally sharp in the solution...

...performing this without formal resolutions or methods, just as <margin>Cratistus.</margin> our friend Cratistus <note>original: "Cratistus" — a mathematician mentioned by Proclus, known for his intuitive rather than systematic approach</note> used to do.
