Nevertheless, methods have been handed down, the best of which is that <margin>Three methods handed down by Plato.</margin> which leads the **Sought-after thing** back to a proven principle through **Resolution** <term>Resolution (or Analysis): the method of assuming the result is true and working backward to known truths to see if they hold</term>. This method, they say, Plato passed on to Leodamas, who is said to have become the discoverer of many things in Geometry because of it. The second method is that which has the power of **Division**, as it divides the proposed class <note>original: "genus"</note> into distinct parts. By removing other possibilities from the construction of the proposal, it provides the opportunity for **Demonstration**. Plato also praised this method as one that assists all sciences. The third method is that which, through **deduction to the impossible**, does not show the sought-after thing in itself, but refutes the opposite and finds the truth indirectly <note>This refers to *reductio ad absurdum*, a proof method where you show that if a premise were false, it would lead to a logical impossibility</note>. **Assumption** <note>original: "Sumptio"</note> shares in this kind of consideration.

<margin>What a Case is.</margin> A **Case**, however, declares the different modes of construction and the change of position when points <note>original: "Signis"</note>, lines, surfaces, or solids are transposed. Indeed, all its variety is seen in the diagram. Therefore, it is called a **Case** because it is a transposition of the construction.

<margin>What a Corollary is.</margin> A **Corollary** <note>Also known as a Porism</note> is spoken of regarding certain problems, such as the Corollaries attributed to Euclid. Strictly speaking, however, a **Corollary** is when another theorem appears from things that have been demonstrated, without us specifically proposing it. For this reason, they called it a **Corollary**, as if it were a kind of gain that occurs beyond the intended purpose of the scientific demonstration. <margin>See Varro in his book *On the Latin Language*. What an Objection is.</margin>

An **Objection** <note>original: "Instantia"</note>, however, blocks the entire path of the argument by opposing either the construction or the demonstration. Just as it is necessary for someone proposing a **Case** to show that the proposition remains true, it is not necessary for the one making an **Objection** to do the same; rather, it is necessary to destroy the objection and show that the person using it is in error.

<margin>What Induction is. † Note the similarity between Geometric Induction and Logical Induction.</margin> **Induction** <note>In this context, Proclus uses "Inductio" to mean "Reduction" (*anagoge*): the process of reducing a complex problem to a simpler one that is already solved</note> is the transition from one problem or theorem to another. Once the second problem is known or compared, the original proposal also becomes clear. For example, when the duplication of the cube was sought, they transferred the question to another problem upon which this follows—namely, the discovery of two mean proportionals. They then sought how, given two straight lines, two mean proportionals could be found.

<margin>Hippocrates was the first inventor of Geometric Induction.</margin> They say that Hippocrates of Chios was the first to perform the **Induction** of the aforementioned titles; he also squared the **Lune** <note>A crescent-shaped figure; Hippocrates is famous for proving that certain lunes can be squared, a step toward squaring the circle</note> and discovered many other things in Geometry, excelling everyone in his natural talent for these titles. So much for these matters.

Let so many things have been said regarding the equilateral Triangle. It is now necessary to <margin>End of the Digression</margin> construct the remaining Triangles, and first the **Isosceles** <note>Latin: *Aequicrus*, literally "equal-legged."</note>. Therefore, let there be a straight Line *a b*, upon which it is necessary to construct an **Isosceles** triangle. Let Circles be described, as was done for the Equilateral triangle, and let the Line *a b* be extended on <margin>Construction of the remaining Triangles.</margin> both sides to the Points *c* and *d*. Therefore, *c b* is equal to *a d*. With Center *b*, and the Interval <note>In this context, "interval" refers to the radius of the circle.</note> *c b*, let Circle *c e* be described. Again, with Center *a*, and the Interval *d a*, let Circle *d e* be designated; and from Point *e*, where the Circles intersect each other, let straight Lines *e a* and *e b* be extended to Points *a* and *b*. Since, therefore, *e a* is equal to *a d*, and *e b* is equal to *b c*, and *a d* is equal to *b c*, then *e a* will also be equal to *e b*. But these are also greater than the line *a b*. Therefore, triangle *a b e* is **Isosceles**, which is what was required to be done. 

Next, let it be ordered to construct a **Scalene** Triangle upon the given straight Line *a b*. Let Circles be described with Centers and Intervals as in the previous examples. Let Point *f* be taken on the Circumference of the Circle having Center *a*, and let a straight Line *a f* be extended, and let it be produced to Point *g*; then let the straight Line *g b* be extended. Since, therefore, *a* is the Center, *a f* is equal to *a d*. Therefore, *a g* is greater than *a d*, which is to say, greater than *g b*. Furthermore, *b* is also a Center, therefore *g b* is equal to *c b*. Therefore, *g b* is greater than *b a*. But *g a* is greater than *g b*. Therefore, the three lines *g b*, *b a*, and *a g* are unequal. Thus, it is a **Scalene** Triangle. 

So the three Triangles have been constructed. And while <margin>A Teaching.</margin> these things are common knowledge, there is something beautiful in them: namely, that the **Equilateral**, being equal in every way, is constructed in only one way. The **Isosceles**, however, having equality in only two Sides, is constructed in two ways; for the given straight Line is either smaller than both equal sides (as we have done here), or it is larger than both. But the **Scalene**, being unequal in every way, is constructed in three ways: for the given straight Line is either the largest of the three, the smallest, or larger than one and smaller than the other. One may practice either assumption by either extending or contracting the lines. For us, however, let the things that have been set forth suffice.

Those which are constructed simply are called (as **Amphinomus** <note>A Greek mathematician and philosopher, likely a student of Plato, known mostly through the writings of Proclus.</note> says) "ordered"; but those which are constructed in multiple ways...

For an **Equilateral** triangle <note>A triangle where all three sides and all three angles (60 degrees each) are equal.</note> is constructed **simply**; but of the remaining two, one is established in a double way, while the other is established in a triple way. 

Moreover, problems of this kind—namely, to divide a given straight line into three proportional parts—could be done in infinite ways. For if it were cut into a double ratio, and that which is formed from the smaller part were applied to the larger as a deficient quadrangular shape, it will be divided into three equal parts. <note>This refers to the "application of areas," an ancient Greek geometric method used to solve what we now consider algebraic equations.</note> But if the larger segment were more than double the smaller, for instance triple, and if a deficient quadrangular shape equal to what is formed from the smaller part were applied to the larger, it will be divided into three unequal proportional parts. Therefore, since a line can be cut into two parts in infinite ways, where the larger is either double or triple (for <note>original: "multiplex . n. ratio in infinitum procedit"</note> a multiple ratio proceeds to infinity), it follows that it can also be divided into three proportional parts in infinite ways. 

<margin>The word "Problem" is defined in multiple ways.</margin> It is necessary to know that "Problem" is also defined in multiple ways. For everything that is proposed is called a **Problem**, whether it is proposed for the sake of learning or for the sake of doing. <margin>Geometric Problem.</margin> Specifically, however, in the mathematical disciplines, that which is proposed for a contemplative operation is called a **Problem**. For that which is done in these matters has contemplation <note>In this context, "contemplation" refers to theoretical understanding or mental insight rather than physical labor.</note> as its end. And frequently, they even call certain things "problems" which are impossible to do. 

More specifically, however, that which can be done, and is neither **Exceeding** nor **Deficient**, has obtained this name. <margin>What an Exceeding Problem is.</margin> An **Exceeding** problem is one that says, for example, to construct an equilateral triangle that has a vertical angle of <term>two-thirds of a right angle</term> <note>A right angle is 90 degrees; two-thirds of it is 60 degrees. Since every equilateral triangle already has 60-degree angles, this condition is redundant.</note>. For this is superfluous and is added in vain, since it is inherent in every equilateral triangle. 

Of those problems which "exceed," those which are redundant with incongruent or non-existent <term>symptoms</term> <note>The author uses "symptoms" (symptomatibus) to mean the properties or characteristics that define a geometric figure.</note>, they call <margin>What an Impossible Problem is.</margin> **Impossible**; but those which are redundant with things that *can* happen, they call <margin>What a Greater Problem is.</margin> **Greater Problems**. 

<margin>What a Deficient Problem is.</margin> A **Deficient Problem**—which is also called "Less than a Problem"—is one that requires another addition so that it may be reduced from indeterminacy into an order and a <term>limit that produces knowledge</term>. For example, if someone were to say to construct an <term>Isosceles</term> triangle <note>original: "Aequicrus" — literally "equal-legged."</note>. For this is mutilated and indeterminate, and it needs something to be subjoined, such as: what kind of Isosceles? Whether it is that which has a base larger than the two equal sides, or that which has a base smaller than both; and also whether it is that which has a vertical angle double each of those at the base (such as a <term>half-square</term> <note>original: "Semiquadrangulum." This refers to a 45-45-90 degree right isosceles triangle.</note>), or that which has each of those at the base...

<margin>Proposition Two. Second Problem.</margin>

Just as with **Theorems**, some **Problems** are indeed without **Case**, while others have many **Cases**. Therefore, whichever ones have the same power appearing in multiple descriptions, and—changing positions—preserve the same mode of **Demonstration**, these are said to have a **Case**. Whichever ones, however, proceed according to only one Position and one Construction, these are "without Case." For simply put, the **Case** itself appears regarding the construction of both Theorems and Problems.

<margin>Commentary 6.</margin>

<margin>Various Cases of this Problem.</margin>
That the various cases of the present problem arise from the different positions of the point is manifest. For either the given point is placed outside the given straight line, or on it. And if it is on the line, it will either be one of its endpoints, or it will lie between the endpoints. The first [proposition] dealt with the origin of Triangles; the Second and Third, however, proposed comparing one straight Line to another equal one. 3. **The Apostles' Creed** or the **Apostolic Faith**.

It is so named because in ancient times it was believed that the Apostles themselves had composed it. Indeed, it is recounted that they came together before their dispersal, and that <gloss>each contributed individual articles</gloss> <note>original: "singuli singulos contulisse articulos"</note>. This account is first found in the writings of **Rufinus** <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–411) was a historian and theologian whose commentary on the Apostles' Creed is one of our most important early sources for its history.</note>. However, this story is now rejected by almost everyone. It is called **Apostolic**, however, because it contains within it the Apostolic doctrine.

In the earliest times, the creed was not the same everywhere. The Roman, African, and Aquileian churches had some variations <note>Early Christian communities often had their own "local" versions of the creed used during baptismal ceremonies before a single version became standardized.</note>. In particular, the words: <gloss>he descended into hell</gloss> <note>original: "descendit ad inferos"</note>, and <gloss>the communion of saints</gloss> <note>original: "sanctorum communionem"</note> were added only later.

4. **Articles**.

Traditionally, twelve articles were counted, matching the number of the Apostles. But **Luther** and others have organized it into only three main parts <note>referring to the sections dedicated to the Father (Creation), the Son (Redemption), and the Holy Spirit (Sanctification)</note>.

5. **Summary**.

The content is the **Rule of Faith** <note>original: "regula fidei"; a term used by early church fathers like Irenaeus and Tertullian to describe the core truths of the Christian faith that must be held by all believers.</note>. It serves as a brief summary of everything a Christian must believe for salvation.

Indeed, the "one" is everywhere the minimum, and it always serves as the measure for the infinity of other things. Furthermore, it is manifest to anyone that the entire demonstration of the present Theorem <note>This refers to Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Proposition 4: the "Side-Angle-Side" theorem of congruence.</note> depends upon common notions <note>Common Notions are what we now call axioms—self-evident truths that require no proof.</note>, and proceeds as if springing spontaneously from nature, emerging from the very evidence of the Suppositions. <margin>Demonstration of the present Theorem</margin> For when two sides are equal to two sides, each to each, they coincide with one another. When the angles contained by those equal sides are also equal, they likewise coincide with one another. With angle fitted to angle and sides fitted to sides, <margin>Book 1.</margin> the endpoints of the sides below will also coincide. If these endpoints coincide, the Base will also coincide with the Base. If three parts coincide with three parts, then the whole Triangle will coincide with the whole Triangle, and all parts will be equal to all parts.

Equality, therefore, when considered in those things which are of the same species, appears to be the cause of the entire demonstration. For there are two Axioms <note>original: "Pronuntiata"</note> here that have the power to contain the entire method of the proposed Theorem. One <margin>The Eighth Axiom.</margin> says that things which coincide with one another are equal; and this is simply true and requires no limitation, which the author of the *Elements* <note>Euclid</note> uses for the Base, the Space, and the remaining Angles. For he says these are equal because they coincide with one another. The other Axiom is that things which are given as equal coincide with one another. <margin>Converse of the eighth Axiom.</margin> This, however, is not true in all cases, but only in those which are similar in species. By "similar in species," I mean such things as a straight line to a straight line, a circumference to a circumference of the same circle, and angles which are contained by similar lines lying in a similar manner. <margin>Note: here he understands "species" in the most specific sense.</margin> Of these, I say that those which are given as equal will coincide with one another.

Thus, the entire demonstration (to speak briefly) is of this kind: These things are given as equal to those—namely, two sides to two sides and the angles contained by them—and these things coincide with themselves. If these things coincide with one another, then the Base coincides with the Base, and everything coincides with everything. If these coincide, they are also equal. Therefore, if these are given as equal to those, it is simultaneously shown that all parts are equal to all parts. This appears as the first mode of recognizing triangles that are equal in every respect. <margin>† Simple.</margin> Truly, let these remarks suffice concerning the whole demonstration. <margin>The distinction between Problems and Theorems according to Carpus.</margin>

In his astrological treatise, he <note>Likely referring to Carpus of Antioch, a mathematician of the 1st or 2nd century AD</note> raised a discussion regarding **Problems** and **Theorems**. He remarked that it was an opportune moment not to let the matter pass in silence. Finally, having attempted a distinction between them, he stated that the category of "Problems" precedes "Theorems" in the order of study. 

<margin>The first difference.</margin>

For the subjects <note>The physical or geometric shapes themselves</note> are sought to be found by means of Problems before their <term>Symptomata</term> <note>original Latin: *symptomata*. In this context, it refers to the essential properties or accidental qualities of a geometric figure, not a medical symptom.</note> are discovered. Furthermore, the **Proposition** of a Problem is simple, 

<margin>The second difference.</margin>

and requires no complex intellectual effort. It clearly commands something to be done: for example, "to construct an equilateral triangle," or "from the larger of two given unequal straight lines, to cut off a segment equal to the smaller." What among these is difficult or obscure? Regarding a **Theorem**, however, the proposition is difficult, requiring a certain great and precise power, and a judgment that produces knowledge, so that it seems neither to exceed the truth nor to fall short of it. This is certainly the nature of the first of the Theorems.

<margin>The third difference.</margin>

Moreover, in Problems there is a single common path found through <term>Resolution</term> <note>original Latin: *Resolutionem*. This refers to the method of "analysis," where one works backward from the desired result to known principles.</note>, by following which we can successfully manage the matter. In this way, the easier Problems are investigated. In Theorems, however, the treatment is so difficult that up to our own time (he says) no one has been able to hand down a common method for their discovery. Therefore, on account of this ease, the class of Problems is certainly simpler. 

Having distinguished these things, he says that in the foundational teaching of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard textbook of geometry</note>, Problems precede Theorems. The foundational instruction of the "Elements" begins with these, and the first Theorem is actually the fourth in the sequence. It is not listed as fourth because it is shown to be fourth among the others, but because even if it required none of the preceding ones for its demonstration, it was necessary for those others to come first because they are Problems, whereas this is a Theorem. For this Theorem uses entirely common notions, and in a way, it treats the same triangle as being placed in different locations; for the <term>congruence</term> <note>original Latin: *congruentia*. The idea that two shapes are identical if they can be laid exactly over one another.</note> and the equality shown by it are perceived as entirely sensible and evident. Nevertheless, even with the demonstration of the first Theorem being of such a nature, the Problems rightly preceded it, because they were assigned the primary place universally.

<margin>Personal opinion.</margin>

And perhaps in order, Problems precede Theorems, especially among those who ascend from the practical **Arts** (which deal with things perceived by the senses) toward contemplation. However, in **dignity**, Theorems surpass Problems. It seems that all Geometry, insofar as it joins itself to many Arts, acts "problematically"; but insofar as it adheres to primary science, it acts "theoretically"—moving from Problems to Theorems, from secondary things to primary things, and from those things that belong more to the Arts to...

The triangle is **isosceles**. However, the founder of the Elements <note>Euclid</note> will perform a **conversion** to show that the angles at the base are equal. We shall state the reason for this later. <margin>See below in the present commentary.</margin> But now, we must first ask for what reason he demonstrated at all that the angles below the base are equal. <margin>A doubt</margin> For he never makes use of this in the construction or demonstration of other problems or theorems. We must say, in response to <margin>The solution.</margin> this question, that although he will nowhere use this fact—namely, that the angles below the base of an isosceles triangle are equal—it will nevertheless be most useful for the **destruction of instances** <term>Instantia: a technical term for a counter-argument or a specific case that challenges a general rule</term> and for the solutions to objections resisting these theorems. It is a matter of great skill, and belongs to the realm of science, to prepare solutions against those who attack what is said, and to arrange in advance the supports for one's responses. This is so that demonstrations of what is true may be formed not only from what was previously demonstrated, but also so that **refutations of the false** may arise from them. 

You may also take from this order in geometry a benefit for **Rhetoric**. <margin>Note also the benefit to Rhetoric from this geometric order.</margin> For the man who is able to do this in his speeches—foreseeing the points that might attack subsequent chapters and preparing the solutions to them before they are even treated (which is indeed beyond the immediate purpose)—will have woven together a most certain and marvelous path for his disputes. Therefore, the founder of the Elements, teaching us this by the very matter itself, demonstrates simultaneously that the angles below the base of isosceles triangles are equal before those theorems in which we solve resisting objections using these current findings, and thus he prepares the refutation of the lies contained within them. That we shall solve the **instances** brought against the seventh and ninth theorems from this will be clear as we proceed. 

From this, it is also evident for what reason he does not convert the sixth theorem <margin>Here is the cause he mentioned above.</margin> from this one, since it does not offer any primary utility, but rather contributes to the whole of science only by accident. <margin>Proposition 7. Theorem 4.</margin> **Upon the same straight line, two other straight lines equal to the same two [original] straight lines (each to its corresponding one) will not be constructed at a different point on the same side, having the same endpoints as the two straight lines originally drawn.**

<margin>Commentary 11.</margin> The present Theorem has suffered a rare fate, which is not frequently accustomed to happen to the Propositions that give birth to knowledge. For it to be formed through a negation, and not through an affirmation, is not quite proper to them; for the most part, the Propositions of both Geometric and Arithmetic Theorems are affirmations. But the cause (as <margin>Aristotle in *Posterior Analytics*, Book 1, text 31.</margin> Aristotle says) is because the universal affirmative is most suitable to the sciences, as being more fit and needing no negation; but the universal negative also needs affirmation if it must be shown; <margin>† For without affirmation there is no demonstration.</margin> † for from negatives alone there is neither Demonstration nor any certain Reasoning. And therefore the Demonstrating sciences show very many things as affirmative, but rarely use negative conclusions. 

However, the Proposition of this Theorem is full of admirable diligence and bound with all the specific conditions <note>original: 'additionibus' — additions or qualifying clauses</note> by which it is made so certain and indubitable that it can by no means be refuted or proven wrong by those who attempt to use sophistry <note>original: 'calumniari' — to bring false or deceptive charges in an argument</note>. 

<margin>The first condition of this Theorem.</margin> For first, indeed, that small part [**upon the same straight line**] is included, lest we should show two lines equal to the original two on a *different* line and thereby deceive the reader by misusing the Proposition. 

<margin>The second [condition].</margin> Secondly, that one straight line exists; he does not say simply to construct "two equal to two" upon it (for this can happen), but "**one to the other**" <note>This means each new line must specifically match the length of the one it corresponds to, rather than just the sum of the two being equal.</note>. For what wonder is it that someone might take both as equal to both in a simple sense, if he stretches out one of the lines being constructed while contracting the other? But he says that matching them "one to the other" is impossible. 

<margin>The third [condition].</margin> Thirdly, he adds the phrase [**at a different point**]; for what if someone, when he had made two other lines equal (each to each) to the first two, had fitted these to the originals at the *same* point which joins the underlying straight lines at the vertex, and had constructed them there? For entirely, when the straight lines are equal, their endpoints will also coincide.

<summary>This page presents Euclid's Proposition 7, which proves that a triangle's vertex is uniquely determined by the lengths of its sides on a given base. The commentary explains that while science usually prefers positive proofs, this negative proof is made "indubitable" through its precise qualifying language.</summary>

**If two triangles have two sides equal to two sides, each to each, and also have the base equal to the base: they will also have the angle equal to the angle that is contained by the equal straight lines.**

<margin>Proposition 8. Theorem 5.</margin>

***

The eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth <note>Proposition 4 is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem.</note>, though it is not taken according to the primary form of conversion <margin>Commentary 12.</margin>. For it does not make the entirety of that theorem's hypothesis the conclusion, nor the entire conclusion the hypothesis. Rather, by weaving together some part of the hypothesis of the fourth theorem with some part of the things sought in that one, it demonstrates one of those things that were given there. 

For this fact—that two sides are equal to two sides—is the hypothesis in both cases. However, this fact—that the base is equal to the base—was one of the things sought in the former [Prop. 4], but in this one [Prop. 8] it is given; and this fact—that the angle is equal to the angle—was given in the former, but is the thing being sought in this one. Therefore, it is only the exchange of things given and things sought that effects this "conversion." 

If anyone should desire to learn the reason why the eighth is placed in this order, <margin>Question</margin> and not immediately after the fourth as its converse—just as the sixth follows the fifth, since it is the converse of the fifth (indeed, many things that are converted follow their precedents and are shown after them with no intermediary)—it must be said that the eighth required the seventh theorem for its proof. <margin>Response.</margin> For it is shown by a reduction to the impossible <note>original: "Deductionem ad impossibile"; a logical method where a statement is proved by showing that its opposite leads to a contradiction.</note>, and that such a thing is impossible is made known by the seventh theorem. 

This seventh theorem, in turn, required the fifth in its own demonstration. Therefore, it was necessary for the seventh and the fifth to be assumed before this theorem which is now being shown. But because the converse of the fifth [Prop. 6] also had an easy demonstration from first principles, it was rightly placed immediately after the fifth because of the kinship it has with it. Furthermore, since Proposition 6 is shown by a reduction to the impossible, it refutes the impossible based on common notions <note>original: "communibus notionibus"; fundamental axioms or self-evident truths that everyone agrees on.</note>, and not (as the eighth does) based on another theorem. For those things which oppose common notions are more evident for the purpose of refutation than those which merely contradict previous theorems. For these...

The poles of the Equator are at a specific distance from the poles of the Zodiac <note>original: *Signiferi*; literally "the sign-bearer," referring to the belt of the heavens containing the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>. Indeed, they are distant from each other by the side of a fifteen-sided figure <note>The angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic was historically estimated using a quindecagon, or 15-sided polygon, inscribed in a circle</note>. Therefore, the teacher of the Elements [Euclid], looking also toward Astronomy, seems to show many things in advance, preparing us for that science as well. <margin>A doubt</margin>
Let these things be said regarding this question. But if anyone should doubt for what reason he did not add as many things in the eighth as he did in the fourth Theorem—

<margin>The solution.</margin>
namely, that the triangles and the remaining angles are equal—we will say that once the angle at the vertex <note>original: *verticali Angulo*</note> was demonstrated to be equal, it followed through the fourth Theorem <note>Euclid's Theorem 4 is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) congruence rule</note> that everything was equal to everything else. Therefore, it was necessary to demonstrate this one thing alone, and to take all the rest as consequences.

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
It seems, moreover, that the equality of the sides enclosing those angles and the equality of the bases bring about the equality of the vertical angles. For if the bases are unequal, the same angles do not remain, even assuming the enclosing sides are equal; rather, while the base becomes smaller, the angle is simultaneously diminished, and while it grows, the angle also grows along with it. Nor does the angle remain the same if the bases stay the same but the sides become unequal; rather, while they are shortened, the angle is increased, and while they are lengthened, it is diminished. For the angle and the sides enclosing it undergo an opposite "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to a property or an effect experienced by a geometric shape</note>. For if you imagine the sides on the same base descending to a lower part, you indeed shorten them, but you increase the angle enclosed by them and create a greater distance between them. But if they are carried upwards and receive an addition, you diminish the angle they contain. For they meet further away, since their vertex is made more remote from the base. It is certain to say, therefore, that both the base being the same and the sides being equal determine the equality of the angle itself.

...considering these things themselves. Since, therefore, he [Euclid] showed in the preceding sections that in a single triangle the equality of the sides follows from the equality of the angles, and vice versa; and similarly in two triangles—except that the mode of conversion <note>In logic and geometry, "conversion" refers to the process of swapping the hypothesis and the conclusion of a theorem.</note> was different in one and in two triangles—he now moves on to problems, and commands us to bisect a given rectilinear angle. Furthermore, the ratio of the division was specified for us, and this again not without reason; for to divide into any ratio whatsoever exceeds the present construction—for example, to divide into three, four, or five equal parts. For it is indeed possible to trisect <note>original: "trifariam secare"</note> a right angle by using a few of those principles to be handed down later; but it is impossible to trisect an acute angle without transcending to other lines of a "mixed species" <note>This refers to curves more complex than simple straight lines and circles, which are the only tools allowed in "elementary" Euclidean geometry.</note>. 

<margin>Regarding this, see Witelo <note>A 13th-century friar and physicist known for his work on optics.</note> in Proposition 28 of the first book.</margin>

This is demonstrated by those who proposed the problem in this way: "To trisect a given rectilinear angle." For Nicomedes, being the inventor of the property of the Conchoid lines <note>The Conchoid of Nicomedes is a curve used to solve the problem of angle trisection, which cannot be solved with only a compass and straightedge.</note>—of which he handed down the origin, order, and characteristics <note>original: "Symptomata"; in Greek mathematics, this refers to the defining properties of a curve.</note>—trisected every rectilinear angle using them. 

<margin>Nicomedes was the inventor of the property of the Conchoid lines.</margin>

Others did the same using the "quadratrix" <note>original: "quadrantibus Lineis"; referring to the curve of Hippias, one of the oldest known curves used for squaring the circle and trisecting angles.</note> of Hippias and Nicomedes, these too using "mixed" quadrant lines. Others, inspired by the spirals of Archimedes, divided a given rectilinear angle into a given ratio. Since their considerations are difficult for those being instructed to contemplate, we omit them for the present. 

<margin>In Proposition 30 of the third book of the Elements.</margin>

...provoked by this problem, they might think that it is taken as an assumed starting point <note>original: "Suppositio," referring to a mathematical postulate</note> among geometers that a line does not consist of **indivisible parts**. For if it consists of indivisibles, it must be composed of either an odd or an even number of them to be finite and complete. But if it consists of an odd number, an "indivisible" would also seem to be cut when the straight line is divided in two; for if one part consists of more indivisible units, the remaining part would be larger. Therefore, it is impossible for a given straight line to be cut exactly in half if <term>Magnitude</term> <note>In Greek geometry, "magnitude" refers to continuous quantities like lines, surfaces, and solids, as opposed to discrete numbers.</note> consists of indivisible atoms. If, however, it does not consist of indivisibles, it is divided to infinity. And so it seems (as they say) that this is accepted by the common consensus of all, and that it is a geometric principle that Magnitude belongs to the class of things that are divided to infinity. <margin>Note 1: The solution according to the opinion of Geminus.</margin>

But we shall say against these arguments what Geminus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician from the 1st century BCE.</note> says: that geometers assume as a <term>Common Notion</term> <note>An "axiom" or self-evident truth that requires no proof.</note> that a **continuum** is divisible. <margin>Note 2: See Aristotle in the treatise *On Indivisible Lines*.</margin> For we call that a "continuum" which consists of joined parts, and it is entirely possible for this to be divided. However, they did not merely presume that the continuum is also divided *to infinity*; rather, they demonstrate this from their own principles. For when they show that <term>incommensurability</term> <note>The discovery that certain lengths, such as the diagonal of a square compared to its side, cannot be measured by any common unit, no matter how small. This implies that lines cannot be made of tiny "bricks" or atoms.</note> exists in Magnitudes, and that not all things are commensurable with one another, what else would one say they are showing except that every Magnitude is divided into things that are always further divisible? We will never arrive at an indivisible part, since even the smallest common measure would still be a Magnitude. This [infinite divisibility], therefore, is a thing to be demonstrated, while the former is an axiom: namely, that every continuum is divisible. 

Therefore, since a finite line is also continuous, it is divisible. And based on this notion, the author of the *Elements* <note>Euclid, the father of geometry.</note> cuts a finite straight line into two equal parts, but not because he is assuming it is infinitely divisible. For it is not the same thing for something to be "divisible" as it is for it to be "infinitely divisible." <margin>Note 3: Here the opinion of Xenocrates regarding indivisible lines is refuted. See Aristotle in the treatise *On Indivisible Lines*.</margin> Moreover, the argument of Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato who argued that there must be "indivisible lines" to avoid the paradoxes of the infinite.</note> introducing "indivisible lines" would be refuted by this very problem. For if a line exists at all, it is either **Straight**, and it can be cut in two; or **Circular**, and it is larger than a certain straight line (since every circular line certainly has a chord that is a smaller straight line); or **Mixed**, and this is all the more divisible since it consists of simple, divisible components. 

But truly, let these matters be deferred to another investigation. The geometer cuts a finite straight line in two, using the first and ninth [propositions] in the **Construction**; but in the **Demonstration**, he uses the fourth alone. For he shows the bases to be equal by means of the angles. <margin>Note 4: The Demonstration of Apollonius of Perge.</margin> And Apollonius of Perge <note>A great geometer famous for his work on conic sections.</note> cuts a given finite straight line in two in this manner. ### On the Divine Nature and Attributes

It is necessary to consider the distinction between the **Absolute** and the **Relative** in our understanding of the Divine. For as we have established in the preceding sections, the essence of the First Cause is not subject to the limitations of time or material composition.

<margin>The distinction of the Schools</margin>
The <term>Schoolmen</term> <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who used a specific dialectical method of learning</note> often argue that while we can know *that* God is, we cannot fully comprehend *what* He is in His infinite majesty. This is because the finite mind cannot contain the infinite.

<column-break/>

#### Of the Divine Will

The Will of God is not like the human will, which is often moved by passion or external necessity. Rather, it is:
1. **Perfectly Free** — acting without any external compulsion.
2. **Immutable** — unchanging in its purpose from eternity.
3. **Sovereign** — over all things visible and invisible.

<margin>See also: *Metaphysics*, Book IV</margin>
As the philosopher states, <note>original: "Primum Movens Immobile"</note> the "First Unmoved Mover" initiates all motion without being moved Himself. This aligns with our understanding of the <insert>Divine Providence</insert> which governs the universe with a steady hand.

<gloss>The Greek term *Logos* here implies both Reason and Word.</gloss>

We must also address the objection that if God's will is unchanging, then prayer is ineffectual. To this, we respond that prayer is itself a part of the divine order, a means by which the creature aligns their own will with the <unclear>Eternal Decree</unclear>.

For let there be a straight line **a b**, and a given point **a** on it, and let any point be taken on the straight line **a b**, and let it be **c**. From this point (just as the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard textbook for geometry in the Renaissance.</note> taught us), let a straight line be raised at right angles to **a b**, and let it be **c e**. From this **c e**, let **d c** be cut off equal to **a c**. Let the angle at point **c** be cut in half <note>Bisected.</note> by the line **c f**. From point **d**, a line raised at right angles to **e c** should meet the straight line **f c** at point **f**, and from point **f**, let it be connected to point **a** as **f a**. I say that the angle which is at point **a** is a right angle. For since **d c** is equal to **c a**, and **c f** is common to both, they contain equal angles (since the angle at point **c** was cut in half). Therefore, **d f** is equal to **f a**, and everything is similarly equal to everything else (through the fourth <note>Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 4, which proves triangle congruence by Side-Angle-Side.</note>). Because of this, the angle at point **a** is also equal to the angle at point **d**. However, the angle at point **d** is a right angle; therefore, the angle at point **a** is also a right angle. Thus, what was sought has been shown. The author of the *Elements* <note>original: "Elementorum institor", referring to Euclid.</note> has no need of this device, for he commanded a line to be raised to right angles <note>In the plural, meaning it creates two right angles with the base line.</note>, not just to one right angle. It is worthwhile, therefore, not to take the point at the very end of the straight line, so that the straight line which is raised makes angles with the subject straight line, rather than just one angle. 

But Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – c. 190 BC), a Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections.</note> raises a line at right angles in this way. <margin>Apollonius’s Demonstration</margin>
Let there be (he says) a given straight line **a b**, and a given point **c** on it. Let any point be taken on **a c**, and let it be **d**. From **c b**, let a segment equal to **c d** be taken away, which shall be **c e**. With center **d** and distance **d e**, let a circle be described; and again, with center **e** and distance **e d**, let a circle be marked out. Let a straight line be drawn from point **f** to point **c**. I say that this is the line which has been raised at right angles. For if **f d** and **f e** are connected, they will be equal. Moreover, **d c** and **c e** are equal, and **f c** is common. For this reason, the angles at point **c** are equal (through the eighth <note>Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 8, which proves triangle congruence by Side-Side-Side.</note>). <margin>He commends Euclid’s Demonstration.</margin> Therefore, they are right angles. Do you see again that...

For the reason that the straight line, to which the perpendicular will be drawn, was given as infinite. However, how the Infinite can subsist is worthy of contemplation. <margin>Digression</margin> It is manifest that if an infinite straight line exists, the Plane will also be infinite, and this would be in actuality if what was proposed by Euclid is true. Therefore, both the divine Aristotle and those who received philosophy from him show abundantly that among sensible <note>Things perceivable by the senses, or physical objects.</note> things, no Magnitude exists as infinite according to any distance. <margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 3, in the chapter on the infinite.</margin> For neither that which moves Circularly, nor any other of the simple bodies can be infinite, since the place of each one is limited. It remains, therefore, that the Infinite subsists only in the **Imagination** <term>Phantasia; the mental faculty that creates images, acting as a bridge between the physical senses and pure logical thought</term>, though the Imagination does not "understand" the Infinite. <margin>The Infinite subsists in the Imagination.</margin> For it simultaneously understands, and imposes Form and Limit upon that which is understood, and by the act of understanding, it halts the transition of the phantom <note>The "phantom" or *phantasma* is the mental image being processed.</note>, runs through it, and embraces it. Therefore, the Infinite does not exist by the Imagination understanding it, but rather by the Imagination progressing infinitely around that which is understood, but not understanding it; and whatever it leaves as innumerable and incomprehensible to the understanding, this it calls infinite. <margin>A most beautiful example.</margin> For just as Sight knows darkness by *not* seeing, so the **Imagination** perceives the Infinite by *not* understanding. It produces it because it possesses an impartible power which can progress continually; <margin>The Imagination has an impartible power. The same is found in Book 2, Commentary 1.</margin> but it understands it as something subsisting, because it does not understand the Infinite. For that which it leaves behind as something that cannot be traversed, this it calls the Infinite. For this reason, since we have placed a given infinite Line in the Imagination—just as indeed we have placed all other Geometrical species, namely Triangles, Circles, Angles, Lines, and all things of this sort—we will not wonder how the line is infinite in actuality, and how, progressing itself into infinity, it applies itself to finite understandings. But **Thought** <term>Cogitatio; here referring to *Dianoia*, or discursive mathematical reasoning</term>, in which there are reasons and Demonstrations, does not use the Infinite for the sake of science (since the Infinite is not perceivable by science at all), but taking it from a supposition, it uses the Finite alone for Demonstration; and it assumes the Infinite not for the sake of the Infinite, but for the sake of the Finite. Because if you grant to it that a given point lies neither in a straight line with a given finite straight Line, nor is so distant from it that no part of it is placed under the Point, it will need nothing more from the Infinite. Therefore, so that Thought may use the finite straight Line without blame or controversy, it supposes the Infinite to exist, since it [the Infinite] [is] of the Imagination...

Again, since segment *f h* is equal to *h b*, and the connected line *c h* is common to both, and the base *c f* is equal to the base *c b* (for they both originate from the center), the angles at point *h* are therefore right angles; for they are equal and adjacent. Since, therefore, both angles *c f h* and *c h f* are right angles, the side *c f* is equal to *c h*. But *c f* is equal to *c e*, for they both originate from the center; and therefore *c h* is not unequal to *c e*, which is quite impossible. <note>This is a proof by contradiction: the author is showing that if certain assumptions were true, they would lead to a logical impossibility where a part of a line is equal to the whole.</note>

It remains now to examine the Third Instance. For let it be said (as they say) that the circle being described cuts the straight line at points *a* and *b*, and also at points *f* and *h*. Thus, by bisecting the straight line *a b* at point *k* and connecting the lines *c a*, *c f*, *c k*, and *c b*, we shall demonstrate that which is impossible. For since *a k* and *k b* are equal, and *c k* is common to both, and the bases *c a* and *c b* are equal, the angles at points *a* and *b* are equal, while those at point *k* are right angles.

<margin>How a <term>Case</term> <note>Latin: *Casus*</note> differs from an <term>Instance</term> <note>Latin: *Instantia*</note>. On this, see also the first commentary of this book above.</margin>

But both <note>lines *c a* and *c b*</note> are equal to *c f*. Therefore, the angles at point *f* are right angles, for they are adjacent and equal. Thus, *c f* itself is equal to *c k*, for they subtend right angles. Yet *c f* is equal to *c d*, since they both originate from the center; therefore, *c d* is equal to *c k*, which is impossible. <note>In this geometric construction, *c d* represents the full radius, while *c k* is only a portion of it; they cannot be equal.</note> Therefore, it is impossible for the circle being described to cut the straight line *a b* at one point, or two, or several other points besides points *a* and *b*. These, then, are the instances.

There are also <term>Cases</term> <note>The author distinguishes between a "case," which is a variation of the proof, and an "instance," which is a specific objection or counter-example.</note> of the construction of this problem, which must be distinguished from <term>Instances</term>. For an instance and a case are not the same thing; the latter shows the same result in a different way, whereas the former leads the person raising the objection into an absurdity.

<margin>Cases of this Problem.</margin>

Other commentators, however, do not distinguish these from one another and treat them all as the same; thus, it is uncertain whether they intend to write of cases or instances. We, therefore, distinguishing between them, have chosen to describe the cases separately after the instances. Let there be, then, an infinite straight line *a b* and a given point *c*. Someone might say that there is no more room on the other side of the straight line, but only on the side where point *c* lies.

When a straight Line standing upon a straight Line has made Angles, <margin>Proposition 13. Theorem 6.</margin> it will make either two right angles, or angles equal to two right angles.

The author has returned again to those Theorems <margin>Commentary 17.</margin> which follow from what was shown through Problems <note>In this context, "Problems" refer to geometric constructions (doing something), while "Theorems" refer to the investigation of properties (proving something).</note>. For since a perpendicular line had been drawn at right Angles to a straight Line, it remained to ask: if the line were not perpendicular, what kind of Angles would it make, and how would they relate to the straight Line upon which it stands? This, therefore, he demonstrates universally: that every straight line standing upon another straight line and making angles, either makes two right angles—if its position is upright, firm, and leaning nowhere—or it makes angles equal to two right angles, if it should incline to one side and stand further away from the underlying Line on the other. For however much it takes away from one Right angle by its inclination toward the other side, it adds just as much to the remaining angle by that distance. 

One must also observe the care and diligence the Geometer <note>The "Geometer" refers to Euclid, the author of the Elements.</note> employed in this Proposition. For he did not simply say that every straight line standing on another makes two right angles or their equivalent, but added: *if it should make angles* <note>original: "si Angulos fecerit." Euclid uses the plural "angles" to exclude the case where a line meets another only at its very end.</note>. For what if it stands at the very end of a straight line and makes only one angle? Does it ever happen that this single angle is equal to two right angles? This is certainly impossible. For every <term>rectilinear angle</term> <note>An angle formed by straight lines, as opposed to curved lines.</note> is less than two right angles, just as every solid angle is less than four right angles. You may take an angle that appears to be the most Obtuse <note>An angle greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees.</note> possible, yet you can still increase it, as it has not yet reached the measure of two right angles. 

It is necessary, therefore, for the straight line to stand in such a way that it makes *angles* (plural). This point, as I have said, regards the diligent precision that gives birth to science. But what did he intend by adding the phrase [either two right angles, or equal to two right angles]? <margin>A Point of Doubt</margin> For when it makes two right angles, it surely makes angles equal to two right angles, since right angles are equal to one another. Is it because one description is "common" <note>Applies to many cases.</note> to all equal angles, <margin>The Solution.</margin> while the other is "proper" <note>Specific to a single case.</note> only to right angles? We are accustomed, when dealing with both a specific and a general case...

...is commonly verified, to express each thing by its own property; but when we do not have that, we must be content with a common expression for the explanation of the underlying things. Therefore, this fact—that the <term>angles which are adjacent</term><note>Latin: "angulos qui deinceps sunt." These are angles formed by one line standing on another.</note> are equal to two right angles—is also common to right angles, yet it is not predicated of them alone. However, this—being right angles—exists as a peculiarity of their equality. Therefore, the phrase "to be equal to two right angles" signifies unequal angles; for it is verified in those alone, but in equal angles, not at all. And the <term>Founder of the Elements</term><note>Euclid.</note> also divides this from its opposite by "two right angles." For when it is spoken of by itself, it has the power of signifying unequal angles in both cases. 

<margin>Digression</margin>
We can also perceive through these things that equality is the measure and the limit of inequality. For although the increase and decrease of <term>Obtuse and Acute</term><note>Obtuse angles are greater than 90 degrees; acute angles are less.</note> angles is indeterminate and infinite, it is nevertheless said to receive its limit and end from the Right Angle. Each of them, taken separately, recedes from that Right Angle by a lack of similarity; yet both are brought back to its limit according to a single union. Since they can by no means be made equal to the simplicity of the Right Angle, they receive equality by its being doubled, their example of infinity being the <term>Dyad</term><note>Latin: "Binarius." In Pythagorean philosophy, the number two (the Dyad) represents duality, division, and the beginning of infinity/multiplicity, as opposed to the Unity of the number one.</note>, since it is infinite in itself. 

<margin>The same [is said] above in Book 2, commentary 10, and in other places.</margin>
And this seems to bring forth a clear image of the progression of primary causes, which always consist in the same way around the infinity of generation according to a single limit. For how else could generation, which participates in the "More and Less" and is carried along indefinitely, agree with <term>intelligible things</term><note>Things understood by the mind/intellect rather than the senses.</note> and be in some way made equal to them, unless through participation, while they progress by secondary powers and merely multiply themselves? For those things which remain in their simplicity and indivisibility are entirely separated from things subject to generation. These are the points to be taken from the present Theorem for the knowledge of the universe.

He shows, however, that it is one straight line which creates these [angles] relative to the aforementioned straight line. What was given in that [previous theorem] is sought in this one, and it is shown through a **Reduction to the Impossible** <note>Also known as *reductio ad absurdum*, a proof where you assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show it leads to a logical contradiction.</note> in this manner. For the **Converses of Theorems** <note>A converse flips the 'if' and 'then' parts of a theorem.</note> ought to be demonstrated this way, while in **Problems** they should also receive primary demonstrations. We can also observe in this the precision of a mind producing the highest and most excellent knowledge. 

For **first**, when he had said "if toward any straight line," he adds **[and at a point on it]** <note>original: *ad eiusque Signum*</note>. For what if, with two ends of a straight line existing, one line was drawn from one end and the other from the other, and they made angles equal to two right angles? Could they then be in a straight line? And how could they be, when they are led out from different points <note>original: *Signis*</note> of the straight line? Therefore, he added this too: **[and at a point on it]**, since he wants both to lie at the same point. 

**Secondly**, since it was possible that the lines being drawn were at the same point but not **consecutively** (since we can take infinite straight lines at one point), he added the phrase **[two straight lines consecutively]**. 

**Thirdly**, since this word **[consecutively]** is considered both in the same direction and on both sides: he explained that it is impossible for lines which are consecutively in the same direction to be in a straight line with each other, but he provided us an opportunity for consideration, that straight lines which are consecutive are to be taken in position on both sides <note>meaning on opposite sides of the line</note>. These indeed can be shown to be in a straight line. 

<margin>Converses of theorems must mostly be shown through a reduction to the impossible, whereas problems [are shown] through a primary demonstration; see the reason for this below in the commentary on Proposition 19.</margin>

<margin>First. Second. Third.</margin>

Let there be, at the straight line **a b**, and at its point **b**, two straight lines **b c** and **b d** on the same side. These are therefore consecutive to one another; for there is no other straight line between them. For those things are "next to each other" between which there is nothing similar. For we say these columns are consecutive between which there is no other column; for although the air is entirely in between, nothing of the same kind is in the middle. 

Since, therefore, they lie on the same side, they are not at all in a straight line, even if they make two angles equal to two right angles—namely, the angles that are at <note>original: *† Signum b*</note> the line **a b**. For nothing prevents angle **a b d** from containing one right angle and a third part of a right angle within itself, while angle **a b c** is the two remaining thirds.

...be, let these suffice concerning the Proposition. In the Construction, however, he uses one **Postulate** <term>Postulate: a fundamental assumption in geometry (Latin: Petitio)</term>, specifically the second one, which requests to produce a straight line in a straight line; just as in the Demonstration of the preceding **Theorem**, and two **Common Notions** <term>Common Notion: a self-evident truth or axiom (Latin: Pronuntiatum)</term>—namely, that which says that things equal to the same thing are also equal to each other, and that which says if equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal. For the collection of the impossible <note>This refers to *reductio ad absurdum*, a proof method where an assumption is shown to lead to a logical impossibility.</note>, he uses the Common Notion which states that the **Whole is greater than its part**; for it is also equal when one common Angle is taken away, which cannot happen.

That it is possible, however, for two straight lines lying consecutively at the same straight line and its Point, yet toward the same parts, to make the angles at that one straight line equal to two right angles, we shall show thus, just as **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentaries on Euclid are often cited in Renaissance editions.</note> does. Let there be a certain straight line *a b*, and <margin>Porphyry's Demonstration</margin> any Point *c* on it, and let there be raised at right angles to *a b* the [A geometric diagram showing a right angle dcb on a line ab, with a bisecting line ce, a perpendicular eb, and an extension bf such that eb=bf, with a line cf connecting c and f.] straight line *c d*. Let the angle *d c b* be **bisected** <term>Bisected: cut into two equal parts (Latin: bifariam)</term> by the line *c e*, and from the Point *e* let a perpendicular *e b* be drawn to the line *a b*. Let *e b* itself be extended, and let *b f* be set equal to *e b*, and let *c f* be connected. Therefore, since *e b* is equal to *b f*, and *b c* is common, and they contain equal angles (for they are right angles), the Base *e c* is therefore equal to the Base *c f*. Consequently, all parts are equal to all parts. Therefore, Angle *e c b* is equal to Angle *f c b*. 

But Angle *e c b* is half of a right angle, since the right angle *d c b* was bisected by the line *e c*. Therefore, Angle *f c b* is also half of a right angle. Thus, Angle *d c f* is one right angle and half a right angle <note>In modern terms, 135 degrees.</note>. Moreover, Angle *d c e* is also half a right angle. Therefore, at the straight line *c d* and at its Point *c*, two straight lines *c e* and *c f* are placed consecutively toward the same parts—namely, *c e* and *c f*—making angles equal to two right angles <note>The sum of 45 degrees (dce) and 135 degrees (dcf) equals 180 degrees, or two right angles.</note>.

Lest we should seek after things that cannot happen—namely, the way in which the straight lines *c e* and *c f*, making angles at the straight line *d c* equal to two right angles, are in a straight line with each other—the **Geometer** <note>A traditional title for Euclid.</note> added the specific phrase [**not toward the same parts**]. It is therefore necessary for the straight lines that make the angles to lie on both sides of the straight line...

<margin>Proposition 15. Theorem 8.</margin>

We say that **Angles** that are "adjacent" <note>Latin: "deinceps"; angles positioned side-by-side along a line</note> differ from "vertical" angles <note>Latin: "ad verticem"; also known as "vertically opposite" angles</note>. <margin>Commentary 19.</margin> For the origin of the latter is caused by the intersection of two straight lines, while the former are produced merely by one line being deflected from the other. For if a straight line, remaining unbroken itself but cutting another with its endpoint, should make two angles, we call these **Adjacent Angles**. <margin>What adjacent angles are.</margin> But if two straight lines cut one another, **Vertical Angles** are produced. They are so named because they have their vertices joined at the same **point**. <margin>What vertical angles are.</margin> Their vertices are the points toward which the planes, as they are contracted, produce the angles. Thus, this Theorem shows that when two straight lines cut one another, the vertical angles are equal. It was first discovered (as Eudemus <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a pupil of Aristotle and historian of mathematics</note> says) by **Thales**; <margin>Thales was the first inventor of this Theorem, according to Eudemus. Euclid, however, was the first to demonstrate it.</margin> but it was deemed worthy of a scientific demonstration by the founder of the *Elements* <note>Euclid</note>. However, it is not demonstrated from all primary principles. For the **Construction** itself is lacking in this instance, but the **Demonstration**, which is absolutely necessary to include, depends upon the thirteenth Theorem. It also employs two **Axioms** <note>Latin: "Pronuntiatis"; literally "pronouncements" or "common notions"</note>, one of which is: *Things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other*; and the other: *If equals are taken away from equals, the remainders are equal*. Indeed, Euclid's Theorem is clear. Moreover, another such theorem is the **Converse** of this Theorem. <margin>Converse of this Theorem.</margin> If, at some straight line and at a point on it, two straight lines not taken on the same side make the vertical angles equal, those straight lines will be in a straight line with one another. <margin>Demonstration of the Converse of the present Theorem.</margin> For let there be a certain straight line **a b**, and any point upon it **c**, and at point **c** let two straight lines **c d** and **c e** be taken, not on the same side, making angles **a c d** and **b c e** equal. I say that **c d** and **c e** are in a straight line. For since the straight line **c d** stands upon the straight line **a b**, it makes angles equal to two right angles, namely **d c a** and **d c b**. But angle **d c a** is equal to angle **b c e**. Therefore, angles **d c b** and **b c e** are equal to two right angles.

<margin>Why Euclid omitted this</margin>
Therefore, since at a certain straight line *bc*, and at its point *c*, two straight lines *cd* and *ce* placed one after the other—not on the same side—make adjacent angles <note>Original: *angulos deinceps*. However, it seems the Geometer <note>The "Geometer" refers to Euclid.</note> omitted this because it is easy to show this also by the same path of deduction to the impossible <note>Original: *deductionem ad impossibile*, commonly known as proof by contradiction.</note> by which we showed the fourteenth theorem.

<margin>Another indirect proof of the same.</margin>
With the same things being supposed, I say that the straight line *cd* is in a straight line with the straight line *ce*. For if it is not, let the straight line *cf* be taken in a straight line with *cd*. Since, therefore, the two straight lines *ab* and *df* intersect each other, they make the vertical angles <note>Original: *angulos ad verticem*. These are the opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines.</note> equal. Therefore, angles *acd* and *bcf* are equal. But angles *acd* and *bce* were also equal. Therefore, angle *bce* is equal to angle *bcf*—the greater to the lesser—which is impossible. Therefore, no other straight line except *cd* itself will be in a straight line with *ce*. Thus, the straight lines *cd* and *ce* are themselves in a straight line with each other, assuming the vertical angles are equal. Since, then, the demonstration is the same as that which was assumed in the fourteenth theorem, how would it not be superfluous to provide this converse?

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
For the sake of practice, however, we have proven it both through deduction to the impossible and through a direct method. It seems that this fifteenth theme <note>The 15th Proposition of Euclid’s Elements: "If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another."</note> relies on the similarity of the parts of straight lines and their position at the extremities. For lines situated in this way and intersecting each other must necessarily have similar inclinations toward each other on both sides. Indeed, circumferences <note>Curved lines or arcs of circles.</note>—and generally non-straight lines—intersecting each other do not necessarily make the vertical angles equal, but sometimes they are equal and sometimes unequal. These are crescent-shaped angles formed by the intersection of two arcs.</note> at the vertex; but they do not do so for the remaining ones—namely, the one that is concave on both sides and the one that is convex on both sides—but one is larger. In straight lines, however, the position at the extremities [results in] an equal [division] of the other segments...

<margin>Commentary 26.</margin>

<margin>The double meaning of Corollary; the same is found in the first commentary of this book.</margin>

A "Corollary" is one of the names used in geometry; however, it signifies two different things. For they call Corollaries those theorems that are proven along with the demonstrations of others, like unexpected gains <note>original: "Lucra inexpectata"</note> and profits arising for those who seek them. They are also those things which are sought and require discovery, yet are not sought solely for the sake of construction <note>original: "generationis," referring to the physical drawing or creation of a shape</note>, nor for simple contemplation. For instance, that the angles at the base of an isosceles <term>isosceles: literally "equal-legged" triangle</term> triangle are equal is something one must contemplate; the knowledge of such existing things is of this nature. However, to bisect an angle, or to construct a triangle, or to cut off or place a straight line of equal length—all these demand that something be *done*. But to find the center of a given circle, or to find the greatest common measure <note>The "greatest common divisor" in modern mathematical terms</note> of two given commensurable magnitudes, or anything else of that kind, are in a way between Problems and Theorems. For in these, there is neither the simple origin of things sought, nor sole contemplation, but rather discovery <note>original: "inuentio"</note>. Indeed, there is a need to place the thing sought in view and before the eyes.

<margin>The first of the third [book]. The third of the tenth [book].</margin>

<margin>Euclid constructed books of Corollaries.</margin>

Such, therefore, are the various Corollaries that Euclid wrote, for he indeed constructed books of Corollaries <note>Euclid's lost work, the *Porisms*, was often referred to as "Corollaries" or "Subsidies" in early modern translations</note>. But let us pass over discussing Corollaries of that kind. The Corollaries found in the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements of Geometry*</note> appear simultaneously with the demonstrations of other things; they themselves are not the primary object of the search, such as the one proposed here. For what was being sought was whether, when two straight lines intersect each other, the vertical angles <note>Angles opposite each other at a vertex</note> are equal. While this was being shown, it was simultaneously demonstrated that the four angles which are formed are equal to four right angles. <margin>Definition of a Corollary.</margin>

A **Corollary** <term>Corollarium: From the Latin 'corolla' (a little crown or garland); originally a tip or bonus given to actors, in mathematics it refers to a "bonus" truth that becomes evident while proving something else.</term> is therefore a theorem that emerges unexpectedly from the demonstration of another problem or theorem. For we seem to fall into corollaries as if by chance; they offer themselves to us without us proposing them or even seeking them out.

<margin>See Varro in his book *On the Latin Language*</margin>
For this reason, we have compared these to "bonuses" <note>original: *lucris*, meaning profits or unexpected gains</note>. Perhaps those skilled in mathematical matters gave them this name to show the common people—who rejoice in visible profit—that these are the true gifts of God and true gains, rather than the things they usually value. This faculty within us produces that power, and the fertile force of science adds these to our primary inquiries, manifesting a rich wealth of theorems. Such is the nature of corollaries.

Only these specific shapes, according to the stated numbers, are equal to four right angles. This is the **Pythagorean Theorem**. Furthermore, by this corollary, if more than two straight lines intersect one another at a single point—for example, three, four, or any number—all the angles that are formed are shown to be equal to four right angles; they occupy the space of four right angles. It is also evident that the number of angles will always be double the number of straight lines. Thus, when two straight lines intersect each other, there will be four angles equal to four right angles; with three lines, there are six angles; with four lines, eight, and so on to infinity. For the multitude of straight lines is always doubled to find the number of angles; as the angles increase in number, they decrease in magnitude, because the total being divided—the four right angles—always remains the same.

In every triangle, if one side is extended, the **exterior angle** of the triangle is greater than either of the **interior and opposite** angles. <margin>Proposition 16, Theorem 9</margin>

Those who stated this proposition with a defect—omitting the phrase "**if one side is extended**"—perhaps provided an opening for many others to criticize, and especially for Philip <note>original: "Philippo"; likely Philip of Opus, a 4th-century BCE mathematician and student of Plato</note> (as Heron the Mechanician reports). <margin>Commentary 21</margin> <margin>The criticism of Philip the Mathematician as reported by Heron</margin> For a triangle does not possess an exterior angle simply by being a triangle <note>An exterior angle only exists if a line is drawn out beyond the shape's boundary</note>. What, then, does the proposition say? That if you extend any one of the sides of a triangle, you will find that the angle formed outside the triangle is greater than either of the internal angles lying opposite it. <margin>This is the second case.</margin>

Again, since line **a b** is equal to line **a d**, Angle **a b d** is equal to Angle **a d b**. However, Angle **a b c** was equal to Angle **a c b**. Therefore, Angle **a c b** is equal to Angle **a d b**—the external angle being equal to the internal and opposite angle—which is impossible. <note>The author is referencing a fundamental geometric principle: in a triangle, an exterior angle must always be greater than either of the opposite interior angles.</note> Therefore, from the same point to the same straight line, three equal straight lines can by no means be drawn. Through this theorem, we shall also demonstrate that if a straight line falling upon two straight lines makes the external angle equal to the internal and opposite angle, those straight lines will not form a triangle, nor will they meet <note>The original Latin *coincident* means to fall together or intersect at a point.</note>, because the same angle would be both larger and equal, which is impossible. 

For example, let **a b** and **c d** be straight lines, and let the straight line **e b** falling upon them make the angles **a b d** and **c d e** equal; these straight lines **a b** and **c d** will not meet further on. For if they were to meet while the angles remained equal, Angle **c d e** would be equal to Angle **a b d**. And since it would be an external angle, it would be greater than the internal and opposite angle. It is therefore necessary that if they meet, the angles can no longer remain equal, but the angle at point **d** must increase entirely. 

<margin>Another Corollary</margin>

For whether you imagine **a b** remaining immobile and **c d** moving toward it so that they meet, you will create a greater distance in Angle **c d e**. For the more **c d** approaches **a b**, the more it recedes from line **d e**. Or even if **c d** remains fixed and you imagine **a b** moving toward it, you will make Angle **a b d** smaller. For it is moved toward **c d** and **b d** simultaneously. Or if you make both move toward each other—**a b** tending toward **c d** and contracting Angle **a b e**, while you find **c d** receding from **d e** because of the movement toward line **a b** and Angle **c d e** increasing. 

<margin>† One line tending toward those parts where it diminishes the internal angle; the other moving away from those parts in which it creates the external angle.</margin>

Necessarily, therefore, if there is a triangle and the straight lines **a b** and **c d** meet, the external angle will also be greater than the internal and opposite angle. For either the internal angle stays the same while the external increases, or the external remains while the internal diminishes, or the internal is contracted and the external is further drawn apart. The cause of these things is the motion of the straight lines, † one indeed tending toward those parts where it diminishes the internal angle, and the other toward those where it increases the external. And from this it is clear to you...

**In any triangle, any two angles, taken in any way, are less than two right angles.**

<margin>Proposition 17</margin>
<margin>Theorem 10</margin>
<margin>Commentary 22</margin>
<margin>On Proposition 32</margin>
<margin>Instruction</margin>

Now, indeed, it is shown in an indeterminate way that any two angles of a triangle are less than two right angles; however, in what follows, it will also be determined exactly how much less they are—namely, by the amount of the remaining angle of the triangle. For the three angles of the triangle itself are equal to two right angles. Therefore, any two angles are less than two right angles by the amount of the remaining angle. 

The demonstration provided by the founder of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid, the author of the foundational geometry textbook</note> follows a clear path, since it makes use of the preceding theorem <note>Proposition 16, which concerns exterior angles</note>. It is worthwhile, however (as in the preceding case), for one who observes the origin of triangles to find the cause of the present <term>characteristic<gloss>symptoma; a mathematical property or attribute</gloss></term>. 

Let there be, again, straight lines **ab** and **cd**, which are at right angles to the line **bd**. Therefore, if a triangle is to be formed, it is necessary that the straight lines **ab** and **cd** lean toward each other <term>incline<gloss>annuere; literally "to nod" or "lean toward"</gloss></term>. This leaning <note>original: "nutus"</note> diminishes the interior angles, which is why they become less than two right angles. For they were right angles before the leaning began. 

Likewise, if we also imagine straight lines standing at right angles on the side **ab**, the same result will occur according to the leaning of the straight lines; and the angles at points **a** and **b** will be less than two right angles. The same applies to the remaining side in the same manner. This, then, is the true cause, and not simply that the exterior angle is greater than either of the opposite interior angles. For it is not actually necessary for a side to be extended, nor for an angle to be formed on the outside, to create a triangle. However, it *is* necessary that any two of the interior angles be less than two right angles. How can that which is not necessary <note>the exterior angle extension</note> be the cause of something that is necessary? Certainly in no way. Rather (as I have already said), the cause is indeed what was stated: namely, the leaning of the straight lines...
