Let there be a triangle $abc$, and let any point $d$ be taken on the side $bc$, and let $ad$ be joined. Therefore, since one side of triangle $abd$ has been extended, namely $bd$, the external angle $adc$ is greater than the internal angle $abd$. Again, since one side of triangle $adc$ has been extended, namely $cd$, the external angle $adb$ is greater than the internal angle $acd$. However, the angles that are around the straight line $ad$ are equal to two right angles, according to the thirteenth [proposition]. <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book I, Proposition 13, which states that angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.</note> Therefore, the angles $abc$ and $acb$ are less than two right angles. 

We shall show in a similar way that the angles $bac$ and $bca$ are also less than two right angles by taking a point on the side $ac$ and connecting point $b$ to that chosen point; and again, we shall affirm that the angles $cab$ and $abc$ are less than two right angles by taking a point on the side $ab$ and connecting a straight line from point $c$ to that chosen point. Thus, the proposition is demonstrated through the same theorem with no side of the triangle being extended. 

It is therefore possible that through this, it may also be shown <margin>Corollary as an assumption.</margin> that from the same point to a single straight line, two perpendicular <term>perpendiculars: lines meeting at a 90-degree angle</term> lines cannot be drawn. For instance, let there be two perpendiculars $ab$ and $ac$ from point $a$ to the straight line $bc$. Therefore, the angles $abc$ and $acb$ are right angles. But since $abc$ itself is a triangle, any two of its angles are less than two right angles. Therefore, angles $abc$ and $acb$ are less than two right angles. Yet they are also equal to two right angles because they are perpendiculars, which is impossible. Therefore, from the same point to the same straight line, two perpendiculars shall not be drawn.

->### THIRD BOOK 181<-

...the Geometer, when in the construction of Triangle **a b c** he had assumed Side **a c** to be greater than Side **a b**, in order to show that the angle at Point **b** is greater than the angle at Point **c**, he cut off <note>The Latin *abscidit* refers to the geometric operation of marking a segment of a specific length on a longer line.</note> a straight line **a d** from Side **a c** equal to Side **a b**. However, should someone say that the subtraction of **a d** <note>The text likely means the point **d** should be taken from point **c** rather than **a**.</note> ought to be made from Point **c**, come, let us show the proposition even under this supposition, just as **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neopythagorean philosopher and logic scholar who wrote commentaries on Euclid’s *Elements*.</note> did. 

<margin>Porphyry’s Demonstration</margin>
For let **d c** be equal to **a b** itself, and let **a b** be extended to Point **e**, and let **b e** be placed equal to **d a**. Therefore, the whole line **a e** is equal to the whole line **a c**. Let **e c** be connected. Since, therefore, **a e** is equal to **a c**, the angle **a e c** is also equal to the angle **a c e**, by the **fifth proposition** <note>original: "per quintum". This refers to Euclid’s Elements Book I, Proposition 5: the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>. Therefore, angle **a e c** is greater than angle **a c b**. Moreover, angle **a b c** is also greater than angle **a e c**. For in the Triangle **c b e**, one side was extended, namely **b e**, and thus since angle **a b c** is an external angle, it is greater than the internal angle lying opposite it. Therefore, angle **a b c** is much greater than angle **a c b**, which was what was to be demonstrated. 

<margin>Instruction</margin>
The geometric demonstrations of the present Theorem are of this kind. It is manifest, however, that the cause of this <term>property</term> <note>original: "Symptomatis". In early scientific Latin, a *symptoma* was a "falling together" or a characteristic property of a figure, rather than a medical symptom.</note> is the amplification or diminution of the Side <term>subtending</term> <note>To "subtend" means to be opposite to an angle in a geometric figure.</note> the Angle according to its magnitude. For indeed, being larger, it amplifies the angle more; becoming smaller, however, it simultaneously diminishes it and contracts it more. Moreover, this happens because of the position of the straight line at its extremities; for being placed at its own extremities, it changes the magnitudes of the angles according to its own increase and decrease. 

And we say these things in the case of a single Triangle, since it is possible for the same angle to be subtended by a larger and smaller straight line: and for the same straight line to subtend a larger and a smaller angle. For let there be, perhaps, an <term>isosceles</term> <note>original: "æquicrus", literally "equal-legged".</note> triangle **a b c**, and let Point **d** be taken on side **a b**, and let a segment equal to **a d** be taken from **a c**, and let **d e** be connected. Therefore, lines **d e** and **b c** subtend the angle which is at Point **a**, of which one is indeed larger, while the other is smaller. And in the same way, infinite...

[The page contains two geometric diagrams. The first shows a triangle **abc** with a point **d** on side **ac**. The second shows a triangle **abc** with side **ab** extended to point **e**, and a line segment **ec** drawn.]

**TO THE READER, ON THE BENEFIT**
**to be gained from Proclus.**

Reader, if you desire now to know the full scope of Mathematics,
   Learn the way to be not merely a Geometer.

He treats everything in summary: either the Doctrines
   Which the Great Plato wrote, or those of Aristotle.
Being full of light, he dispels the dark shadows of both,

Believe me, for many years the good Publisher <note>original: "Bibliopola"; in the Renaissance, the bookseller and publisher were often the same person.</note>

   What of his own name, *Proclus*? It is nothing other than what I think:

->TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS DANIELE BARBARO,<-
->DESIGNATED PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA,<-
->FRANCESCO BAROZZI<-
->SENDS HIS FONDEST GREETINGS.<-

[Floral ornament]

**L**OVE <note>The author uses the Neoplatonic concept of Love as a cosmic force that binds the universe together, rather than just a human emotion.</note>, the oldest and yet the newest of the Gods, the author and preserver of all things, was not without reason—most worthy Patriarch—called so by the wisest philosophers, as I believe. For since Love is a certain divine thing, and flows from divine causes, it is not undeservedly that philosophers and poets have fashioned him as a God, and indeed one born of the Gods. They assert he is the **oldest** of the other Gods because he took his origin then, when the Supreme Good—which is that first father of the universe and author, God—created the triple World out of a certain formless essence (which the ancients called Chaos), through the turning of that essence back toward its own beginning from which it arose: first, indeed, the **Angelic mind**; then the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Mundi... animam." This refers to the *Anima Mundi*, a concept where the entire universe is treated as a living, breathing entity.</note> which we perceive; and lastly the body of that same soul, which consists of the heavens, the elements, and mixed things. All of these, according to the likeness of their **Ideas** <note>technical term: "Idearum." Barozzi refers to Platonic Ideas—the perfect, eternal patterns in the mind of God upon which all physical things are modeled.</note> that shine forth in the divine mind, are called Gods, such as Coelus, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Apollo, Venus, Mercury, Diana, Vulcan, Juno, Neptune, Pluto, and others.

But he is called the **newest** because Love is twofold: one, by which God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." or *Optimus Maximus*, a title originally for Jupiter, here applied to the Christian God.</note>, loving the perfection of things, brought all things forth; the other, by which all lower things—having arisen as if from a certain footprint and divine seed—follow their recognized parent and desire to enjoy the goal of their own perfection. The former is indeed older than all things, while the latter is younger. Thus, philosophers of ancient authority and divine men have not hesitated to call him the beginning and the end of things: the first and the newest of the Gods.

Furthermore, they have called him the **author** and **preserver** of all things, not without justice in my opinion. For Love—which for this reason is commonly defined by all philosophers as the "desire to enjoy beauty"—because it is his nature to seize toward beauty and to join the deformed with the beautiful, is truly seen to stretch through all things that exist. For (to embrace the matter in few words), all things that have been brought forth by the **First Cause** <note>A philosophical term for God as the initial creator of everything.</note> in the nature of things have been assigned an order and relation among themselves: either of superiors, inferiors, or equals. If they are superior, they are the causes of the inferior; if inferior, they are the works of the superior; if equal, they enjoy the same nature. And if indeed they are causes, they love their own works, and the highest...

<summary>This page features a formal dedication from the mathematician Francesco Barozzi to the scholar-prelate Daniele Barbaro, utilizing Neoplatonic philosophy to define 'Love' as the primary cosmic force that created and sustains the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Francesco Barozzi, Daniele Barbaro, Neoplatonism, Anima Mundi, Chaos, Platonic Ideas, Cosmology, Renaissance philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 208 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the nature of Love as a cosmic force. The previous page likely established the relationship between beauty and the desire for perfection.</meta>

...they desire their supreme beauty and supreme perfection. If, however, works seek to enjoy the beauty and perfection of their causes; and if they are endowed with the same nature, then, as similar parts of the Whole, they are mutually moved by Love, so that together all may fully enjoy the perfect beauty of the Whole. Since this is the case, it is evident from every perspective that Love exists in all things and penetrates through all things. Nothing can be found that pursues another with hatred, except by accident <note>original: *per accidens*; in philosophical terms, this means something happening incidentally rather than by the essential nature of the thing</note>. For a thing does not hate or flee its opposite by its own nature, but by accident, and out of Love for itself, lest it be destroyed by that opposite. Since, therefore, Love is implanted and innate in all things, both divine and human, who could doubt—if it were shown that the actions of all things happen for the sake of Love, and that the works resulting from those actions are preserved by Love—that Love is the creator and preserver of all? Indeed, the desire to propagate the inherent perfection of each thing is the greatest Love.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;God, in whose immense power alone absolute perfection is found, produced all things for the sake of propagating His perfection, and He likewise granted to all things the desire for propagation. These things have been so allotted that whatever happens in the World seems to happen for the sake of Love. Furthermore, the union of parts preserves the Whole, while division destroys and scatters it. Love has the power to bring about this union. Therefore, Love not only creates all things but also preserves them. For this reason, it is rightly called the author and preserver of all. But if Love has the power to create and preserve all things, it is clear enough to anyone—more than clear, in fact—that it is also the author and guardian of the sciences <note>In this context, *scientiarum* refers to all structured knowledge or branches of learning</note>. For (if we are to believe Aristotle) the same ideas and the same sciences often appear and vanish among men according to certain ordered cycles of the Universe. And as it pleased other great philosophers to believe, all sciences and arts, all human inventions, and finally all things—both those produced by Nature and those devised and discovered by men across the whole world—flourished for infinite ages, only to perish and fall away in turn due to infinite fires and floods. In the same way, they will flourish and perish again. Since this is indeed how things are,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Love was needed for the restoration <note>original: *redintegrationem*; the act of making something whole again or renewing it</note> and preservation of all things, especially the sciences. For after the Deucalionean rains <note>A reference to the great flood in Greek mythology; Deucalion was the son of Prometheus who survived the deluge sent by Zeus</note>, due to the excessive abundance of water, not only did cities, buildings, and living creatures of every kind perish (except those which divine providence guarded), but also all memory of things contained in books was so extinguished that those first humans, who sprang from the few who remained, lived as if they were brand new and unskilled in all matters. They led a simple, pure life, free from all malice and craftiness—the kind of life that poets call the *golden age*. In this golden age, those unrefined people were guided first by that Love with which God pursues the World, and then by the natural human desire for knowledge...

<summary>The author argues that Love is the universal force of creation and preservation, acting as the catalyst for the restoration of human knowledge and "sciences" following cyclical global catastrophes like the Great Flood.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmic Love, Universal Cycles, Aristotle, Deucalion's Flood, Golden Age, Restoration of Knowledge, Divine Providence</keywords>

--- Page 209 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the historical development and recovery of scientific knowledge, likely following a description of a period of intellectual decline or the initial curiosity of early thinkers.</meta>

...aroused by desire, they began to wonder and be amazed, and finally to contemplate the entire **machine of the world** <note>original: *Mundi machinam*; a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, orderly system</note>, its movements, and the various effects of those movements, as well as to investigate the cause of now this thing, now that. It so happened that all the sciences again took their start from a seemingly small beginning; from there they gathered strength daily, and gradually raised themselves to the height of their perfection. 

But afterwards, both due to the **revolution of the whole world** <note>original: *Mundi totius reuolutionem*; likely referring to the cyclical nature of history or the passage of great ages</note> and due to the many and varied wars that followed throughout the universe, by which all the provinces had been devastated, many excellent works of ancient authors in every branch of knowledge perished utterly. Many others emerged into the light obscured and corrupted. Indeed, lest these—or at least the teachings contained within them—be completely torn away from the human race, such that barely a shadow of them might ever reach us, a love seized many people to both find those teachings again by their own efforts, and... <meta>The text ends mid-sentence at "ha," likely the beginning of "habendi" (holding/having) or "hanc" (this).</meta>

...which were just as if they had never been published. However, since divine providence—for the common benefit of all students—had decreed to aid this burning desire of mine through its greatest Love, it brought it about that while I was on the Island of Crete three years ago, a certain very ancient copy of those same commentaries of Proclus on Euclid (which had already been printed) came into my hands. This copy had belonged to Andrea Doni, my teacher, a man truly the most outstanding in Greek literature among all the Greeks of his age. From this copy, I diligently corrected the printed version as much as I could, for even that ancient manuscript was imperfect in several places. 

Afterward, when I had returned to Italy and recognized the profound teaching and utility of these commentaries, I burned daily with a greater and unquenchable desire and Love to restore them. Therefore, to satisfy this desire of mine, I first traveled to Bologna, where I found two handwritten copies. One was in the library of Saint Salvatore <note>The library of the San Salvatore monastery in Bologna was famous for its collection of Greek manuscripts.</note>, as they call it, which I was permitted to transcribe along with other small books by the Reverend men Floriano Cedroplano of Bologna, then the Prior of that monastery, and Raphael Campiono, the Procurator. These men, moved by nothing other than kindness and a certain Love toward me, bestowed the greatest favors upon me. The other copy was in the library of the most excellent man Fabrizio Garzoni, who publicly professes the faculty of medicine at the University of Bologna <note>original: "Bononiensi Gymnasio"</note>. With great liberality, he even allowed his own copy to be brought away with me, which truly brought me no small benefit.

Then, having departed from there, I betook myself to Padua, where from all those copies I made one complete version as far as was possible. Finally, I translated this from the Greek language into Latin <note>The author, Francesco Barozzi, is explaining his process of creating the first reliable Latin translation of this work, published in 1560.</note>, partly for the sake of practice, partly driven by the Love with which I have pursued this book and the <term>Mathematical disciplines</term> <note>At this time, "mathematics" included geometry, astronomy, music, and arithmetic.</note> since my early youth, and also to comply with the persuasions of my friends and consult the common benefit of those students who are not skilled in the Greek tongue. And finally, when I saw this work—so long expected by many—finished and restored, and after I had sought out many critics for it (as Plato and Horace prescribe to me), I was unwilling to follow the opinion of Horace when he says:

*Such is your judgment, such your mind; yet if ever you should*
*Write anything, let it enter the ears of Metius the judge,*
*And your father’s, and mine; and let it be suppressed until the ninth year.*
*While the parchment is stored away, you will be able to erase*
*What you have not published. A voice once sent forth knows not how to return.*
<note>original: "Id tibi iudicium est..." This is a famous passage from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, advising authors to wait nine years before publishing to ensure the work's quality.</note>

But instead, studying the common benefit, I decided it ought to be printed. While it was being printed, I saw two more Greek copies, one in Venice—

In Venice, in the library of Saints John and Paul; the other in Padua, from the library of Gian Vincenzo Pinelli of Genoa, a man most noble in his lineage, his spirit, and his character. Out of all the copies which I have seen until now, this most useful and clear volume of Proclus Diadochus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a hugely influential philosopher in the Neoplatonic tradition; "Diadochus" is Greek for "Successor," marking him as the head of Plato’s Academy.</note>, having been rescued from near destruction, now for the first time rises up like a reborn phoenix. 

For its most happy birth, immortal thanks must be given first to God, the supreme craftsman of all things, and then to Love—who is the author and preserver not only of the sciences, but indeed of all things. You see, therefore, most worthy Patriarch, that both my current scholarly labors <note>original: "lucubrationem," referring to work performed by lamplight or late at night</note> and all things that have arisen or arise daily in the natural world, arise and come to be by the grace of Love. 

Since, therefore, this work was produced by me out of Love, it is only right that it should also bring me some gift of Love in return. The greatest gift of Love, it seems to me, is Friendship. I mean that friendship which is true Friendship. For since Love is threefold: one based on what is pleasant, another on what is useful...

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle of a scholarly work, likely a commentary on the Neoplatonist philosopher Proclus, as indicated by the mention of "my work on Proclus" toward the end of the text. ...is clearly established. From these principles, Friendship indeed arises. For there is nothing that attracts men more to loving one another than a similarity of virtue and good character, as well as a fellowship of shared studies; indeed, because of these things, we even love strangers in a certain way. This, finally, is the kind of Friendship I have long desired to exist between us. For "someone must always be sought," as Cicero says, "whom we may love and by whom we may be loved." <note>original: "semper enim aliqui (ait Cic.) acquirendi sunt, quos diligamus, & à quibus diligamur." The author is quoting Marcus Tullius Cicero’s famous treatise *De Amicitia* (On Friendship).</note> For once charity and benevolence are removed, all joy is removed from life. I have always proposed to myself that this sentiment must be observed most diligently.

Therefore, in recent days, as I weighed your various and manifold gifts of mind, and noticed the greatest harmony and kinship in our ideas, stars, genius, and dispositions of soul and body, <note>The author uses "sidere" (star) and "genio" (guiding spirit), suggesting that their friendship is written in the stars or part of their inherent nature.</note> I chose you above all others. Since you are already joined to me by our shared homeland, I wished to join you also in perfect Friendship and to always follow in your footsteps. For I hope and desire that our friendship (which was perhaps a mutual benevolence, but hidden until now) will be true, perfect, indissoluble, and eternal. For every friendship that arises from the best principles is true and perfect, and cannot be violated or dissolved by any means. 

Indeed, if one of the friends violates the friendship, his own greatest good surely collapses; and no one seeks the destruction of their own good. Therefore, friendship—which is produced and sustained not by utility or pleasure, but by the good and by virtue—remains inviolable, eternal, and indissoluble (whether they wish it or not) when found in such men, and from it, the greatest utility and the greatest joy always blossom forth. <note>The author is drawing on Aristotelian ethics, which distinguishes between "accidental" friendships based on usefulness and "perfect" friendships based on virtue.</note>

But since Nature has given us this law, that we should not approach friends without some gift, and since I had nothing I thought would be more pleasing to you than this <term>lucubration</term> <note>original: "lucubratione." A term for scholarly work produced by "burning the midnight oil."</note> of mine on Proclus, I decided it should be dedicated to you, such as it is. You will not be reluctant to accept this small pledge of my love for you, with the kindness you usually show, for I have found no one whom I thought should be preferred over you. 

Receive, then, this new gift of Mercury and Minerva, <note>In this context, Mercury represents eloquence and the transmission of knowledge, while Minerva represents wisdom and the arts.</note> so that under the protection of your most distinguished name, it may pass daily into the hands of men with the greatest authority. As for me, so that our friendship may be true and perfect, love me always with a mutual and not hidden love. Farewell.

->Padua. November 20, 1559.<- <note>original: "XII. Cal. Decembreis M. D. LIX." Using the Roman calendar, the 12th day before the Kalends (1st) of December is November 20th.</note>

# PREFACE OF FRANCESCO BAROZZI TO THE READER.

->[A decorative floral ornament]<-

**[Historiated initial Q depicting a scholar in a study]** SINCE the work, which was undertaken by me many months ago through the supreme providence of the first cause of all things <note>A common Renaissance reference to God as the "First Cause."</note>, has finally been completed and finished by divine help after many labors, studious Reader, I believe it will be done with prudent counsel (as I am persuaded) if, before you approach the writings of Proclus himself, I remind you of several matters that are of no small importance. Equipped with these, you will more easily be able to attain an understanding of those things which you read in this book. For it is worthwhile, before any discipline, both to remove those things which might be an obstacle to the soul's ability to recollect its own principles <note>This refers to the Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, or "recollection," where learning is seen as the soul remembering eternal truths it once knew.</note>, and to recognize those things from which the discipline itself arises.

Firstly, therefore, I would like you to know that among many other men named Proclus, there was one most famous of all, with the surname **Diadochus** <note>original: "Diadochum, hoc est successorem"</note>, which means "the Successor." He was a Lycian by birth, a Platonic Philosopher, and a most outstanding Mathematician. He (if Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and its author.</note> is to be believed) was a disciple of the great Syrianus, and when he presided over the Athenian School, he had other disciples himself, among whose number one was the distinguished Marinus of Naples, his successor; another was Marcus Antonius, by whom (as Spartianus reports) he was even promoted to the consulship. This same Proclus left many writings to us: on the art of Grammar, on Philosophy, commentaries on Homer, as well as on Plato, on Hesiod’s *Works and Days* <note>original: "Ἔργα καὶ ἡμέρας"</note>, on the Theology of Orpheus, and others besides these. Chiefly, however, he wrote these commentaries on the first books of Euclid’s *Elements*, which I judge to be worthy of the highest admiration and to be held in one's hands with the greatest study, since they open the way for us to all Mathematics and universal Philosophy. And they offer themselves to everyone now especially because they have been restored to a whole and perfect state (as far as was possible) from their previously mangled and corrupt condition.

For which reason I also wish you to be warned that you should not compare this labor of mine with the Greek edition from Basel <note>Referring to the 1533 edition by Simon Grynaeus, which Barozzi considered full of errors.</note>, which was torn apart rather than printed, nor with any other edition. For I have seen many copies filled with the greatest variations, from all of which I have gathered whatever good there was and transferred it into this single work, which I am also the first to translate from the Greek into the Latin language. In the course of translating it, although I was not unaware that Horace said, *Nor should you care to render word for word as a faithful translator* <note>original: "Nec uerbum uerbo curabis reddere fidus Interpres"</note>, I nevertheless decided that nothing should be added or diminished. Instead, I have rendered the Greek words, the meanings of the words, and the truth of the text everywhere into Latin. I have not imitated those who, in translating books, add not a few things of their own, omit many others, or change the order of the authors by disturbing their sequence.

I have set before me, above all, Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator known for his skill in bridging Greek and Latin.</note> as the Prince of all translators. For many have translated, but he alone seems to me a true translator. Indeed, I have seen various translations by many people which are certainly to be ridiculed by everyone. For some (as I have already said) add, omit, and change many things for some reason or another. Others render the most beautiful and lucid meanings of the authors as most obscure and false: either because they are not perfectly skilled in the Greek tongue, or because they are ignorant of the sciences and arts about which those authors treat; or finally because, when they wish to express technical terms of the sciences in Ciceronian language <note>The ornate, classical Latin style of Cicero, which was often criticized for lacking the precise vocabulary needed for technical subjects like math.</note> (which cannot be done), they enter into inextricable Labyrinths, and drag down with them those who read their writings. Others, however, loving a certain barbarism everywhere, translate books from the Greek tongue into Latin in such a way that they might be said to be translated into almost any other language rather than Latin. These people have not observed the sentiment of Quintilian, who said, *Those translating Greek authors may use the best words.* <note>original: "Græcos Autores transferentibus, uerbis uti optimis licet"</note> Finally, others possessing neither the languages nor the sciences, while they write down Greek expressions in Latin and Greek characters in the manner of schoolmasters, hallucinate egregiously.

**2**

# P R E F A C E

...are designated. Therefore, farewell, honest reader; let all those stay far away who defile and overturn the authors themselves. However, I must not pass over in silence the fact that in this, my translation of Proclus, you will find many and various things that ought to be noted. First, I have endeavored to make this author speak English <note>original: "latinum" (Latin). The translator is describing his process of translating Proclus from Greek into Latin; for this English version, we treat his "Latin" as the target language of his time.</note> to the best of my ability, not merely by following the words and forms of speech used by Cicero, but also those of Quintilian and other men of Latin authority who treated the sciences contained in this volume. Next, I wished to translate the technical terms of the sciences everywhere (as far as was possible) in a legitimate and pure manner. Furthermore, for the sake of clarity, I have sometimes altered the flow or "circuit" of the speech, and I have used that figure of speech which the Greeks call <term>the last-first</term> <note>original: ὕστερον πρότερον (hysteron proteron); a figure of speech where what should come second is placed first for emphasis.</note>. Moreover, I have avoided and escaped ambiguities, sometimes by doubling words, or by using softer expressions, or by resolving participles and Greek formulas of speech; and also through the knowledge of correct writing, as will be evident to you as you read. Finally, out of necessity and because of the poverty of the Latin language, I did not abstain from certain words such as: **Identity, Simplicity, Immateriality, Totality, Indivisibility**, and others of that kind. I also used certain adverbs, such as **Uniformly, Multiformly, Indivisibly**, and others; as well as some specific scientific terms, such as **Symptom, Requirement, Predicate, Subject**, and the like. I have also used the proper names of the sciences, such as **Perspective** and **Catoptrics** <note>original: "Specularia," the study of mirrors and reflection.</note>, which names are so widely known that if they were expressed otherwise, they might not be easily understood by everyone. Similarly, regarding certain Greek words—since many older writers used the Greek forms, while some more recent writers whom I have followed have lately rendered them in Latin—I have, for example, used **Obtuse-angled** and **Acute-angled**, which the former called *Amblygonium* and *Oxygonium*, though they nonetheless called a "Rectangle" what the Greeks call <term>right-angled</term> <note>original: ὀρθογώνιον (orthogonion)</note>. Likewise, we have said **Five-angled** and **Six-angled** for what they called *Pentagon* and *Hexagon*. For if they translate <term>right-angled</term> <note>original: ὀρθογώνιον (orthogonion)</note> as "Rectangle," why should <term>sharp-angled</term> <note>original: ὀξυγώνιον (oxygonion)</note> and <term>blunt-angled</term> <note>original: ἀμβλυγώνιον (amblygonium)</note> not be translated as "Acute-angled" and "Obtuse-angled"? If they use **Triangle** and **Quadrangle**, why not **Five-angled, Six-angled**, and likewise **Seven-angled, Eight-angled, Nine-angled**, and **Ten-angled**, even if we proceed no further? Nevertheless, we have also used certain Greek words because, if they were translated, they would exceed the proper limits of the science, such as: **Theorem, Problem, Dodecagon, Dodecahedron, Octahedron, Icosahedron, Sphere, Cube, Pyramid, Cone, Cylinder**, and others of this sort. You will find all these things, benevolent reader, noted with purpose in our translation, along with many others which I will wrap in silence for the sake of brevity at present; for from these things we have mentioned, those too will become known to you.

Now, therefore, it remains for me to exhort you with all my strength to be willing to receive, love, practice, and learn thoroughly from Proclus the **Mathematical Philosophy** which he so elegantly delivers—if, indeed, you desire to know your Soul and yourself. For our Soul (as the most wise Plato teaches) was allotted a mathematical essence. Hence, mathematics is even called "mathematical" by Proclus, and not only by the common name of mathematics, but also **Arithmetic, Harmonics, Geometry**, and **Spherics**. This does not seem ridiculous to me, as it might to those who are ignorant of the cause. For our Soul pre-assumed all these disciplines into its own essence: **Arithmetic** according to the multitude and the essential Units and Numbers existing within it; **Harmonics** according to the ratios of these Numbers which they have to one another. For who does not see that the multitude within the Soul is harmonious and composed? And (as the divine Plato shows in the *Timaeus*) all harmonic ratios are found in it—namely, the **fourth**, the **fifth**, and the **octave** <note>original: διατεσσάρων (diatessaron), διαπέντε (diapente), διαπασῶν (diapason)</note>, and those composed from these. It possesses **Geometry** according to its union, its integrity, its form, and its linear essence. Insofar as it is one, whole, and a Totality, it participates in the Continuous; but insofar as it is Number, it claims a discrete nature for itself. But as something continuous, it has within itself two "rectitudes" <note>In this context, "rectitudes" refers to straight directions or axes of movement.</note>, one of which produces the **Circle of the Same**, while the other propagates the **Circle of the Other** or the **Different**. Furthermore, since these Circles intersect each other at angles that are not right angles, they bring to us the image of the **Zodiac** <note>original: "Signiferi," the star-bearer or the belt of the zodiac.</note> and the **Equator**. For the Equator, which is in the heavens, always effects the "Same"; but the Zodiac effects the "Other" and the "Different." Through these two principles (the Same and the Different, I mean), the whole nature of things is preserved in its most beautiful order. Since, therefore, the essence of our Soul is Linear and Circular, and even Triangular and Quadrangular—as is manifest to the Platonists and (to use a Peripatetic term) like a **triangle within a quadrangle**—it is clearly a doubt to no one that the Soul...

He argues that studying mathematics is essential for self-knowledge because, according to Platonic thought, the human soul is composed of mathematical and harmonic ratios that mirror the structure of the cosmos.</summary>

->P R E F A C E<-

[The Soul] has also taken Geometry into itself beforehand. Moreover, since the Circles which are within the Soul are both immobile and move by themselves—immobile according to their essence (for everything that is moved by itself is simultaneously moved and immobile, since moving pertains in a certain way to an immobile power)—but mobile according to their vital action and their twin circuits, it is not without reason that the Soul also took up Spherics <note>original: "Sphæricam"; here referring to the study of the celestial spheres or astronomy</note> beforehand. Since, therefore, our Soul is mathematical according to all the parts of Mathematics, I consider it a worthwhile effort for anyone who desires to know their own Soul and themselves—and thereby to excel over other living creatures—to be exercised in the Mathematical sciences, without which one will certainly never be able to know oneself perfectly. For this reason, I urge you again and again, most Kind Reader, to embrace these sciences above all others; and if you desire to become a Mathematician in a short course of time, read and re-read this most learned and lucid Volume by Proclus. <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Euclid’s Elements is a primary source for the history of Greek mathematics.</note>

Secondly, while the third book was being printed, two final copies came into our hands, in which we found several things to be different in the first and second books which had already been printed. Therefore, we have had those printed among the beginnings of the book, which follow in this order:

Furthermore, if perhaps some other things besides these have escaped my diligence, it will be your part, kind Reader, to wisely correct them. If, however, you find that those things which I am convinced were observed in this my version (as was said above) were not observed in places, you will forgive this small failing.

BUT LEST by chance you think, most prudent Reader, that this work was published by me rashly in this my youthful age, let this not be hidden from you: that when I had already made these books Latin <note>original: "latinos fecissem"; meaning he had completed the translation from the original Greek into Latin</note>, I wished to spend nearly a whole year before publication so that I might employ several critics <note>original: "censores"; here meaning scholarly reviewers or editors rather than restrictive censors</note> for myself and for this work. These included, foremost, Marcus Antonius Passerus of Padua <note>Marc'Antonio Passeri (1491–1563), a famous philosophy professor at the University of Padua</note>, a second Aristotle of our age; Marcus Antonius Muretus of France <note>Marc-Antoine Muret, a renowned humanist scholar</note>; Giovanni Faseolo of Padua; and Vincenzo Cardini of Florence—men most skilled in the Latin and Greek languages and endowed with all forms of knowledge. I also consulted Felice Paciotto of Urbino, a young man of the greatest promise, who is both thoroughly learned in both languages and exceptionally well-versed in the studies of Philosophy and Mathematics. I will never deny that I very often made use of his advice and his most sharp judgment. Relying indeed upon the authority of these most celebrated men, for the common benefit of students, I preferred to undergo no small amount of danger by bringing this long-awaited Author into the light, rather than to allow him to remain further in the shadows without any risk to myself.

# OF PROCLUS DIADOCHUS OF LYCIA
# COMMENTARIES
### ON THE FIRST BOOK OF EUCLID’S ELEMENTS

## BOOK ONE.

## TRANSLATED BY FRANCESCO BAROCIO,
### VENETIAN NOBLEMAN.

[Decorative floral ornament]

### On the Intermediate Nature of Mathematical Essence
### Chapter I.

[Large historiated initial M depicting a scholar with a compass and globe] ATHEMATICAL Essence <margin>Universal conclusion.</margin> must be seen as consisting neither of the primary kinds of things that exist, nor of the final things that are separated from simple essence, but rather it occupies a middle place between substances that are indivisible, simple, uncompounded, and impartible, and those that are partible and limited by manifold compositions and various divisions. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> For the fact that the principles <note>original: *rationibus*</note> involved in mathematics are always consistent, firm, and cannot be refuted, declares that it is superior to those forms that are found in matter. Yet that power of proceeding through reasoning—which further uses the dimensions of subject matters and prepares some things from other principles—gives it an order lower than that which is allotted to the indivisible nature, which is perfectly constituted in itself. Therefore (as I believe), Plato also divided the knowledge of things according to primary, middle, and final substances. <margin>Plato’s division of knowledge in the *Republic* and other places.</margin> And to indivisible things he assigned the intellectual faculty <term>intellectilem: pertaining to the pure "intellectus" or *nous*, the highest form of intuitive understanding</term>, which collectively and by a certain simple power distinguishes those things perceived by the mind; and since it is without matter, endowed with a certain supreme purity, and applies itself through a single form of reasoning to grasp the things themselves, it excels all other forms of knowledge. But to partible things, which have received the lowest nature, and to all sensible things, he assigned opinion <note>Greek: *doxa*</note>, which has obtained only an obscure truth. To the middle things, however (of which kind mathematical forms certainly are)—inferior to the indivisible nature but superior to the partible—he assigned discursive thought <term>cogitationem: translating the Greek *dianoia*, the step-by-step reasoning used to reach mathematical conclusions</term>. For this is indeed lower than the mind and supreme science, yet more perfect than opinion...

<summary>This page introduces Proclus’s philosophical argument that mathematics is an "intermediate" science, positioned between the perfect, unchanging world of the divine intellect and the imperfect, changing world of material objects. It references Plato’s hierarchy of knowledge, placing mathematical "thought" (dianoia) above mere opinion but below pure intellectual intuition.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Euclid, Mathematics, Plato, Republic, Dianoia, Intellectual Faculty, Essence, Neo-Platonism, Francesco Barocio</keywords>

->FIRST [BOOK]. 3<-

...stable existence, they are brought to perfection by the **Limit**; but because of their division into a multitude, and the abundance of their generative power, and their divine diversity and progression, they take on the nature of **Infinity**. <note>The author is discussing the Pythagorean and Platonic concept that all things are composed of two principles: "Limit" (which provides form and boundary) and "Infinity" (which provides the capacity for growth and multiplicity).</note> Mathematical entities, however, <margin>How the types of mathematics arose from these principles.</margin> have arisen from the Limit and Infinity, yet not only from the primary, intelligible, and hidden principles, but also from those principles which have moved from the first to a second order of existence. These are sufficient to produce the intermediate arrangements and the variety found within them.

For this reason, in these mathematical realms, the <term>ratios<note>original: "rationes." In this context, it refers to the logical proportions or governing principles of mathematical objects.</note></term> indeed proceed toward infinity, yet they are restrained by the principle that acts as the **Limit**. For **Number**, starting from **Unity** <note>original: "Vnitate." In ancient mathematics, "Unity" or the Monad was not just the number one, but the indivisible source from which all numbers spring.</note>, accepts an unceasing increase, yet any number actually selected is always finite. The division of **magnitudes** <note>In this context, magnitudes refer to continuous things like lines, surfaces, or solids, as opposed to "numbers" which are discrete.</note> likewise goes on to infinity, yet all things being divided are bounded, and the small parts of the whole exist as finite in their actual state. <summary>This page explains how mathematical concepts like numbers and shapes are born from the tension between the "Limit" (which keeps them finite) and "Infinity" (which allows them to be divided or increased forever). It notes that while numbers can grow forever and lines can be divided forever in theory, any specific number or piece of a line we encounter is always finite.</summary>

### 4 BOOK

<margin>Divine science</margin>
Now we shall also consider their common theorems, which are both simple and derived from a single science that encompasses all mathematical knowledge within itself. We will examine how these theorems apply to everything, and how they may be observed in **Numbers**, in **Magnitudes**, and in **Motions**.

<margin>Common mathematical considerations</margin>
Included in this category are all matters of *Proportions*, *Compositions*, *Divisions*, *Conversions*, and *alternate Permutations* <note>original: "alternarum Immutationum"; this refers to the mathematical practice of swapping terms in a proportion (if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d)</note>. Likewise, this includes all *Ratios*—such as *Multiples*, <term>Superparticulars<note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part of it (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</note></term>, and <term>Superpartients<note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus more than one part of it (e.g., 5:3 or 7:4).</note></term>, as well as their opposites. Indeed, we shall look at everything considered universally and generally regarding *Equality* and *Inequality*—not merely as they appear in Figures, Numbers, or Motions, but insofar as each of these possesses a certain common nature in itself and offers a simpler form of understanding. But the beauti— <note>The text breaks off here mid-word, likely "pulchritudo" (beauty) or "pulchrum" (beautiful).</note>

<summary>This page describes a "universal" mathematical science that governs proportions and ratios across different fields like geometry and physics. It emphasizes that certain mathematical truths are common to all things, regardless of whether one is dealing with shapes, numbers, or physical movement.</summary>

--- Page 223 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the hierarchy of sciences, specifically how universal principles govern mathematical concepts like proportions. It transitions from the nature of "First Philosophy" to the specific mental tools used to understand mathematics.</meta>

->FIRST. 5<-

...they will also be proportional. This must be demonstrated from the specific principles of one’s own science. For who is it that understands **alternating ratios** <note>original: *alternam Rationem*; a mathematical property where if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d</note> by themselves, whether they exist in Magnitudes or in Numbers? Or who understands the division of composite Magnitudes or Numbers, and likewise the composition of those that have been divided? <margin>These common principles are known neither by Natural Science nor by Mathematics, but by Divine Science.</margin> These are certainly not the sciences or cognitions of "divisible" things. We do not possess a science of those things which are without matter and which are established closer to intellectual contemplation; rather, the knowledge of those things is a much earlier science, and from it, many common sciences receive their principles. An ascent occurs toward such great knowledge from more particular things to more universal ones, until we return to the very science of **being insofar as it is**. <note>original: *quatenus est*; a reference to Aristotle's definition of Metaphysics</note> For this science does not think it right to contemplate only what is inherent in Numbers, nor even what is common to all quantities; instead, it contemplates the one, firm essence and existence of all things that are. 

Consequently, it is the most capable of all sciences, and from it, all others assume their own principles. For the higher sciences always provide the primary suppositions for demonstrations to the lower ones. <margin>Divine Science is the most capable of all sciences, which Aristotle calls the "Mistress of Sciences" in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, text 23. Also Socrates in the *Theaetetus*.</margin> That science, however, which is the most perfect of all sciences, bestows principles upon all from itself—to some more universal, and to others more particular. Therefore, in the *Theaetetus*, Socrates, mixing humor with serious matters, compares the sciences within us to **pigeons**; he says they fly, some in flocks and others separately from the rest. For those that are more common and more "capable" encompass many more particular sciences within themselves. But those which are distributed into specific forms and touch upon things subjected to cognition are distant from one another, and can in no way be joined together, since they are stirred by different primary principles. <margin>Epilogue. First Philosophy, which Plato calls **Dialectic** in the seventh book of the *Republic*.</margin> Let one science, therefore, precede all sciences and doctrines, namely that which knows the common things that permeate through all categories and supplies principles to all Mathematical sciences. And here let our teaching on this matter be concluded.

### What the instrument is for judging Mathematics. Chapter V.

Next, we shall consider what instrument is fit for judging Mathematical things. In explaining this matter, we shall establish **Plato** as our leader, who in the books of the *Republic* <margin>Plato’s division in the seventh book of the *Republic* and other places.</margin> divides those things which fall under cognition on one hand, and the types of cognition themselves on the other; he then distributes these cognitions in pairs to the things that are known.

<summary>This page argues that a "Divine Science" (Metaphysics or Dialectic) provides the foundational principles for all other disciplines, including mathematics. It uses Socrates's "aviary" metaphor to explain the hierarchy of knowledge before beginning a new chapter on the mental tools used to judge mathematical truths.</summary>

<keywords>First Philosophy, Metaphysics, Dialectic, Plato, Aristotle, Theaetetus, Republic, alternating ratio, hierarchy of sciences, mathematical principles</keywords>

--- Page 224 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plato's epistemological hierarchy, specifically focusing on the mathematical sciences' position between pure intellect and sensory opinion, as described in the "Divided Line" analogy of the Republic.</meta>

6 BOOK

...established. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought about how Plato structured the levels of reality.</note> For of those things which exist, he placed some as intelligible <note>original: "intellectilia," referring to things grasped by the mind alone</note> and others as sensible. Furthermore, among the intelligibles, some are again purely intelligible, while others are subjects for **thought**; and among the sensibles, some are indeed sensible, while others are **conjectural**. To the intelligibles (which are truly the first of the four kinds), he assigns the cognition of **intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentiam," often translated as "intellection" or "nous"</note>; to those subject to thought, he assigns **thought** <note>original: "cogitationem," referring to "dianoia" or discursive reasoning</note>; to sensibles, he assigns **faith** <note>original: "fidem," meaning "belief" or "conviction"</note>; and to conjectural things, the **power of conjecture**. <margin>The proportion of cognitions according to Plato.</margin> He shows that the power of conjecture has the same relation to the sense as thought has to intelligence. For the power of conjecture recognizes the images <note>original: "spectra"</note> of sensible things when they are observed in water and other bodies that clearly reflect an image. Indeed, these have obtained a place, in a way, at the very end in the waters, and have truly become reflections of reflections. Similarly, thought inspects the images of intelligibles, which have fallen away from the primary, simple, and indivisible forms into multitude and division. Therefore, the knowledge of these [mathematical] things depends on other more ancient hypotheses; but intelligence reaches the non-hypothetical principle itself.

<margin>Mathematical things are subject to thought, and Thought is the instrument judging them.</margin> If, therefore, mathematical things have obtained neither an indivisible substance (separated from all division and variety) nor that substance which is grasped by the senses (which is subject to many changes and divisible in every way), it is clear to anyone that, according to their essence, they are subjects of **thought**. Thought, like a suitable instrument for judging, presides over them, just as sense does over sensibles and the power of conjecture over conjectures. <margin>Socrates in the seventh [book] of the Republic.</margin> Hence, Socrates indeed determines that the knowledge of these things is more obscure than the "first science" <note>Dialectic or pure philosophy</note>, but more evident than that which is placed in opinion. <margin>The same [is said] above in chapter one.</margin> For they [mathematical objects] possess something beyond intelligence insofar as they are unfolded and have the power to proceed; yet, by the stability of the reasons found in them, which cannot be refuted, they surpass opinion. And that they take their origin from a hypothesis is due to their falling short of the first science; but that they are constituted in those forms which exist without matter is due to their perfection compared to the knowledge of sensibles. <margin>Epilogue.</margin> Thus we establish, according to Plato's view, that the instrument suitable for judging all mathematical things is such: namely, **thought**, which establishes itself as superior to opinion but is surpassed by intelligence.

<margin>The first opinion, which is Aristotle's.</margin>
<margin>The second opinion, which is Plato's.</margin>

...[the essence of] mathematical forms and types, and whether we must admit that they flow from sensory objects and exist in the nature of things—either through **abstraction** (as is commonly said) or through the collection of particulars into one common principle—or whether we must confess that they exist even before these things, as Plato asserts and as the progression of all things shows.

<margin>Refutation of the first opinion. Argument.</margin>
First, if we say mathematical forms arise and exist from sensory objects, and our soul finally forms within itself a circular or triangular shape from triangles or circles residing in matter, where then does that precise power and that certainty—which can by no means be refuted or overcome—come from in mathematical reasoning? These must be drawn out either from sensory objects or from the soul. 

<margin>Mathematical certainty emanates from the soul itself.</margin>
But it is impossible for these to be drawn from sensory objects. For much greater certainty would have to be granted to those physical objects than they actually possess. Therefore, they are drawn out from the soul itself, which provides perfection to the imperfect and adds certainty to things that are not certain. For where among those things that fall under the senses could an **indivisible** <note>original: "impartibile" — meaning a point that has no parts or dimensions</note> thing be perceived, or one lacking width or thickness? Where, further, is the equality of lines emerging from the center of a circle? Where are the always stable ratios of sides? Where are the straightnesses of angles? Indeed, I do not see them. 

Since all things that fall under the senses are mixed together, nothing pure is found in them that is free from its opposite; instead, all things exist as divisible, full of dimensions, and subject to motion. How then shall we attribute an immutable and firm essence to the immobile principles derived from those things which move and are different at different times? For there is no one who would not admit that whatever derives its origin from moving essences has a changeable existence. 

<margin>Conclusion of the argument.</margin>
Finally, how shall we add certainty to uncertain forms through forms that are certain and cannot be refuted? For whatever is the cause of immobile knowledge is itself even more so. Let it be confessed and accepted, then, that the soul is the **mother** <note>original: "genitricem"</note> of mathematical forms and principles. 

<margin>Another question.</margin>
<margin>The first opinion, which is Plato's.</margin>
But if she [the soul], having models according to her essence, establishes them—and if such origins are certain emissions of the forms that pre-existed in her—we will agree with Plato in saying these things, and the true essence of mathematical disciplines will be found by us. 

<margin>The second opinion, which is Aristotle's, and its refutation.</margin>
<margin>The first argument.</margin>
But if she does not have them, and has not previously grasped the principles, but merely weaves together a decoration devoid of matter and produces such a contemplation, how can she judge whether what has been produced is vital <note>living or real</note> or empty <note>original: "subuentanea" — literally "wind-eggs," meaning unsubstantial or hollow</note>, and images instead of truths? By what rules does she measure the truth that is in them? Finally, not having their essence, how can she produce such a great multitude of principles?

Let the beginning be made, then, in the name of God, and let this first part be placed here.

### What Alchemy is in itself.

Alchemy is a glorious part of **natural magic**, <note>In the 17th century, "natural magic" referred to the study of the hidden but natural properties of physical substances, distinct from supernatural or "black" magic.</note> which through the wise preparation and composition of natural things—such as precious stones, metals, minerals, and other things—raises their nature to a more glorious state.

Secondly, it is the highest art of nature in the separation of things that must be divided from one another, to bring them to a pure clarity, purity, and perfection.

Thirdly, it is an investigator of the inner hidden spirit of all things, which resides in all creatures and maintains them through its power, effect, and **virtue**. <note>The original term is *Tugend*, which in this context means the inherent medicinal or spiritual potency of a substance.</note>

Fourthly, it is an inventor of the best medicines against all diseases of the human body.

Fifthly, it is an art of coming to the aid of nature through the help of art, so that she may achieve her desired ripeness <note>Or maturity; the alchemical belief that metals "grow" in the earth toward a state of gold.</note> which in many places has been hindered by cold, dampness, or the inconsistency of the weather; therefore man, as a **servant of nature**, <note>A common alchemical trope: the practitioner does not create from nothing but assists nature in finishing her work.</note> should step in and offer her a hand so that she might reach her goal.

Sixthly, it is a wise distributor and orderly housekeeper of the wonderful gifts of God, which He has placed into nature.

### Another objection by certain Platonists against the utility of mathematics, and its solution.
### Chapter 10.

Perhaps, however, some arising from **our own school** <note>The author refers to fellow Platonists or Neoplatonists</note>, putting forward Plato as a witness for their arguments, will attempt to provoke the unlearned into a contempt for the study of mathematical disciplines. For they will say that the Philosopher himself, in his books on the ***Republic***, excludes this mathematical knowledge from the **choir of sciences**, <note>The "choir of sciences" refers to the traditional grouping of the liberal arts</note> and rebukes it as being ignorant of its own principles—as something whose beginning is something it does not even know, and whose end and middle are composed of things it does not know. To these they will add whatever other reproaches were leveled there by Socrates against this form of contemplation. 

Speaking, therefore, against these men who are our friends, we shall remind them that Plato himself clearly asserted that mathematics is a **purifier of the soul** and a **guide that leads it upward**, <note>original: "animæ purgatricem, sursumque ductricem"</note> insofar as it removes the darkness from the intelligent part of the mind...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the classification of knowledge, specifically addressing Plato's view of mathematics as a bridge between mere opinion and supreme wisdom.</meta>

->18 BOOK<-

<margin>Plato in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Plato in Symposio"</note></margin>
...there he attributes the name of **science**; but to experiences, not at all. For he says in the *Symposium*, by what means could a thing which possesses no **reason** <note>The Latin *ratio* carries multiple meanings here: reason, logical proportion, and mathematical ratio.</note> be a science? And therefore, every cognition that contains the reason and the cause of the things to be known is a certain type of science. Again, he divides this science—which has its power from knowing by way of the cause—according to the property of its **Subjects**. He posits one part as being conjectural regarding divisible things, but the other part as being the knower of those things which exist through themselves and always remain in the same state. According to this division, he separates **Medicine**—and every faculty that deals with material things—from science; but **Mathematics**, which possesses the power of contemplating eternal things entirely, he calls a science.

<margin>Aristotle shows how art differs from science in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, chapters 3 and 4. <note>original: "Quo differat ars a scientia, ostendit Aristo. sexto Moralium cap. 3. & 4." The "Moralium" refers to the Nicomachean Ethics.</note></margin>
Finally, dividing this science which we distinguish from the arts, he wills that one part be free of **supposition** <note>Plato’s "unhypothetical" first principle.</note>, while the other flows from a supposition. That which is free of supposition has the power of knowing the universe: it climbs all the way to **the Good** and the supreme cause of all things, and it makes that Good the end of its ascent. 

<margin>On the Good and the supreme cause, see Plato and Proclus in the 7th book of the *Republic*; [it says] at the beginning, but it is at the end. <note>original: "De bono, & suprema causa vide Platonem, & Proclum in 7. de Rep. † in principio, sed in fine esse."</note></margin>
However, this [mathematical] science, which provides for itself defined and determined principles from which it demonstrates those things that follow the principles themselves, tends not plainly toward the ultimate principle, but toward an end. And thus he says that Mathematics, insofar as it uses suppositions, falls short of that perfect science which lacks supposition. For there is truly only one science through which we are fit to know all things that exist, from which also the principles for all sciences emerge—some being closer and others more remote. 

<margin>Refutation of the argument <note>original: "Destructio Argumenti"</note></margin>
Therefore, let us not say that Plato expels Mathematics from the number of the sciences, but that he asserts it is second to that unique science which holds the supreme seat. Nor does he say that it is ignorant of its own principles, but rather that since it has received them from that [higher science] and held them without any demonstration, it demonstrates those things which follow from them. 

<margin>Regarding this, see Plato in the *Timaeus*. <note>original: "Circa hoc vid Platonem in Timaeo."</note></margin>
Indeed, he concedes that the **soul**—which is constituted from mathematical ratios—is sometimes the principle of motion, but at other times receives motion itself from the "kinds" <note>The Platonic Forms or Ideas.</note> which are subject to the intellect. These points harmonize with one another: for those things which are moved by another, there is a certain cause of motion, but not all motion has a cause. In this very same way, Mathematics is second to the first science, and as if imperfect in respect to it; yet it is nonetheless a science—not as being immune from supposition, but as the knower of the soul’s own ratios, and as providing the causes of its conclusions, and containing the reason of those things which are subject to its cognition.

<margin>Conclusion <note>original: "Epilogus"</note></margin>
Let all these things, therefore, be said on behalf of Mathematics according to the opinion of Plato.

### What should be required of a mathematician, and in what manner anyone might judge him correctly.
### Chapter XI.

<margin>Aristotle, in Book 1 of *On the Parts of Animals*, and in the first book of the *Ethics*, Chapter 3</margin>
Now, let us speak next of what one should require from a mathematician, and in what way anyone might be able to judge him correctly. For that man, as Aristotle says, who is generally educated in all things, is fit to judge all things; but he who is educated only in mathematical disciplines can pass judgment on the correctness of the reasoning found within them. It is necessary, therefore, to first establish the boundaries of judgment, and to recognize, first of all, in which areas they demonstrate things in common, and in which areas they look toward the unique properties of individual things. For many identical properties exist in things that differ in species—for example, the property of having **two right angles** <note>original: "duo Recti"; this refers to the theorem that the sum of the interior angles of any triangle is 180 degrees, or the sum of two right angles.</note> belongs to all triangles. Many other things, however, share the same classification, but the common species differs in individual cases, such as the concept of **similarity** in both geometric figures and in numbers. However, one should not seek a single type of demonstration from the mathematician in these matters. For the principles of figures and the principles of numbers are not the same; rather, they differ in their underlying subject matter. But if a property belongs to a thing essentially, the demonstration will also be singular. For having two right angles is the same in all triangles. <margin>Terms by which a mathematician is to be judged. First term.</margin> † And that which causes this to happen is the same in all cases (namely, that a triangle has external angles equal to the internal ones) <note>original: "Triangulum nempe Rectis æquales habere externos"; the author is referencing the geometric rule that an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note> and the very definition of a triangle. <margin>† And that which causes this to happen is the same in all, namely the triangle, and the triangular ratio.</margin> Just as having external angles equal to four right angles belongs not only to triangles, but to all **rectilinear** <note>Shapes made of straight lines, such as squares or polygons.</note> figures, and the demonstration applies to all insofar as they are rectilinear. For every ratio simultaneously brings with it a certain distinct property and "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" (passio) refers to a characteristic or attribute that a subject possesses.</note> in which all things participate through that ratio, such as "triangularity," or "rectilinearity," or the nature of "figure" in general.

<margin>Second term:</margin>
Secondly, one must judge if he demonstrates according to the subject matter—that is, if he provides **necessary** <note>Logic that must be true and cannot be otherwise.</note> reasons and such arguments that can by no means be refuted or proven wrong, rather than merely "probable" ones or those full of likelihoods. <margin>Aristotle, first book of the *Ethics*, Chapter 3.</margin> For it is the same thing, says Aristotle, to demand demonstrations from an orator as it is to accept a mathematician who argues only from probability. Indeed, anyone endowed with science or art ought to provide reasons appropriate to the things of which he treats. <margin>Plato in the *Timaeus*.</margin> Similarly, Plato in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world.</note> requires "likely" reasons from the natural philosopher, as one dealing with physical things; but from one who discourses on intellectual things and stable essence, he requires reasons that can neither be refuted nor even shaken. <margin>Metaphysics, Book 6.</margin> For the subject matters immediately cause the sciences or arts to differ—for instance, if some are immobile while others are moved, and some are simpler while others are more complex.

...to stand still, or to be moved. Indeed, they consider **Arithmetic** as that which deals with quantity in itself; **Music** as quantity in relation to another; **Geometry** as magnitude <note>original: "Quantum"</note> insofar as it is immobile; and **Spherics** <note>The study of the heavens and celestial motion, often called Astronomy.</note> as that which moves by itself. They consider, furthermore, that these sciences deal with "How Many" <note>discrete quantity</note> and "How Much" <note>continuous magnitude</note> not as absolute size or multitude, but as that which is defined by a limit. For by removing these sciences from the realm of the infinite, they prevent the mind from the vain task of trying to grasp infinity through knowledge.

<margin>How "How Many" and "How Much" are considered by the Mathematician.</margin>

Since these most wise men say these things, we certainly shall not think that they mean the "How Many" found in physical things we can touch, nor the "How Much" that is imagined concerning physical bodies. For the study of these (as I believe) belongs to natural science <note>Physics</note>, not to Mathematics itself. 

<margin>Digression.</margin>

But since the **Creator** <note>The "Opifex" or Demiurge, the craftsman of the universe in Platonic thought.</note> of all things undertook the union and division of the universe—along with identity and diversity, and besides these, stability and motion—to complete the soul, and constituted the soul from these categories as the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the world.</note> taught us, we must say that when the soul's thought stands by its own diversity and its division of reasons and multitude, and understands itself to be both one and many, it proposes and produces **Numbers** for itself, and the knowledge of these is **Arithmetic**. 

<margin>From what elements the Creator constitutes the Soul according to the Timaeus.</margin>

<margin>How thought produces the mathematical sciences.</margin>

In contrast, when looking toward the union of multitude and its communication and binding together with itself, the soul prepares **Music** for itself. Therefore, **Arithmetic** excels **Music** in antiquity <note>Arithmetic is considered "older" or more fundamental than Music.</note>, since the soul itself was first divided by the Creator and then collected back together by reasons, as Plato relates. 

<margin>The Soul is first divided, then collected, according to the mind of Plato in the Timaeus; therefore Arithmetic precedes Music.</margin>

Again, by that stability which is within the soul, establishing its action, it brought forth **Geometry** from itself, as well as the one essential **Figure** and the creative principles of all Figures. But by its motion, it brought forth **Spherics**. For the soul itself also moves through **Circles**, yet it always remains in the same state because of the causes of the Circles—namely, the **Straight** and the **Circular**. 

<margin>Geometry precedes Astronomy, because stability is prior to motion.</margin>

And for this reason, here too **Geometry** precedes **Spherics**, just as stability precedes motion. Furthermore, since thought itself does not look toward the convolution of its forms (which is endowed with infinite power), but rather looks toward the boundary of the **Limit** <note>The "Finis" or "Limit" is a Pythagorean concept representing order and definition against the chaos of the Infinite.</note> according to its types, it generated these sciences. Therefore they say that these sciences took the infinite away from multitude and magnitude, and finally occupy themselves with the finite. For the mind placed the principles of all things—both of multitude and of magnitude—within thought itself. 

<margin>Why the Pythagoreans say Mathematics deals with the finite.</margin>

For since the soul is whole and made of similar parts to itself, and is both one and indivisible yet also divisible, and brings forth the ornament of forms, it participates in the essential **Limit** and **Infinity** from the intelligible realms. It understands, indeed, because of the **Limit**, but it generates various lives and reasons because of **Infinity**. Its intelligence, therefore, established these sciences according to the **Limit** that is within them, but not according to the infinity of life...

<margin>The intelligences of thought established the mathematical sciences according to their own Limit.</margin>

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
...infinity. Indeed, they represent an image of the mind, but not of life. This is the opinion of the Pythagoreans and their division of the four sciences. <note>The "four sciences" refers to the Quadrivium: Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy.</note>

### Another division of the entire mathematical science according to Geminus. Chapter 13.

<margin>Another division of mathematics according to the opinion of Geminus.</margin>
Again, some believe mathematics should be divided in another way, as does Geminus <note>Geminus of Rhodes (c. 10–60 AD) was a Greek astronomer and mathematician whose work often categorized scientific knowledge.</note>. They want one part of it to deal only with **intellectual things** <term>intellectibles: objects grasped by the mind alone, independent of matter</term>, while the other part deals with **sensible things** <term>sensibles: physical objects perceived by the five senses</term>. They call "intellectuals" whatever investigations the soul stirs up by itself, separating itself from material forms. Of that part which deals with intellectuals, they place two as by far the primary and most important parts: **Arithmetic** and **Geometry**. 

<margin>The parts of mathematical science: Arithmetic, Geometry, Mechanics, Astronomy, Perspective, Geodesy, Canonics (or Regularity), and Calculation.</margin>
Of that part which explains its duty and work in sensible things, they list six: **Mechanics**, **Astronomy** <note>original: "Astrologiam"; in this context, it refers to the mathematical study of celestial movements rather than modern astrology.</note>, **Perspective** <note>original: "Perspectiuam"; this refers to Optics, the mathematical study of light and sight.</note>, **Geodesy** <note>The practical measurement of land and earth.</note>, **Canonics** <note>original: "Canonicam"; the mathematical study of musical intervals and harmony.</note> (also called the Regular Art), and **Calculation**. 

However, they do not believe the **military art**—specifically that which pertains to the arranging and coordinating of battle lines, which the Greeks call *tactics* <note>original: τακτικὴν (taktikēn)</note>—should be called one of the parts of mathematics, as some others have wished. Instead, they say it merely *uses* mathematics: sometimes the art of calculation (as in counting legions) and sometimes geodesy (as in dividing and measuring the spaces for a camp's layout). 

<margin>Military art and others are excluded from the mathematical sciences.</margin>
Furthermore, they say that neither the writing of history nor the art of medicine is a part of mathematics, even though historians and doctors frequently use mathematical theorems. Writers of history use them when reporting the location of climates, the sizes of cities, or when calculating diameters, perimeters, and circuits. 

<margin>Hippocrates in the book *On Places*.</margin>
Doctors, meanwhile, clarify many things in their art through such methods. Even Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC).</note> himself showed the utility that comes to medicine from astronomy, as have nearly all who have spoken about the right times and places for health. 

<margin>How the military art uses mathematics.</margin>
For the same reason, the commander who works on arranging battle lines will use mathematical theorems, but he is not a mathematician for that reason. This is true even if he occasionally chooses—when he wants to make a small number of troops look very large—to form his camp and armies into the shape of a **Circle**; or at other times into a **Square**, a **Pentagon**, or some other **Polygon** when he wishes a great number to appear even larger. 

<margin>There are two types of Geometry: the consideration of planes and Stereometry.</margin>
Since these are the types of the whole mathematical science, Geometry is further divided into the study of **Planes** and the measurement of **Solids**, which is called **Stereometry**. For indeed...
