<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion of the mathematical sciences, this page details the specific divisions of Geometry, Arithmetic, Geodesy, and the arts of Optics and Music.</meta>

->BOOK ONE. 23<-

Since there is no specific treatment of Signs <note>original: "Signa," here meaning points</note> and Lines on their own, because no Figure <margin>in these</margin> can be made from them without Planes or Solids. Indeed, no part of Geometry does anything other than either construct Planes or Solids, or compare and divide those already constructed. <margin>The principal duty of Geometry.</margin> Likewise, the distribution of Arithmetic lies in the contemplation of linear, planar, and solid numbers. <margin>Three parts of Arithmetic: the consideration of linear, planar, and solid numbers.</margin> For it considers the types of numbers as they proceed from Unity, the origin of planar numbers—both similar and dissimilar—and the progression of solid numbers up to the third degree of growth. 

However, Geodesy <term>Geodesy: the practical art of measuring land or physical volumes</term> and Calculation <note>original: "Supputatrix," referring to the art of practical logistics</note> are similar to these (Geometry and Arithmetic) in their divisions, although they speak not of intellectual Numbers or Figures, but of sensible <note>Meaning: objects perceived by the senses rather than abstract concepts</note> ones. <margin>Geodesy and Calculation are divided in the same way as Arithmetic and Geometry.</margin> For it is not the task of Geodesy to measure the abstract Cylinder or Cone, but rather piles of material things as if they were Cones, and wells as if they were Cylinders. It does not achieve this with intellectual straight Lines, but with sensible ones—sometimes indeed with those that are more certain in a way, such as solar rays, but at other times with coarser ones, such as Cords and Plumb-lines. 

Similarly, the Calculator does not inspect the properties of numbers in themselves, but as they exist in sensible things. <margin>What Geodesy and Calculation consider.</margin> Hence he even gives them names based on the things he measures, calling some "apple-counters" <note>original: "μηλίτας" (melitas)</note> and others "cup-counters" <note>original: "φιαλίτας" (phialitas)</note>. He does not grant that there is any "minimum," as the Arithmetician does, who accepts that minimum as a kind of relative genus. For a single man is to him a measure for the whole multitude of men, just as Unity is the common measure of all Numbers. 

Again, Optics <note>original: "Perspectiva"</note> and Music <note>original: "Canonica"</note> are born from Geometry and Arithmetic. <margin>Understand "Canonica" to be Music.</margin> And Optics indeed uses visual rays as Lines, and the Angles that are formed by these rays from the eyes. It is divided into that which is called Optics in the proper sense—which provides the cause for those appearances that usually present themselves to us differently than they truly are, due to the various positions and distances of the things that fall under our sight (such as the convergence of parallel lines, or the appearance of squares as if they were circles); <margin>Three parts of the whole of Optics.</margin> <margin>Optics.</margin> and into the whole of Catoptrics <note>original: "Specularia," the study of mirrors</note>, which deals with various and manifold reflections and is connected to imaginary or conjectural knowledge; <margin>Catoptrics.</margin> and also into that which is called Scenography <note>original: "Sciographice," the art of perspective drawing</note>—that is, the designer of shadows—which shows how it is possible for things appearing in images to not seem awkward or deformed due to the distances and heights of the objects drawn. <margin>Scenography.</margin> 

Moreover, Canonics <term>Canonica: the mathematical study of musical scales and intervals using a "canon" or monochord</term> or the science of the Canon considers the ratios of audible harmonies, finding the divisions of the Rules and using the aid of the senses everywhere, being (as Plato says) such that for the mind, the ears... <margin>What Canonics considers, about which Plato [speaks] in the 7th book of the Republic.</margin>

-> BOOK I. 25 <-

...and perfects that very process from within itself. In the same way, **Dialectic**, being the purest part of **Philosophy**, clearly surpasses the mathematical disciplines in its simplicity. It encompasses their entire sphere and provides from within itself the various powers needed by those sciences—the power to perfect, to judge, and to understand. I mean the powers of **resolving** <term>Resolution (analysis): the process of breaking a complex idea down into its simplest principles</term>, **dividing**, **defining**, and **demonstrating**. Aided and perfected by these, Mathematics finds some things through resolution and others through **composition** <term>Composition (synthesis): the process of building complex proofs up from basic axioms</term>. It explains some things by dividing and others by defining, and it gathers the answers to its inquiries through demonstration. It adapts these paths to its own subjects, using each of them to examine its intermediate arguments. Hence, resolutions, definitions, divisions, and finally demonstrations are proper to it, operating according to the specific mode of mathematical knowledge.

Not without reason, then, is **Dialectic** the peak and summit of the mathematical sciences. It perfects everything that is intelligible within them; it renders what is certain immune to all criticism; it keeps what is unchanging stable; and it refers what is pure and free of matter back to the simple nature of the mind, which is secluded from matter. Furthermore, it distinguishes the first principles of these sciences through definitions. It shows the distinctions of the **genera** <note>Categories or 'families' of things</note> and the **forms** <note>Specific types or species</note> that fall under those genera. It also teaches the compositions that produce consequences from principles, as well as the resolutions that rise and climb back toward the first things and the principles themselves.

Furthermore, the "connection" <margin>The connection of the mathematical sciences is not proportion, as Eratosthenes claimed.</margin> of the mathematical disciplines is not to be found in **proportion** <note>original: *proportio*; likely referring to the Greek *analogia*</note> itself, as **Eratosthenes** <note>A famous Greek polymath and librarian at Alexandria, known for calculating the Earth's circumference</note> thought. Indeed, proportion is said to be—and is—only one of the things common to mathematics. Many other things besides apply to all mathematical disciplines (to be brief) which are inherent in the common nature of mathematics itself.

But as it seems we must say, their closest connection is a single, **Total Mathematics**, which encompasses the principles of all the specific sciences within itself in a simpler way. It considers their commonality and their difference, teaching what is found to be the same in all of them, what is found in many, and what is found in only a few. For those who learn aptly, there is a return to this "Total Mathematics" from many other subjects.

But above even this, **Dialectic** <margin>The second connection of the mathematical sciences. Plato in the Republic.</margin> is also a connection of the mathematical disciplines. As I have already said, **Plato** in his book *The Republic* called this their "summit." For Dialectic perfects the whole of Mathematics and, through its powers, leads it back to the **Mind**...

...a deep surface, or the equality of lines from the center to the circumference, or entirely multi-angled figures of many bases, and all those figures of which Geometry teaches? In what way, finally, can the reasons of this <margin>Third argument</margin> science remain such that they can in no way be refuted? For while sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses."</note> forms and figures admit of "more or less," they all exist as mobile and changeable, and are filled with material variety; and equality itself exists alongside its contrary, inequality. But have <margin>Second part</margin> indivisible things progressed according to partition and <term>interval</term><note>Latin: *intervallo*; in this context, it refers to spatial extension or distance.</note>? For extension, swelling, and every kind of interval happens to forms because of their material receptacle, which receives indivisible things in a divisible way, things lacking dimension together with dimension, and immobile things in a mobile way.

How then do we cut a straight line, a triangle, or a circle? <margin>First argument</margin> How do we speak of the differences of angles, and the <margin>Second argument</margin> additions and subtractions of the figures themselves, such as those of triangles or quadrangles? Yet such doubts exist, in addition to the fact that Plato <margin>Fourth argument from the authority of Plato in Book 7 of the *Republic*; see also Aristotle, Book 2 of the *Physics*, and Book 3 *On the Soul*.</margin> calls the forms of Geometry "positioned in thought," and he allows that we proceed from sensible things to forms of this kind, rising from sense to the mind—even though (as we said above) the reasons that are in thought are indivisible, and are separated by no interval, and exist according to the property of the Soul. 

But if reasons are to be rendered that are consistent both with the things themselves and with the doctrine of Plato, let us speak by <margin>Solution</margin> dividing them in this way. Every <term>universal</term><note>A "universal" is a general concept or category that can be applied to many individual instances (e.g., the concept of "Circularity" vs. a specific drawn circle).</note>, and every single thing containing many <margin>Division of the universal itself</margin> parts, is either:
1.  Natural to be thought of within singular things, or to appear as such, having its existence in them; it exists as inseparable from them, is arranged and distributed within them, and either moves together with them or stands firm and immobile; 
2.  Or, it exists *before* the many, having the power to generate a multitude, providing images of itself to the many; it is pre-structured for those things which participate in it in an indivisible way, yet it suggests various ways for fertile participation;
3.  Or, it is formed by thought *from* the many, having a generative existence, and finally residing in the many. 

Indeed, according to these three ways of existing, we shall find (as I judge) that some things are "before the many," others are "in the many," and others exist through the respect they have toward the things themselves and their "predication" <note>Predication refers to the act of affirming or asserting a property of a subject.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of mathematical objects, specifically circles and triangles, distinguishing between how they exist in the physical world, the imagination, and the higher intellect.</meta>

-> SECOND [BOOK] <-                                     31

In sensible <note>original: "sensilibus" — things perceivable by the physical senses</note> circles, a universal is distributed which brings each of those circles to completion; they are all similar to one another, existing by a single principle, though differing in their magnitudes or their underlying materials. In those circles that exist in the imagination <note>original: "phantasia" — the faculty of the mind that holds mental images</note>, there is also something common in which all those circles participate, and according to this they all have the same form. However, a difference exists in them here only in the imagination, namely, in their magnitude. For when you imagine several circles around the same center, they all have their existence in a single immaterial subject and in life, which is inseparable from the simple body <note>meaning the "luminous" or "astral" body of the soul in Neoplatonic thought</note> and surpasses partible essence by its extension. They differ, however, in greatness and smallness, and by whether they contain or are contained. 

Therefore, let that universal which exists in many things be understood as twofold: one indeed in sensible things, and the other in imaginable things. And the principle <note>original: "ratio" — here meaning the essential definition or formative principle</note> of the circle and the triangle—and of figures in general—is twofold. One exists in the <margin>The principle of the circle and triangle is twofold.</margin> intellectual matter, the other in sensible matter. But the principle that resides in thought <note>original: "cogitatione" — the higher discursive reason</note>, and which is established in nature itself, precedes these and is more ancient. This is the author of both the imaginable circles (and the one form existing within them) and of the sensible circles. For let there be circles in the heavens, and those produced by nature in general: just as the principle in thought does not fall under their distribution, neither does the natural principle. For those things which possess extension exist without any extensions; partible things exist indivisibly; and magnitudes exist without magnitude in incorporeal causes, just as, conversely, indivisible things exist divisibly and things lacking magnitude exist with magnitude in corporeal things.

For this reason, that circle which exists in thought is one, simple, and free from extension; magnitude itself is there without magnitude, and the figure is not expressed by any physical shape. For principles without matter are of such a kind. But the circle in the imagination is partible, shaped, possesses extension, and is not merely one, but one and many—not just a form, but a distributed form. Whereas the circle in sensible things is composite, distant in magnitude, diminished by a certain proportion, and full of "ineptitudes" <note>meaning physical imperfections or irregularities</note>, falling far short of the purity of immaterial things. 

Therefore, when Geometry speaks anything concerning the circle, the <margin>Geometry considers that universal which is distributed in imaginable things.</margin> diameter, and the passions <note>technical term: the properties or attributes of a geometric shape</note> and affections that relate to the circle—such as contacts, divisions, and things of this sort—we say that it neither teaches nor discusses sensible things (since it strives to separate itself from them), nor the form that exists in thought (for that circle is one, whereas geometry makes its arguments about many, proposing something about each one and contemplating the same things in all of them). That higher form is indivisible, but this one is divisible,

## What Science Geometry Is.

Thus, it may show more varied things proceeding from the simpler, and then returning to them again. The subjects of Geometry, then, are Triangles, Quadrangles, Circles, and all Figures and Magnitudes, along with their limits. The things that belong to these essentially are Divisions, Ratios, Contacts, Equalities, Applications, Excesses, and Defects, and all such things. Then there are the Postulates and Axioms by which it demonstrates each point: such as, "to draw a straight line from any point to any other point"; and "if equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal," and those things that follow from these. Therefore, not every problem or question is geometric, but only those that flow from the principles of geometry. And anyone who is refuted and convicted by these will be refuted specifically as a geometer. 

But whatever does not come from these is not geometric at all; rather, it is foreign to geometric contemplation. These are of two kinds: either the question is from entirely different principles—just as we say a musical question is foreign to geometry because it arises from completely different suppositions and not from geometric principles—or it is a question that uses geometric principles but does so perversely, as if someone should say that parallel lines meet. Because of this, geometry also provides us with tools for judging, by which we can distinguish which things follow from its principles and which fall away from the truth of those principles. For the methods by which we can disprove falsehoods according to how they err fulfill this promise. For some principles accompany geometry, while others accompany arithmetic. 

What indeed should be said of other sciences, since they differ so much from these? For one science is more certain than another (as Aristotle says <note>original: "Aristoteles 1. post. t. 42." refers to the *Posterior Analytics*</note>): specifically, that which arises from simpler suppositions is more certain than that which uses more varied principles; and that which explains the "why" <note>the cause</note> is more certain than that which only knows "that" a thing is so; and that which deals with intelligible things <note>abstract concepts understood by the mind</note> is more certain than that which touches on sensible things <note>physical objects perceived by the senses</note>. According to these definitions of certainty, Arithmetic is indeed more certain than Geometry, for its principles excel in their simplicity. For Unity <note>the number one</note> is without position, whereas the Point has position. And the Point, once it has taken on position, is the principle of Geometry; whereas Unity is the principle of Arithmetic. Geometry, however, is more certain than Spherical Geometry <note>the study of the heavens</note>, and Arithmetic more certain than Music. For these parent sciences provide the causes of the theorems contained under them in a universal way. Geometry, again, is more certain than Mechanics, Optics, and the study of mirrors <term>Specularia: the science of catoptrics, or reflected light</term>, because these latter deal with physical, sensible things. Therefore, the principles of Arithmetic and Geometry [differ] from the principles of others...

<margin>Which theorems are common to Arithmetic and Geometry, and which are proper to each.</margin> For instance, the idea that every ratio can be expressed <note>original: "exprimere." It also deals with points of contact; for "touching" is found only in continuous things <note>surfaces or lines.</note>. It concerns those proportions that cannot be expressed; for where division proceeds to infinity, there also exists that which cannot be expressed.

<margin>The distinction between common theorems.</margin> What they have in common are matters of division, such as those Euclid teaches in the second book <note>referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book II, which deals with geometric algebra.</note>, except for the division of a straight line into extreme and mean ratio <note>The "Golden Ratio." For permutation, conversion of ratios, compositions, and divisions are common to both in this way. Arithmetic first examines what is commensurable <term>commensurable: magnitudes or numbers that can be measured by the same exact unit.</term>; afterwards, Geometry follows, imitating it. From this, Geometry determines that commensurable things are whatever have a ratio to one another like that of a number to a number, seeing as commensurability exists primarily in numbers. For where there is number, there is also the commensurable; and where there is the commensurable, there also is number.

Finally, Geometry first examines triangles and squares; Arithmetic then receives them by adapting their proportions. For in numbers, figures exist according to their cause <note>The author suggests numbers are the primary "logic" or cause behind physical shapes.</note>. Therefore, moved by the effects [seen in Geometry], we pass to their causes, which reside in numbers. And sometimes we observe the same properties without distinction, such as when every polygon is resolved by us into triangles. But at other times, we are satisfied with an approximation, such as when we find a square double another square in Geometry; in numbers, however, since we do not have this exactly, we say one is double the other though falling short by one unit. ->**From where all Geometry began, and how far it extends, and what its utility is.**<-

**[A]**gain, taking up the beginning from a higher point, let us contemplate the whole of Geometry: where it began and how far it extends. In this way, we shall rightly perceive the <term>order</term><note>original: "ornatum"; refers to the beautiful and mathematical structure of the universe.</note> that exists within it. We shall certainly understand that Geometry extends itself through all things that exist, applying its observations to all, and containing the forms of all things within itself. 

At its highest level—which possesses the supreme power of understanding—Geometry surveys those things that truly exist. Through images, it teaches the properties of <term>divine orders</term><note>original: "diuinorum... ornatuum"; in Neoplatonic thought, these are the celestial or divine structures that govern the universe.</note> and the powers of <term>intellectual forms</term><note>original: "intelligentium formarum"; the abstract, perfect blueprints of reality that exist in the mind of the Creator.</note>. For Geometry holds the reasons for these within its own contemplations. It demonstrates which figures are appropriate to the Gods, which belong to the primary essences, and which belong to the substances of souls. 

Turning to middle-level cognitions, Geometry unfolds the reasons for our thinking; it explains and inspects the variety found within them, showing their existence, the <term>affections</term><note>original: "passiones"; in a mathematical sense, these are the properties or characteristics that "happen" to a shape, like the angles of a triangle.</note> inherent in them, as well as their commonalities and differences. From these, it captures the imaginable shapes of figures within defined limits and leads them back to the essential substance of their underlying logic. 

Finally, regarding the third level of the expansion of the thinking intellect, Geometry considers nature. It teaches how the forms of the <term>sensible elements</term><note>original: "sensilium elementorum"; the physical components of the world—earth, air, fire, and water—which can be perceived by the senses.</note> and the powers within them are pre-contained within these logical reasons. For Geometry possesses images of all intellectual types and serves as a model for sensible things; it has fulfilled its own essence according to those things subjected to thought. 

Through these levels, as if through a middle path, Geometry ascends and descends to all things that are and all things that come to be. By always philosophizing geometrically about those things that exist, it encompasses the images of intellectual beings, living creatures, and natural things within all the principles of <term>virtues</term><note>original: "virtutum"; Proclus suggests that even moral virtues have a geometric or proportional structure.</note>. It transmits the orderly arrangement of all <term>Republics</term><note>original: "Rerumpublicarum"; the structures and constitutions of political states.</note> and shows the various mutations they undergo. Geometry performs these tasks by a certain immaterial and cognitive power; yet, when it touches upon matter, it produces from itself many...

<margin>A twofold purpose.</margin>
# What the Purpose of Geometry Is.
### Chapter VI.

Someone might perhaps ask what the purpose of this treatise is. I, however, would tell them that the purpose must be distinguished in two ways: both according to the subjects being sought, and according to the student learning them. Regarding the subjects themselves, we say that the discourse of every geometer is about **Cosmic Figures**.
<margin>The first purpose of Geometry</margin>
Indeed, he begins with simple things and ends with the variety of their composition. He establishes each figure separately, and simultaneously hands down their inscriptions into the **Sphere** <note>The "Sphere" here refers to the universe or the perfect geometric container for the five Platonic solids.</note>, and the ratios they possess.
<margin>The opinion of some.</margin>
For this reason, some have been of the opinion that the purposes of the individual books are to be referred to the Universe, and they have recorded the use and utility which they bring to us for the contemplation of the Whole.

However, distinguishing the purpose by looking toward the student, we shall say that the purpose is that which is called <term>Elementary Instruction</term> <note>original: "Stichiosis" (στοιχείωσις). This refers to the systematic arrangement of the basic building blocks of a science.</note>: that is, the teaching of the **Elements**, as well as the perfection of the students' thinking for the whole of Geometry.
<margin>The second purpose of Geometry</margin>
For by starting from these, we will be able to know the remaining parts of this science and comprehend the variety existing within it. Without these, the discipline of the rest is impossible and incomprehensible to us. For here, the most fundamental, simplest, and most closely related theorems to the primary assumptions are gathered in a fitting order. The demonstrations of the rest use these as if they were the best-known things, and they proceed from these.
<margin>Archimedes.</margin>
Just as indeed **Archimedes** also, in those things which he wrote concerning the **Sphere and the Cylinder**, and **Apollonius**, and all the rest, seem to use the things shown in this treatise as if they were self-evident principles.
<margin>Apollonius.</margin>
The purpose, therefore, is this: namely, to instruct students in the **Elements** for the sake of the whole science, and to hand down the determined structures of the **Cosmic Figures**.
<margin>The whole purpose of Geometry</margin>

<margin>A triple theorem.</margin> <margin>What an Element is.</margin> <margin>What "Elementaries" are.</margin> <margin>Theorem: What a theorem is that is neither an Element nor Elementary.</margin> <margin>The double meaning of "Element" according to the opinion of Menaechmus.</margin> <margin>Postulates are the Elements of theorems.</margin> <margin>Why Euclid’s theorems are called "Elements."</margin> <margin>It is difficult to construct Elements.</margin> ...what reasoning it holds, so that we may truly inquire something regarding the title itself? Of theorems, therefore, some are accustomed to be called **Elements**, others **Elementaries**, while others are defined as being outside the power of these two. Those are named **Elements** whose consideration passes into the knowledge of other things, and from which the solution to the doubts that arise within them assists us. For just as there are certain first, most simple, and indivisible principles of the spoken voice, which we call by the name of "Elements," and all speech and oratory is constituted from these; so indeed in the whole of Geometry there are certain principal theorems that hold the status of a principle for those that follow, looking toward all things and providing demonstrations for many <term>accidents</term><note>In this context, "accidents" (accidentium) refers to the non-essential but observable properties or characteristics of geometric figures.</note>; these they call **Elements**.

**Elementaries**, on the other hand, are those which extend to several things and possess a certain simplicity and <italic>sweetness</italic> <note>The author uses "suauitatem" (sweetness/smoothness) to describe the elegance or clarity of these proofs.</note>, yet they do not possess the same dignity as the Elements. This is because their contemplation is not common to every science. For example: the fact that in triangles, the <term>perpendiculars</term> drawn from their angles to the opposite sides coincide at a single point. Finally, whatever theorems neither possess a knowledge extended to a great multitude of things, nor further reveal anything skillful or elegant, these fall even outside the power of the **Elementaries**.

Again, the term **Element** (as <note>Menaechmus was a 4th-century BCE Greek mathematician and friend of Plato, famous for discovering conic sections.</note> Menaechmus says) is used in two ways. For that which confirms is an **Element** of that which is confirmed; as, in Euclid, the First [book] is the Element of the Second and the Fifth, and the Fourth [is likewise]. Thus, many things may also be said to be Elements of one another in turn, for they are mutually confirmed. For from the fact that the external angles of rectilinear figures are equal to four right angles, the multitude of internal angles equal to right angles is shown; and conversely, from the latter, the former is demonstrated. Such a premise is likened to an **Element**.

In another way, **Element** is defined as that into which a composite is dissolved because it is more simple. In this sense, however, not every thing will be called an Element of every other thing; rather, only those that are most fundamental among those things established in the reasoning of the completed effect. In this way, <term>Postulates</term> <note>original: "Petitiones." In Euclidean geometry, these are the fundamental assumptions or axioms required to begin proofs.</note> are the **Elements** of theorems. According to this meaning of "Element," the **Elements of Euclid** were also constructed. Some belong to that part of Geometry which deals with planes, others to <term>Stereometry</term> <note>The study of three-dimensional shapes and volumes (solid geometry).</note>. Truly, in the same manner, many have written **Elementary** institutions in matters of Arithmetic and Astronomy. It is difficult, however, to choose and to arrange the **Elements** conveniently in every science...

...from which all other things proceed, and into which they are resolved. And among those who have devoted effort to this matter, some were able to collect more [principles], others fewer. It is necessary, however, for this treatment to remove everything that is superfluous, for such things are an impediment to science. One must choose all things that contain and conclude the intended subject, for this is most convenient and useful in science. Its universality of demonstration is achieved by the migration from the first and principal Theorems to the things being sought.

## II. The individual is nothing definite in itself.

One might object that the general system of the objective—that is, Nature—is indeed the object for the subject, and yet it is not the "I," for we perceive it as a real external world independent of us. — Yet that is precisely the error. The world outside of us does not exist in itself; rather, it exists only insofar as we have it within our knowledge. — There is no object without a subject. — The "I" is the primary principle, and everything objective exists only for an "I" and through an "I". — What we call matter is merely a form of the "I." What we understand as space and time are only the forms of our intuition <note>original: "Anschauung". In this context, it refers to the way the mind structures sensory experience.</note>. But the individual is nothing definite in itself; it is rather a mere point of transition, a point of the "I’s" reflection into itself. It is the organ through which the universal "I" comes to self-intuition. In every individual, the whole "I" is present.

This "I," which encloses everything within itself and beholds itself in everything, is the Absolute. We thus come to the proposition:

**The Absolute is the identity of the subjective and the objective.**

This identity, however, cannot be grasped through mere thinking, but only through intellectual intuition <term>intellectual intuition (intellektuelle Anschauung): An immediate, non-logical grasp of the absolute unity between thought and reality.</term>. Philosophy is nothing other than the doctrine of the construction of the Absolute in its various potencies <term>potencies (Potenzen): The different stages or levels through which the Absolute manifests itself in the world.</term>.

**Art is the organon of philosophy.** — <note>An "organon" is a tool or instrument for gaining knowledge.</note>

If philosophy accomplishes the synthesis of the ideal and the real by way of knowledge, art accomplishes the same synthesis by way of representation. In the work of art, the infinite is represented in the finite. It is the objective in which the subjective objectifies itself. The work of art is therefore the highest stage of the objectification of the spirit. It is the completion of philosophy.

<summary>This page outlines a core tenet of Transcendental Idealism: that the external world exists only through the "I," and that art serves as the ultimate bridge (organon) between the subjective mind and objective reality.</summary>

<keywords>The Absolute, Subjective and Objective, Intellectual Intuition, Potencies, Organon of Philosophy, Transcendental Idealism, Nature, Art, Objectification of Spirit</keywords>

position. Often, however, some also call all these things Suppositions <margin>Opinion of the Stoics</margin>, just as the Stoics called every simple Statement an Axiom. Therefore, according to their view, Suppositions will also be Axioms; whereas according to the opinion of others, even Axioms will be called Suppositions.

Furthermore, <margin>Those things which flow from principles are divided into Problems and Theorems.</margin> those things which spring from principles are divided into Problems and Theorems. The former <note>Problems</note> contain the Origins, Sections, Subtractions, or Additions of Figures, and absolutely all the properties concerning them; the latter <note>Theorems</note> show what happens to individual things by themselves. For just as the productive Sciences <note>The "practical" sciences that make physical things.</note> participate in contemplation, in the very same way, those who contemplate have also pre-assumed Problems in the place of operations.

In the past, among the ancient mathematicians <margin>Opinion of Speusippus and Amphinomus</margin>, some wanted to call everything "Theorems," as did the followers of Speusippus <note>Speusippus (c. 408–339 BC) was Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy.</note> and Amphinomus, judging that the name "Theorems" was more proper to contemplative sciences than "Problems." <margin>Their reasoning.</margin> Especially since they speak of eternal things. For in eternal things, there is no "Origin" <note>Speusippus argued that because mathematical truths are eternal, they are never "created" or "made," only discovered.</note>. Therefore, a "Problem" will have no place in these; for a Problem announces the origin and production of that which did not exist before—such as the construction of an Equilateral Triangle, or the description of a Square given a straight line, or the positioning of a straight Line at a given Point. It is better, therefore (they say), to say that all things are of this kind. We do not perceive their "origin" by making them, but by knowing them, treating those things that exist eternally as if they were coming into being. Therefore, we shall say that everything is accepted "Theorem-wise," and not "Problem-wise."

Others, on the contrary, thought that everything should be called "Problems" <margin>Opinion of Menaechmus</margin>, such as the mathematicians who followed Menaechmus <note>Menaechmus (c. 380–320 BC) was a mathematician known for discovering the conic sections.</note>. Now, the function of a Problem is twofold <margin>The twofold function of a problem according to Menaechmus</margin>: sometimes to provide what is sought, but sometimes, when they have received something determined, to see either what it is, or of what kind it is, or what property it has, or what relations it has to something else.

And indeed, both speak correctly. For the followers of Speusippus judge well. <margin>Reconciliation of the two above opinions.</margin> For the Problems of Geometry are not like those of Mechanics. For those <note>Mechanical problems</note> are perceptible to the senses, having a physical origin and every kind of change. And those who followed Menaechmus do not dissent from the truth. Since the discovery of Theorems cannot in any way exist without some access to matter—I mean, <term>intelligible matter</term> <note>original: "materia intelligibilis"; this refers to the mental "space" or substance in which a mathematician imagines geometric shapes, as opposed to physical wood or stone.</note>. Therefore, when the rational principles proceed into that matter and give it form, they are not without reason said to be assimilated to "generations" <margin>Intelligible matter.</margin> <note>Meaning the "creation" of a shape in the mind.</note>. For the motion of our thought, and the production of the rational principles existing within it: [the production] of Figures,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the fundamental distinctions between "Theorems" and "Problems" in geometry, likely within a commentary on Euclid’s Elements.</meta>

->46 BOOK<-

of things that are in the Imagination, as well as the properties that concern them, we say their origin is there. For there are found Constructions, and Sections, and Positions, and Applications, and Additions, and Subtractions. However, all things that exist in Thought <note>The author distinguishes between *Phantasia* (Imagination), which deals with mental "images" of shapes, and *Cogitatio* (Pure Thought), which deals with universal truths.</note> exist without origin and without any change. Thus, there are both Geometrical Problems and Theorems. Since contemplation <term>contemplatio: the act of viewing or theorizing without physical action</term> abounds in Geometry itself, just as manual construction does in Mechanics, all Problems also participate in contemplation; however, the reverse is not true. For Demonstrations are entirely the work of contemplation, and all things in Geometry that follow the first principles are obtained through Demonstration. Therefore, the Theorem is the more general category. Not all Theorems require Problems, for there are some which possess the Demonstration of the thing sought from within themselves.

<margin>The opinion of others on how a theorem differs from a problem.</margin>
Others, distinguishing a Theorem from a Problem, say that while every Problem admits both the property predicated of its matter and its opposite, every Theorem admits the predicated "symptom" <note>original: *symptoma*—here meaning an essential attribute or property that follows naturally from a definition</note>, but not its opposite. 

<margin>The matter of a Problem and a Theorem: what it is.</margin>
By "Matter," I mean the genus <term>genus: the general class of thing being studied</term> under inquiry, such as a Triangle, a Square, or a Circle. 

<margin>The predicated symptom: what it is.</margin>
By "Symptom," I mean the predicate <note>The "predicate" is what is being asserted about the subject; e.g., in "The circle is round," "round" is the predicate.</note>, which is called an "essential accident" <note>A technical term for a property that is not part of the basic definition but is always true for that object, such as a triangle's angles adding up to 180 degrees.</note>, such as Equality, or Section, or Position, or something else of this kind. 

Therefore, when someone proposes to inscribe an equilateral triangle within a Circle, they are stating a Problem. This is because you could also choose to inscribe a triangle that is *not* equilateral. Or again, to construct an equilateral triangle upon a given finite straight line. This is a Problem because it is also possible to construct one that is not equilateral. 

However, when someone proposes that the angles at the base of an Isosceles <note>original: *Aequicrurium*—literally "equal-legged" triangle</note> triangle are equal, we must say they are proposing a Theorem. For it is impossible for the angles at the base of an Isosceles triangle *not* to be equal. 

Because of this, if someone, formulating a proposition in the manner of a Problem, says they "wish to extend a right angle within a semicircle," they will be considered ignorant of Geometry. For every angle that exists within a semicircle is, by necessity, a Right angle. 

Therefore, in cases where the property is universal and accompanies the whole matter, these are to be called Theorems; but in cases where the property is not universal, nor follows the subject by necessity, it must be classified as a Problem. For example: to cut a given finite straight line in two, or into equal parts—for it is also possible for it to be cut into unequal parts. Or to divide any rectilinear angle in half, or into equal parts—for a division into unequal parts is also possible. Or to describe a Square from a given straight line—for it is possible to describe something that is not a Square...

<summary>This page defines the difference between a geometric "Problem" (a construction that could be done in various ways) and a "Theorem" (a statement of universal, necessary truth). The author explains that Theorems deal with essential properties that must be true, whereas Problems deal with specific actions that can have multiple outcomes.</summary>

<margin>How a Theorem differs from a Problem according to the opinion of Zenodotus.</margin>...be described. And all things of that kind fall into the category of Problems. But the followers of Zenodotus, who was familiar with the teachings of Oenopides and a disciple of Andron, distinguished a <term>Theorem</term><note>A statement that proposes a mathematical truth to be proven.</note> from a <term>Problem</term><note>A task or construction to be performed using geometric tools.</note> in this way: a Theorem seeks to understand the property <note>original: "symptoma"</note> that is predicated of the subject matter itself, while a Problem seeks to find what exists under certain conditions. 

<margin>The definition of Theorem and Problem handed down by the followers of Posidonius.</margin>For this reason, the followers of Posidonius <note>Posidonius was a Stoic philosopher and polymath who influenced late Greek mathematics.</note> defined a Theorem as a proposition through which one asks whether a thing is so or not; whereas a Problem is a proposition in which one asks what a thing is, or what kind of thing it is. They said we ought to form a "contemplative proposition" (a Theorem) by stating a fact, such as: "Every triangle has two sides that, together, are greater than the remaining side," or "In every isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal." On the other hand, they described the "problematic proposition" as a request, such as asking whether it is possible to construct a triangle upon a specific straight line. For they argued there is a difference between asking in an absolute and indefinite way whether it is possible to erect a perpendicular line at right angles from a given point on a line, and looking to see what that perpendicular actually is. 

<margin>Euclid’s *Elements* contains both Problems and Theorems.</margin>Furthermore, it is clear from what we have already said that there is indeed some difference between a Problem and a Theorem. That Euclid's *Elements* likewise contains some Problems and some Theorems will become clear from the individual cases. Indeed, at the end of his demonstrations, Euclid himself added a concluding phrase: sometimes "which was to be shown" <note>original: "quod ostendendum erat," commonly known as Q.E.D.</note> and sometimes "which was to be done" <note>original: "quod faciendum erat," commonly known as Q.E.F.</note>. This latter phrase, "which was to be done," designates a Problem, while the former, "which was to be shown," designates a Theorem. 

<margin>See the reason for this matter below in Book 3, in the commentary on propositions 4 and 9, and in other places.</margin>For even though a demonstration is also performed in Problems (as we have said), the demonstration is sometimes used for the sake of the construction—to show that what was commanded has actually been performed. At other times, the demonstration is worthy in its own right, since it can bring the very nature of the thing sought into the light. You will find that Euclid sometimes weaves Theorems together with Problems, using them alternately, as in the first book; at other times, he favors one over the other. For the fourth book is entirely composed of Problems, while the fifth consists of Theorems. Let this be enough said by us on these matters.

## A Certain Admonition to the Readers. Chapter XI.

As we begin to inquire into each individual point, we forewarn those who are about to read: do not demand from us those <term>minor lemmas</term> <note>original: "Sumptiunculas." Small assumptions or trivial side-proofs often found in basic textbooks.</note>, cases, or anything else of that kind which has already been published by those who preceded us. We have grown weary of such things, and therefore we will rarely touch upon them. Instead, we shall make special mention of those matters that involve more difficult contemplation and look toward universal philosophy. In this, we imitate the Pythagoreans, who had this riddle ready at hand: *A Figure and a Step; not a Figure and three Obols.* <margin>Pythagorean Enigma</margin> <note>original: "Figura, & Gradus: non autem Figura, & tres Oboli." This slogan emphasizes that every geometric "figure" should be a "step" for the soul to ascend, rather than a tool to earn "obols" (small coins).</note> This shows that one ought to pursue that philosophy which, through every theorem, climbs a step and raises the soul on high—not allowing it to remain among sensible things, nor to fulfill a common use among mortals, nor to neglect the elevation found here in favor of worldly concerns.

I say, therefore, that those things which are devoid of matter, and which exist in separate "reasons" <note>original: "rationibus"; here referring to the divine blueprints or formative principles of things.</note> and in the **Forms** themselves which are arranged beneath them, have always been granted a more primary existence of the simpler over the existence of the composite. For this reason—both in the **Intellect** <note>original: "Mente"; the higher divine Mind or Nous.</note>, and in the **Cosmic Orders** <note>original: "Ornatibus"; referring to the structured layers of the universe.</note> (both the middle ones and those belonging to the **Soul**), and in the **Natures** themselves which directly give life to bodies—the **Boundaries** <term>Termini: the limits or definitions that give shape to a thing</term> excel the things that are bounded in terms of their essence. They are more "impartible" <note>indivisible; something that cannot be broken into parts.</note>, more uniform, and more primary than the things themselves. For in immaterial Forms, the **One** is more perfect than the **Many**; the **Indivisible** is more perfect than that which proceeds in every direction; and that which **Limits** is more perfect than that which receives its **Limit** from another.

However, those things which lack matter, yet consist in other things—degenerating from their own essence, scattered around subjects, and possessing a joined union—are granted composite "reasons" before simpler ones. Because of this, the things which appear in the **Imagination** <note>original: "Phantasia"</note> and the matter of those **Figures** which fall under the Imagination appear shaped. Likewise, those things in the world of the senses which are produced by **Nature** have the principles of the "bounded" coming first, while the principles of the "limiters" follow after as something added from the outside. 

For instance, so that a thing which extends in three dimensions does not expand into an infinite size (whether in thought or in sense), it was bounded on all sides by a **Surface**. And so that the flat **Surface**, moving onward, does not hide in infinity, the **Line** took it up beforehand and determined it. Likewise, the **Point** <note>original: "Signum"</note> limits the **Line**—the composite things subsisting for the sake of the simple. 

Furthermore, this is again manifest: in separate Forms, the principles of the **Boundaries** exist within themselves, and not in the things that are bounded. Remaining as they truly are, they have the power to establish secondary things. But in **inseparable Forms** <note>Forms that cannot exist apart from physical matter.</note>, they have given themselves over to the things they bound; they are situated within them, becoming like parts of them, and are filled with inferior qualities. Therefore, in that realm, the **Indivisible** is found in a **Divisible** essence, and that which lacks width is found in things endowed with width. The **Boundaries** can no longer guard their own simplicity and purity. Since they exist in something else, they have changed their nature into the matter of the subject. Indeed, the matter of these things has disturbed their perfection: the principle of the **Plane** creates a deep plane; the principle of the **Line**, by obscuring its single dimension, becomes divisible in every direction; and the principle of the **Point** is made bodily and simultaneously pulled apart...

For **Infinity** in those higher realms (I mean the intellectual ones) was the primary cause and the fertile power of the universe. In material things, however, it is imperfect, and exists as all things only in potential.

<meta>This page continues a mathematical discussion regarding the classification of lines, specifically debating whether the cylindrical helix should be considered a "simple" line or a "mixed" line. It follows a tradition of geometric commentary, likely drawing on the works of Proclus or similar Renaissance mathematical syntheses.</meta>

-> **BOOK SECOND. 61** <-

However, the **Cylindrical Helix** consists of similar parts in exactly the same way as the **Straight** and the **Circular Line**. <note>original: "similium partium"; this refers to "homoeomerous" lines, where any segment of the line is identical in shape to any other segment of the same length, allowing them to be perfectly superimposed.</note> Are there, therefore, three simple lines, and not only two? We shall meet this doubt by saying that a helix of this kind consists of <margin>Solution</margin> similar parts, just as **Apollonius** <margin>Apollonius</margin> <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BCE), known as "The Great Geometer," famous for his work on conic sections.</note> also taught, but it is by no means "simple." For to be "composed of similar parts" and to be "simple" are not the same thing. Indeed, even among those things that exist in nature, **Gold** and **Silver** consist of similar parts <note>i.e., they are homogeneous throughout</note>, yet they are in no way simple elements.

The composition of the Cylindrical Helix from simple elements is revealed by its very **Generation** <note>In geometry, "generation" refers to the way a shape is created by the movement of points or lines.</note>. For it arises while a straight line is moved in a circle around the axis of a cylinder, while a **point** is carried along that same straight line. Thus, two simple motions have constituted it. For this reason, it is numbered among the **Mixed Lines**, and not the simple ones. For that which is constituted from dissimilar things is not simple, but mixed.

And **Geminus** <margin>Geminus</margin> <note>Geminus of Rhodes (1st century BCE), a mathematician and astronomer who sought to classify all possible geometric forms.</note> correctly allowed that while some simple lines can be produced from multiple motions, he did not grant that every such line is "mixed." Rather, he argued that a line is mixed only when it arises from *dissimilar* motions. For if you imagine a **Square**, and two motions occurring with equal speed—one along the length and the other along the width—the **Diagonal** <note>original: "Dimetiens"; refers to the diameter or diagonal of the square.</note> will be produced. Although this results in a straight line, the straight line is not "mixed" because of this. For no other line precedes it which was produced by a simple motion, as we were saying regarding the Cylindrical Helix.

Furthermore, if someone should imagine a straight line being moved within a right angle, and describe a circle by its midpoint <note>original: "bipartita sectione"; literally a "two-part section." This refers to a kinematic mechanism where a rod slides with its ends on two perpendicular axes; the midpoint of that rod traces a perfect circle.</note>, the circular line is not produced by a "mixture" for this reason. For when the endpoints of the line moved in this way move equally, they describe a straight line; but the midpoint, because it revolves unequally, designates a circle. The remaining points on the line describe an **Ellipse**. Therefore, the generation of the circular line resulted from the inequality of the motion made at the midpoint, because it was assumed that the straight line is drawn down within a right angle, rather than moving according to its own nature.

But let these things suffice regarding these matters. It will appear, however, that while both are simple lines (namely, the **Straight** and the **Circular**), the <margin>Proof</margin> **Straight** is the simpler of the two. For in the straight line, not even in our imagination can a dissimilarity be found. In the **Circular**, however, the **Concave** and the **Convex** <note>The "hollow" inner curve and the "bulging" outer curve.</note> indicate a dissimilarity. Furthermore, the Straight line does not conceptually imply a circumference; but the Circumference brings the Straight with it—not by its generation, but by its relationship to the **center** <note>The writer suggests that a circle cannot be defined without the concept of the radius, which is a straight line.</note>. 

What if someone should even say that the Circumference requires a straight line for its constitution? <margin>Doubt</margin> For if either end of a finite straight line...

Since He took up the beginning, middle, and ends of all things that exist, "He terminates straight lines while moving around according to nature," says Plato <margin>Plato in the *Timaeus*</margin>. For He proceeds toward all things through providential actions, and yet is turned back toward Himself, "remaining in His own custom," says Timaeus <margin>Timaeus</margin>. 

Note then, that the **straight line** <margin>Of what the straight line is a sign</margin> is a mark of a providence that is undeviating, unpervertible, immaculate, never-failing, omnipotent, and present to all things. The **circumference** <margin>Of what the circumference is a mark</margin>, however, and the circular motion, is the mark of an action that returns into itself, which is converted to itself, and which rules over all things according to a single intellectual limit. Since, therefore, the Maker of all things had placed these two principles—the Straight and the Circular—within Himself, He produced two Unities from Himself <margin>Two Unities which are from God</margin>. One acts according to the Circular and is the maker of intellectual essences; the other acts according to the Straight and provides the origin for sensible things <note>objects that can be perceived by the senses</note>. 

Because the Soul occupies a middle place between the intellectual and the sensible, insofar as it adheres to the intellectual nature, it acts according to the Circle; but insofar as it presides over sensible things, it provides for them according to the Straight <margin>End of Digression</margin>. Let these words suffice regarding the similarity of these geometric forms to the nature of existence. 

Now, Euclid indeed handed down this definition of a Line <margin>He weighs Euclid's definition</margin>, which we have set forth: through which he shows that the straight line alone is equal to the distance situated between its own points <note>The text cuts off here, likely leading into a technical proof that a straight line is the shortest distance between two points</note>.

**A surface is that which has length and breadth only.**

<margin>The error of Theodorus the Mathematician.</margin>
<margin>Surfaces are mixed through tempering.</margin>
<margin>The origin of the cone.</margin>
<margin>Beautiful.</margin>
<margin>Common to lines and surfaces.</margin>
<margin>The wonderful property of surfaces.</margin>
<margin>The origin of the spiral.</margin>
<margin>There are three types of spirals.</margin>
<margin>1. Continuous spiral.
2. Implicit spiral.
3. Divided spiral.</margin>
<margin>There are three spiric sections.</margin>
<margin>Mixed surfaces are formed in two ways.</margin>
<margin>Four bodies, which have mixed surfaces, are produced from three conic lines. And their surfaces...</margin>

Regarding lines, Theodorus the Mathematician <note>Likely Theodorus of Cyrene, a 5th-century BC Greek mathematician known for his work on irrational numbers.</note> does not think correctly. In the case of **surfaces**, however, "mixture" occurs neither through **composition** <note>original: "Compositionem"; the simple stacking of parts</note> nor through **confusion** <note>original: "Confusionem"; a blending where individual traits are lost</note>, but rather through a certain **tempering** <note>original: "Temperationem"; a harmonious blending where the properties of the original parts are balanced to create a new form.</note>. For instance, if we imagine a circle on an underlying **plane**, and a point high above it, and then draw a straight line from that point to the circumference of the circle and rotate that line, we will surely create a **conical surface**, which is a "mixed" surface. 

Furthermore, by cutting this surface, we can resolve it back into its simple components. For if we draw a section from the peak to the base, the plane that cuts it will create a circular shape. However, the conceptual "Idea" of lines shows that the method of mixture is not achieved through tempering; for it does not send us back to the simple nature of the elements. But if surfaces are cut, they immediately show us the very lines through which they were created. Therefore, the mode of mixture (as has been said) is not the same for lines as it is for surfaces. 

Just as there were certain simple types of lines—namely the **straight** and the **circular**—of which even the common person has a preconceived notion without any prior instruction, the types of "mixed" lines required a more skillful discovery. In the same way, regarding surfaces, we have innate notions of those which are most elementary, such as **planes** and **spheres**. But for those surfaces constituted through mixture, scientific study and reason must investigate their variety. 

There is something wonderful in these surfaces: namely, that a mixture of a surface is often created even from a circular line during its generation. We say this happens, for example, with a <term>spiric surface</term> <note>A surface shaped like a doughnut or torus, or parts thereof.</note>. This is understood to be formed by the revolution of a circle that remains upright and turns around a single point that is not its own center. Because of this, the <term>spiral</term> is also formed in three ways: for the center of the rotation is either on the circumference, inside the circumference, or outside it. 

If the center is on the circumference, it becomes a **Continuous Spiral**; if it is inside the circumference, it is **Implicit** <note>original: "Implicita"; also translated as "entwined."</note>; if it is outside, it is **Divided**. There are also three "spiric sections" corresponding to these three differences. Nevertheless, every spiral is "mixed," even though the circular motion that produces it is a single type. 

Mixed surfaces are created both from simple lines (as we have said) when they are moved in such a manner, and also from mixed lines. Therefore, since there are three <term>conic lines</term> <note>The parabola, ellipse, and hyperbola.</note>, they produce four mixed surfaces, which are called <term>conoids</term> <note>Solid shapes resembling a cone but generated by rotating a conic section other than a triangle.</note>. From a **parabola** rotated around its axis, a **Rectangular Conoid** is formed. From an **ellipse**, those surfaces called **Spheroids** are named: if the rotation is around the major axis, it is **Oblong**; if around the minor axis, it is **Broad** <note>Known today as prolate and oblate spheroids.</note>. Finally, from a **hyperbola**, an **Obtusangular Conoid** is formed. It should be known, however, that sometimes we arrive at a knowledge of surfaces from lines, and sometimes the opposite: for from conic and spiric surfaces, we can discover **conic** and **spiric lines**.

Finally, how would you observe sections of circles or straight lines on a Cone or a Cylinder? It is not without merit, therefore, that he both defined this Surface and treats his subjects by presenting everything within it. For this reason, he called the present treatise "Plane." And in this way, one ought to understand the Plane: as something projected and set before the eyes. **A plane angle is the inclination toward each other of two lines in a plane that touch one another and do not lie in a straight line.**

<margin>Eighth Definition.</margin>
<margin>Commentary 8.</margin>
<margin>Digression: Threefold opinion on the Angle.</margin>
<margin>1st opinion, which is Euclid's.</margin>
<margin>2nd opinion, which is Eudemus's.</margin>
<margin>3rd opinion, which is Plutarch's, Apollonius's, and Carpus's, and their foundation.</margin>

Some of the ancient philosophers, placing the **Angle** in the category of **Relation** <note>original: *Prædicamento eorum, quæ sunt ad Aliquid*. In Aristotelian logic, this refers to things defined by their relationship to something else.</note>, said it was an **Inclination** either of lines or of planes that are inclined toward one another. Others, including it under **Quality**, like straightness or crookedness, say it is a property <note>original: *passionem*. A "passion" or property in classical philosophy is an attribute or state of a substance.</note> of a surface or a solid. Others, however, referring it to **Quantity**, claim it is the surface itself or the solid. For an angle is divided in surfaces by a line, and in solids by a surface. They say that what is divided by these is nothing other than **Magnitude**, and this is not linear magnitude (since a line is divided by a point <note>original: *Signo*. Mathematically, the "sign" refers to the dimensionless point.</note>); it remains, therefore, that the angle is either a Surface or a Solid.

However, this definition seems, in the first place, not to allow an angle to be completed by a single line. And yet the <term>Cissoid</term> <note>original: "Cissoides"; the "ivy-leaf" curve, which has a sharp point or cusp</note>, though it is one line, forms an angle. Therefore, since each is a single line, it forms an angle with itself, not with another line.

Secondly, in defining an angle as an "Inclination," he errs. For how, if there is only one Inclination, can there be two angles? <note>Referring to the fact that two lines meeting create multiple angles, like adjacent or vertical angles</note> How indeed do we still speak of "equal" and "unequal" angles? Many other such objections are customarily raised against this opinion.

Thirdly and finally, some parts of the definition are superfluous for certain angles—specifically the part [**and not lying in a straight line**]—as in the case of those angles formed from circular lines. For even without the help of this clause, the definition is perfect; the inclination of one of these lines to the other will produce the angle itself. Indeed, it is entirely impossible for circular lines to "lie in a straight line." We have judged that these points should be said regarding Euclid's definition, partly interpreting it and partly raising doubts against it.

# SECOND BOOK. 75

->**THE TEXT**<-
<margin>Definition 10.</margin> When a straight line standing upon another straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is **Right**; and the straight line which stands upon the other is called **Perpendicular** to that upon which it stands.

<margin>Definition 11.</margin> An **Obtuse Angle** is one which is greater than a Right angle.

<margin>Definition 12.</margin> An **Acute Angle**, however, is one which is less than a Right angle.

<margin>Commentary 10.</margin>
These are the three species of angles, of which **Socrates** also speaks in the *Republic* <note>original: "Republica"; referring to Plato's dialogue where mathematical "suppositions" are discussed as the foundation of geometric reasoning.</note>, which are accepted as "suppositions" among Geometers. These angles—the **Right**, the **Obtuse**, and the **Acute**—constitute the division of rectilinear angles <note>Angles formed by straight lines.</note> into their specific kinds. The Right angle is defined by equality, identity, and similarity; the others are established through the nature of the "Greater" and the "Lesser," and finally through inequality, diversity, and the indeterminate "More" and "Less."

<margin>A Digression</margin>
While many Geometers are unable to give any reason for this threefold division, and instead merely use this as a supposition—namely, that there are three types of angles—they respond that one should not demand a cause from them when they are questioned. <margin>The Pythagorean Geometers give the reason why there are three rectilinear angles.</margin> The **Pythagoreans**, however, by tracing the solution of this triple distribution back to first principles, are not at a loss in providing the causes for this difference in rectilinear angles. 

<margin>Limit. The Infinite.</margin> For since one of the principles exists through **Limit** <note>original: "Finis"; in Pythagorean philosophy, 'Limit' (Peras) is the principle of order, beauty, and stability.</note>, and is the cause of boundaries, identity, equality, and the entire "better" side of the cosmic order; while the other principle is the **Infinite** <note>original: "infinitum"; the 'Unlimited' (Apeiron) represents change, growth, and disorder.</note>, which grants to its offspring an endless progression, increase, decrease, inequality, and every kind of diversity, and presides entirely over the "inferior" series; it is therefore right that rectilinear angles are also formed through those same principles. 

<margin>The Principle that comes from Limit makes a Right angle.</margin> The **Principle** <note>original: "Ratio"</note> which proceeds from **Limit** produces the **Right angle**, which is single, endowed with equality in respect to any other Right angle, possesses similarity, is always finite and determined, remains the same, and undergoes neither increase nor decrease. 

<margin>The Principle that comes from the Infinite produces the Obtuse and Acute angle.</margin> But the Principle which comes from **Infinity**, since it is secondary and **Dyadic** <note>original: "Dyadica"; referring to the "Indefinite Dyad," a Pythagorean term for the principle of duality and plurality.</note>, produces two types of angles surrounding the Right angle, characterized by inequality according to the nature of the "Greater" and the "Lesser"...

It explains that the right angle represents the principle of "Limit" (stability), while the obtuse and acute angles represent the "Infinite" (change and inequality).</summary>

<margin>A most beautiful comparison of rectilinear angles to the Gods.</margin>

<margin>A beautiful comparison of rectilinear angles to those things which exist.</margin>

Furthermore, in those things which exist, the rectitude of essence is assimilated to the **Right** angle, preserving the same limit of its own being; whereas the **Obtuse** and **Acute** are assimilated to *accidents* <note>In philosophy, 'accidents' are non-essential properties that can change without changing the nature of the thing itself.</note>. For the distribution of a certain suitability and conjunction of nature, or (as the Greeks say) *Sympathy*, leads the soul down into material error and indefinite variety.

<margin>A beautiful consideration and comparison of the perpendicular.</margin>

The **Perpendicular** line is also a mark of inflexibility, purity, immaculate power, and the unwavering nature of all such things. It is also a sign of divine and intelligent measure. For we measure the heights of figures by the perpendicular, and we define other rectilinear angles by their relation to the **Right** angle, since they are themselves indefinite and indeterminate.

<margin>We measure the heights of figures by the perpendicular. See the reason for this below in comment 19.</margin>

SECOND [BOOK]. 77

And not rectilinear. Moreover, many curvilinear angles <note>Angles formed by curved lines rather than straight lines.</note> will appear larger than Right angles, yet they are not for that reason Obtuse. If indeed an angle is Obtuse, it must be Rectilinear. <margin>Second.</margin> This, then, we note first. Next, when he [Euclid] proposed to define the Right Angle, he took a straight line standing upon another straight line, making the adjacent angles equal to one another. But for the Obtuse and Acute, he did not likewise take a straight line inclined toward one side or the other; instead, he handed down their definitions by their relation to the Right Angle. For the Right Angle itself is the measure of non-right angles, just as equality is the measure of unequal things. <note>original: "ipse .n. & non Rectorum mensura est, quemadmodum & inaequalium aequalitas"</note> Indeed, lines inclined toward one side or the other were innumerable, and not just one, as is the case with the Perpendicular. <margin>The Right angle is the measure of non-right angles, just as equality is the measure of unequal things.</margin> After this, we judge that his saying "[angles equal to one another]" looks toward a certain supreme geometric precision. For it could happen that angles were equal to others, yet were not Right. But when they are equal to *one another* <note>Meaning the two adjacent angles created by the intersection.</note>, they must be Right angles. Furthermore, that little word <term>adjacent</term> <note>Latin: "deinceps," referring to angles that share a side and a vertex.</note> added there does not seem to me to be superfluous, as it wrongly seemed to some; rather, it shows the reason for its "rightness." <margin>Third, Fourth.</margin> For both angles are Right because, while being adjacent, they are equal. Since the straight line that stands upon the other is, because of its lack of inclination <note>original: "inflexibilitatem," here meaning it doesn't lean to one side.</note> toward either side, the cause of equality for both, and the cause of "rightness" for each. Therefore, it is not absolute equality to each other, but the resulting position together with equality that is the cause of the angles' rightness. Beyond all these things, I think the purpose of our Author [Euclid] should be recalled to memory here: namely, that he is speaking of those angles which exist in a single Plane. <margin>Fifth.</margin> Therefore, this is not the definition of just any perpendicular, but of that which is in one and the same Plane. However, it is not the time to define that which is called a <term>solid perpendicular</term> <note>A line perpendicular to an entire surface or plane, rather than just another line.</note>. Just as he defined the Plane Angle, so also he defined this kind of Perpendicular. Since a solid perpendicular must make right angles not only to a single straight line, but to all lines that touch it and are in the underlying Plane; this is indeed its unique property.

78                                 B O O K

<margin>Geometry as it was from the beginning</margin>
A Boundary is also an Edge: but this applies to Spaces that are on Surfaces, and to solid Bodies. For now, the author calls the Perimeter a "Boundary," which bounds and distinguishes each individual Space. He defines this kind of Boundary as being the Edge—not in the same way a Point <note>In original geometry, a "Signum" or "Point" marks the end of a line, but does not "enclose" area.</note> is called the Edge of a Line, but in the way that something encloses and excludes its surroundings. This name is proper to that Geometry which existed from the beginning, through which fields were measured and those same boundaries were kept distinct and unconfused; it is from this practice that they arrived at the knowledge of the present science. Therefore, since Euclid had called the external Perimeter a "Boundary," he quite rightly defined it as also being the Edge of the Spaces. For by this boundary, anything contained within is circumscribed.

<margin>The circle is a type of plane space. See the opposite above in Commentary 1.</margin>
For example, I say that in a Circle, the Circumference is indeed the Boundary and the Edge, while the Plane itself is a certain Space; and similarly in other things.

->**TEXT**<-
**A Figure is that which is enclosed by one or more Boundaries.**

<margin>Commentary 12. "Figure" is used in many ways.</margin>
<margin>The first type of Figure.</margin>
Since the word "Figure" is used in many ways and is divided into various types, it is worthwhile first to look at its differences, and afterward to discuss that Figure which is proposed in this definition. There is, then, a certain type of Figure that is created through change and arises from an external action <note>original: *passione*. In this context, it refers to a "passive" state where an object is acted upon by outside forces.</note>, when those things that receive a Figure are shaken, or divided, or taken away, or receive additions, or are altered, or suffer other various influences.

<margin>The second.</margin>
There is also a Figure that is made by Art, such as Painting or Sculpture, according to a pre-existing Logic <note>original: *Rationem*, referring to the internal design or rational concept in the artist's mind.</note> within the Art itself; here, the Art produces the form, while the Matter receives the shape, beauty, and grace from it. 

<margin>The third.</margin>
But there are Figures even more noble and more excellent than these: the works of Nature. Some of these exist in the Elements beneath the Moon <note>In the classical world, the "sublunary" sphere (the Earth) was the realm of change, while the heavens were considered eternal.</note>, having the power to contain the Logics existing within them; others are in the heavens, which distinguish their powers and movements. For through themselves and in relation to each other, the celestial bodies display a very great and wonderful variety of Figures; and they show different forms at different times, offering an image of intellectual forms, and by their harmonious revolutions they describe the incorporeal and immaterial powers of Figures. 

<margin>The fourth.</margin>
Again, beyond these, there are the purest and most perfect beauties of Souls
