[...of Souls] <note>The text begins mid-word: "Animarum" (of Souls).</note> Figures, which, while they are indeed full of life and are self-moving by their own nature, exist prior to those things moved by another. Since they exist immaterially and without any physical dimension, they excel over those things that possess dimension and matter. Concerning these, Timaeus <margin>Timaeus <note>Timaeus is the speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name, which describes the mathematical and geometric construction of the universe and the soul.</note></margin> has also taught us, explaining the craftsman-like and essential Figure of Souls. Furthermore, the Figures of Minds <margin>Fifth <note>Referring to the fifth rank in the author’s ontological hierarchy.</note></margin> are far more divine even than the Figures of Souls. These Minds are superior in every way to those essences that can be divided; they shine everywhere with an indivisible and Intellectual light. They are the bearers, creators, and perfecters of all things. They are present equally to all things and remain firmly within themselves. They bring a sense of unity to the Figures of Souls, and they recall the changing nature of sensible Figures <note>Physical shapes perceived by the senses.</note> back to their proper Limit. Finally, separate from all these are those perfect, <margin>Sixth and final type of Figure, the most perfect of all.</margin> uniform, unknown, and inexpressible Figures of the Gods. These sit upon the Figures of Minds; they bound all other Figures together and encompass everything within their unique Limits. Expressing the properties of these Divine Figures, Theurgy <margin>Theurgy <note>Theurgy, or "god-working," refers to ritual practices intended to invoke the presence or influence of the divine.</note></margin> also surrounds the statues of the Gods with various Figures. Some it fashions inexpressibly through characters <note>original: "characteribus"; these are "sigils" or sacred symbols believed to hold divine power.</note>, for characters of this kind reveal the unknown powers of the Gods. Others it imitates through forms and images: making some standing and others sitting; some heart-shaped, others spherical, and others expressed by different Figures. Some are simple, while others are composed of many forms. Some are sacred and venerable, while others are "domestic" and show the specific gentleness of the Gods. Others are constructed as grim, attributing different signs to different figures according to their kinship with the Gods. Since, therefore, <margin>Digression</margin> Figure takes its beginning from the Gods themselves, it descends down to the lowest things, appearing even in these from the primary causes. For it is necessary to place the perfect before the imperfect; and before those things that exist in others, those which are situated within themselves; and before those things full of their own privation <note>Lacking their own inherent form.</note>, those which preserve their own pure nature. Therefore, Figures that are material <margin>A consideration of all Figures.</margin> participate in material ugliness and do not possess a purity suitable to themselves. Celestial figures are divisible and exist in other things. Those of Souls are endowed with division, variety, and every kind of entanglement. Those of Minds, however, possess a progression into multitude alongside their unity. But the Figures of the Gods themselves—free, uniform, simple, and generative—exist before all things, holding all perfection within themselves and extending the fulfillment of forms from themselves to all others. We must not, therefore, listen to or tolerate the many who <margin>The opinion of Democritus, and his [refutation]. <note>Democritus was an atomist who believed shapes were merely accidental arrangements of matter.</note></margin> say that certain additions, subtractions, and alterations create the physical Figures...

...to produce figures (since movements, being imperfect, certainly could not be the principal or primary cause of effects; nor would the same Figures often arise from contrary movements. For through addition and subtraction, the same Form will sometimes be made). However, we shall judge that these serve others in the process of generation, and we shall say that their perfection is assigned to them by other primordial causes. Therefore, it is not the case that those Figures devoid of matter cannot exist, while only those in matter do exist, as some people say in certain places. Nor is it true (as others claim) that they are indeed outside of matter, but exist only according to thought and abstraction. For where can the certainty, beauty, and order of Figures be kept intact in those things that exist only through abstraction? For since these are of the same kind as things perceived by the senses, how far they fall short of unassailable and pure certainty! 

Since they do possess certainty, order, and perfection, from where will they receive these? For it must be either from the sensible things <note>Things perceived through the five senses.</note> (but these traits were not in them) or from the <term>Intellectibles</term> <note>Original: *Intellectibilibus*. These are "Intelligible" realities—perfect forms that exist in the realm of pure thought or the divine mind, beyond the physical world.</note> (though they will exist more perfectly in those). To say they come from that which does not exist is the most absurd thing of all. For Nature did not produce imperfect Figures while leaving perfect ones without any existence at all. Nor is it right to believe our Soul produces more certain, more perfect, and more ordered Figures than the Divine Mind or the Gods themselves. 

There are, therefore, before there are figures perceived by the senses, certain <term>Ratios</term> <note>Original: *Rationes*. In this context, these are "formative principles" or "logical blueprints" that define the essence of a shape.</note> of Figures, which are divine, self-moving, and intelligent. And while we are indeed stirred by sensible things, we bring forth internal Ratios, which are images of the others. Through these, we know sensible Figures as examples, and we recognize the Intelligent and Divine Figures through their images. For as the Ratios within us emerge and propagate themselves, they reveal the forms of the Gods and the uniform <term>Limits</term> <note>Original: *Terminos*. The boundaries or definitions that give structure to the universe.</note> of all things. Through these limits, they inexplicably turn all things back toward themselves and contain all things within themselves. 

In the Gods, therefore, there is both an excellent knowledge of all Figures and the power to generate and establish all lower things. In the realm of Nature, however, Figures possess the efficient power of those things that appear to us, but they lack knowledge and intellectual perception. In individual Souls, there is indeed an immaterial understanding and a self-acting knowledge, but it is not a fertile or effective cause of physical things. Just as Nature rules over sensible Figures through the act of making, in the same way, the Soul—acting according to its knowing part—brings forth the Ratios of Figures into the <term>Phantasy</term> <note>The "Phantasy" or imagination was viewed in this era as a mental mirror or screen where thoughts are visualized as images.</note> as if into a mirror. And as the Phantasy receives these into its visions and holds the images of the Ratios existing within, it provides the Soul with an inward turning through these very images, leading to an action upon itself from those very visions.

<summary>This page argues that geometric forms (Figures) are not merely human abstractions from the physical world, but exist as divine "Ratios" or blueprints that the human soul "remembers" or reflects when it perceives physical objects. It distinguishes how these forms function differently in the Divine Mind, in Nature, and in the human imagination (Phantasy).</summary>

For everything that possesses matter—whether intellectual or sensible—receives its boundary from elsewhere. It is not the boundary itself, but rather the thing being **bounded**. It is not its own limit, but rather one thing in it acts as the limit, and another is limited. It does not exist *as* the boundary, but is contained *by* it. For a figure is joined to Quantity and exists together with it; Quantity is subject to it. Indeed, the **Reason** and appearance of that Quantity is nothing other than Figure and Form. The figure limits the quantity and adds to it a specific character and boundary, whether simple or <margin>How the Figure shows the Limit and the Infinite in its own Forms.</margin> composite. Since this too shows the double progress of the **Limit** and the **Infinite** in its own Forms (just as the nature of the Angle does), it brings a single boundary and simple form to those things it encompasses, according to the Limit; but it brings many boundaries according to Infinity.
